shots.B12C074S02H01: Bhishma says the man who gives relief from fear for even a moment is most worthy of heaven, and urges Yudhishthira to rule cheerfully, protect the good and punish the wicked.

B12C075.summary: Yudhishthira asks how Brahmanas who keep to their duties differ from those who do not. Bhishma says learned, even-minded Brahmanas match Brahma and the gods, while the ill-born and those who abandon their duties are like Sudras. He adds that the king may tax or discipline the unworthy and should support a learned Brahmana who has turned to theft out of want before banishing him for continued theft.

scenes.B12C075S01: Bhishma sorts Brahmanas by conduct and tells the king how to treat each group, including the unworthy and the thief.

shots.B12C075S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how Brahmanas who keep to their duties differ from those who do not.
shots.B12C075S01H02: Bhishma says learned, even-minded Brahmanas match Brahma and the gods, the unworthy are like Sudras, some callings rank as outcasts while others match Kshatriyas or Vaisyas, and the king may tax or discipline the unworthy and banish a learned thief who ignores support.

B12C076.summary: Yudhishthira asks whose wealth a king may claim and how he should conduct himself. Bhishma says the king may take wealth from everyone except worthy Brahmanas, but must keep Brahmanas supported, since a Brahmana who turns thief reflects on the king. He illustrates this with the story of the Kaikeya king, who wins release from a Rakshasa by listing how righteously his kingdom is run.

scenes.B12C076S01: Bhishma explains the king's duty to support Brahmanas, then tells how the Kaikeya king escapes a Rakshasa by reciting his righteous rule, and closes with advice to protect Brahmanas.

shots.B12C076S01H01: Yudhishthira asks whose wealth the king may claim and what conduct he should adopt.
shots.B12C076S01H02: Bhishma says the king may take wealth from all but worthy Brahmanas, should not spare unworthy ones, should keep Brahmanas provided for, and introduces the Kaikeya king seized by a Rakshasa.
shots.B12C076S01H03: The Kaikeya king answers the Rakshasa by listing how his kingdom has no thieves or drunkards, how each order keeps its duties, and how the helpless and ascetics are cared for.
shots.B12C076S01H04: The Rakshasa lets the king go, saying that a king who protects cows and Brahmanas has nothing to fear and wins heaven.
shots.B12C076S01H05: Bhishma advises kings to protect Brahmanas, who will bless them in return, and to discipline unworthy Brahmanas and separate them from the rest.

B12C077.summary: Yudhishthira asks whether a Brahmana in distress may take up Vaisya work and what goods he may sell. Bhishma says he may farm or keep cattle, but must not sell items such as wine, salt, honey, meat or cooked food, while fair exchange by agreement is lawful. Asked what happens when the orders rise against a weakened king, Bhishma says that Brahmanas and others may take up arms to protect the Brahmanas and the people, and that whoever shields the helpless deserves to rule.

scenes.B12C077S01: Bhishma permits a distressed Brahmana to farm or keep cattle, lists the goods he must not sell, explains lawful exchange, and Yudhishthira asks how a king can stay protector if the orders revolt.
scenes.B12C077S02: Bhishma says the orders should strengthen a weakened king, that fighting for Brahmanas brings heaven, that others may take up arms when Kshatriyas fail, and that whoever protects the helpless deserves to rule.

shots.B12C077S01H01: Yudhishthira asks whether a Brahmana in distress may follow the duties of a Vaisya.
shots.B12C077S01H02: Bhishma says a Brahmana who cannot manage Kshatriya duties may farm or keep cattle to make his living.
shots.B12C077S01H03: Yudhishthira asks which goods a Brahmana may sell without losing his hope of heaven.
shots.B12C077S01H04: Bhishma lists goods a Brahmana must never sell, such as wine, salt, honey, meat and cooked food, says that selling animals or Soma brings specific sins, and holds that fair exchange by agreement is lawful while force is sinful.
shots.B12C077S01H05: Yudhishthira asks how a king can remain the protector and refuge of his people if all the orders take up arms against him.
shots.B12C077S02H01: Bhishma says that when the king is weakened, all the orders should seek their good through gifts, penance and peace, and that Brahmanas should help strengthen him.
shots.B12C077S02H02: Yudhishthira asks who will protect the Brahmanas and the Vedas if the Kshatriyas turn hostile to them, and what the Brahmanas should do then.
shots.B12C077S02H03: Bhishma says Kshatriya power is defeated when it is turned against Brahmanas, that those who fight for them win heaven, and that a Brahmana may take up arms in three cases.
shots.B12C077S02H04: Yudhishthira asks whether a strong man of any order may suppress robbers and protect the people when the Kshatriyas have failed.
shots.B12C077S02H05: Bhishma says anyone who shields the helpless, of whatever order, deserves respect and rule, and that a king who cannot protect is as useless as a barren cow.

B12C078.summary: Yudhishthira asks what conduct and character the priests who serve at his sacrifices should have. Bhishma describes the learning, honesty and self-control a fit priest needs. Yudhishthira then questions the fixed gift of dakshina, and Bhishma says a sacrifice needs its dakshina and sound character, and that true penance lies in harmlessness, truth and compassion.

scenes.B12C078S01: Bhishma describes the qualities of a good sacrificial priest, and then answers Yudhishthira's questions about dakshina, sacrificial character and penance.

shots.B12C078S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what conduct and character suit the priests who perform his sacrifices.
shots.B12C078S01H02: Bhishma lists the qualities of a fit priest, including Vedic learning, loyalty, equal regard for all, honesty, freedom from usury, modesty, self-control and harmlessness.
shots.B12C078S01H03: Yudhishthira asks why the dakshina gift is not fixed by ordinance and whether devotion can help a sacrificer who is stained by falsehood.
shots.B12C078S01H04: Bhishma says dakshina is a required part of sacrifice, that a sacrifice must rest on good character, and that true penance lies in harmlessness, truth and compassion rather than bodily hardship.

B12C079.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a king should choose and trust his ministers, since no task is done alone. Bhishma sorts friends into four kinds, adds a fifth who serves righteousness, and warns that a king must weigh trust and mistrust with care. He advises giving each task to one capable, honest minister and treating kinsmen with outward trust and inner watchfulness.

scenes.B12C079S01: Bhishma explains how to classify friends, when to trust or mistrust them, how to choose ministers, and how a king should deal with his kinsmen.

shots.B12C079S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a king's minister should behave and whom the king should trust or avoid.
shots.B12C079S01H02: Bhishma sorts friends into four kinds plus a righteous fifth, warns that trust must be balanced with watchfulness, advises one capable, honest person per task, and urges outward trust but inner caution toward kinsmen.

B12C080.summary: Yudhishthira asks how to win both friends and foes when kinsmen turn hostile. Bhishma tells of Vasudeva confiding to the sage Narada that his kinsmen wound him with cruel words and split the Vrishnis and Bhojas. Narada says the trouble is internal and self-made, that the wealth given away cannot be reclaimed, and that the remedy is gentle speech, generosity and forgiveness, not steel.

scenes.B12C080S01: Vasudeva describes his troubles with his kinsmen to Narada, who answers that the trouble is of his own making and that gentle speech and generosity are the right remedy.

shots.B12C080S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a man can win the hearts of both friends and foes when his kinsmen have turned against him.
shots.B12C080S01H02: Bhishma introduces a talk between Vasudeva and Narada, in which Vasudeva says his kinsmen wound him with cruel words and that he cannot side with either Ahuka or Akrura.
shots.B12C080S01H03: Narada says Vasudeva's trouble is internal and of his own making, since he gave away wealth that cannot be taken back, and warns that trying to recover it would bring bloodshed.
shots.B12C080S01H04: Vasudeva asks what weapon, not made of steel, could soften the hearts and tongues of his kinsmen.
shots.B12C080S01H05: Narada answers that generous feeding, forgiveness, sincerity, gentleness and honour are such a weapon, and urges Vasudeva to lead his people so that the Bhojas and Vrishnis are not ruined.

B12C081.summary: Bhishma gives a second means: a king must protect the person who reports ministers embezzling the treasury. He tells of the sage Kalakavrikshiya, who used a crow in a cage to expose the corrupt officers of King Kshemadarsin of Kosala, and was saved only after the officers killed the crow. The sage warns the king of the dangers of royal service and urges him to weaken the guilty men one by one, and the king makes him his priest and rules well with his counsel.

scenes.B12C081S01: Bhishma tells how the sage Kalakavrikshiya exposes the king's corrupt officers, how the king is warned about his servants, and how the king takes the sage as his priest and rules successfully.

shots.B12C081S01H01: Bhishma gives a second means: protect the one who reports embezzlement by ministers, and tells how the sage Kalakavrikshiya, touring the kingdom with a crow in a cage, named the thieving officers of King Kshemadarsin and then came to the king after they killed his crow.
shots.B12C081S01H02: The sage warns the king of the perils of royal service, says the officials are plotting against him and the people, and says he will leave the kingdom because of their hostility.
shots.B12C081S01H03: King Kshemadarsin asks the sage to stay, promising him honour, and asks him to see that the rod of chastisement is used properly.
shots.B12C081S01H04: The sage advises the king to weaken the guilty men one by one, reminds him that he was once his father's friend, and the king then makes a Kshatriya minister and the sage his priest, after which he conquers the whole earth.

B12C082.summary: Yudhishthira asks what qualities a king's legislators, war ministers, courtiers, generals and counsellors should have. Bhishma answers at length: choose people of good birth, proven loyalty, learning and self-control, test their records, and avoid the greedy, cruel or self-serving. He also advises that counsel be kept secret, sought in quiet places, and given by at least three ministers.

scenes.B12C082S01: Bhishma explains how a king should choose and test his legislators, war ministers, courtiers, counsellors and generals, and how he should consult with them in secret.

shots.B12C082S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what qualities a king's legislators, war ministers, courtiers, generals and counsellors should have.
shots.B12C082S01H02: Bhishma says the king should appoint men of good birth, loyalty, learning and self-control, avoid the greedy and unreliable, never confide in one who is not devoted to him, hold secret consultations in a quiet place, and keep at least three ministers.

B12C083.summary: Bhishma tells a short story in which Sakra (Indra) asks his priest Vrihaspati which single act wins the regard of all creatures. Vrihaspati answers that agreeable speech does so, since sweet, smiling words win love while frowns breed hatred. Even a king who must punish should speak sweetly, and Bhishma says Sakra followed this advice and urges Yudhishthira to do the same.

scenes.B12C083S01: Bhishma recounts Vrihaspati's teaching to Sakra on the value of agreeable speech, and urges Yudhishthira to practise it.

shots.B12C083S01H01: Bhishma says he will cite an old conversation between Vrihaspati and Sakra.
shots.B12C083S01H02: Sakra asks Vrihaspati which single act wins the regard of all creatures and brings great fame.
shots.B12C083S01H03: Vrihaspati answers that agreeable speech does this: smiling, sweet words win love, frowns and silence breed hatred, gifts without kind words please no one, and a king who must punish should still speak sweetly.
shots.B12C083S01H04: Bhishma says Sakra followed this advice and urges Yudhishthira to practise the same virtue.

B12C084.summary: Yudhishthira asks by what method a king can earn lasting blessedness and fame. Bhishma says a pure king who protects his subjects gains merit and fame here and hereafter. He then sets out the make-up of a royal council drawn from all four orders, and rules for fair justice, punishments matched to offences, the protection of envoys, and the advice never to trust anyone fully.

scenes.B12C084S01: Bhishma explains the composition of the king's council, the rules of justice and punishment, and the duties of envoys, aid-de-camps, ministers and commanders, closing with advice on trust.

shots.B12C084S01H01: Yudhishthira asks by what method a king ruling his subjects can gain great blessedness and eternal fame.
shots.B12C084S01H02: Bhishma says a king of cleansed soul who protects his subjects earns merit and fame here and hereafter by conducting himself righteously.
shots.B12C084S01H03: Yudhishthira observes that the virtues described so far are rarely found together in any one person, and asks how the king should deal with people.
shots.B12C084S01H04: Bhishma agrees such perfection is rare, names the mix of Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaisyas, Sudras and a Suta who should serve as ministers, and gives rules for fair judgement, graded punishment, the protection of envoys, and the advice that a king should trust no one fully, not even his son.

B12C085.summary: Yudhishthira asks what kind of city a king should live in, and whether he should use an existing city or build one. Bhishma says the king should choose among six kinds of citadels: water, earth, hill, human, mud and forest. He describes a well-defended, well-stocked and righteous capital, and advises the king to keep spies, stores, craftsmen and learned ascetics close at hand.

scenes.B12C085S01: Bhishma describes the six kinds of citadel, the features of a good capital, the stores and people a king should keep, and his duties toward ascetics and friends.

shots.B12C085S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what sort of city a king should dwell in, and whether he should use an existing one or have one built.
shots.B12C085S01H02: Bhishma names six kinds of citadels and describes the ideal well-defended, well-stocked and righteous city, along with the stores, craftsmen, spies and ascetics the king should keep close.

B12C086.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a kingdom can be consolidated and protected. Bhishma describes a layered administration, with a headman for each village and superiors over ten, twenty, a hundred and a thousand villages, all reporting upward and watched by spies. He advises taxes that the people can bear, likening the king to a herdsman who must not drain the cow, and urges kindness toward the Vaisyas who sustain trade and farming.

scenes.B12C086S01: Bhishma describes the tiered village administration, the principles of fair taxation, and the care the king should show toward the Vaisya traders and farmers.

shots.B12C086S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a kingdom can be consolidated and how it should be protected.
shots.B12C086S01H02: Bhishma describes a layered administration with headmen over ten, twenty, a hundred and a thousand villages, moderate taxes that leave the people able to work, and kindness toward the Vaisyas.

B12C087.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a king should act if he still craves more wealth despite his riches. Bhishma says a king should draw revenue gently, like a bee gathering honey or a leech drawing blood, raising demands by degrees. He also says the king shares in his subjects' sins and merits, so he must check drinking, gambling and other vices and keep beggars off the streets. He closes with a charge to love all creatures and rule with truth and restraint.

scenes.B12C087S01: Bhishma advises gradual, mild taxation, checking vice and idleness, honouring the wealthy, and ruling with truth and restraint.

shots.B12C087S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a king should behave if, though wealthy, he still desires more.
shots.B12C087S01H02: Bhishma advises taking revenue gently and gradually like a bee or a leech, restraining drinking, gambling and other vices, keeping beggars off the streets, and honouring the wealthy as partners in the people's welfare.
shots.B12C087S01H03: Bhishma closes by urging the king to love all creatures, practise truth and sincerity, and use his power to strengthen his treasury, friends and kingdom.

B12C088.summary: Bhishma says fruit-bearing trees must not be felled, and that a Brahmana in want should be supported rather than driven away. He advises the king to use spies to watch his people and to examine his own conduct and reputation. When Yudhishthira asks how one man among equals comes to rule the rest, Bhishma answers that the strong prey on the weak and that the king must protect traders and farmers from heavy taxes.

scenes.B12C088S01: Bhishma gives advice on protecting trees, Brahmanas, spies and the king's own reputation, and then, answering Yudhishthira, explains how the strong rule the weak and why traders and farmers must be spared.

shots.B12C088S01H01: Bhishma forbids felling fruit-bearing trees, says a Brahmana in want should be supported rather than lost, and advises the king to keep spies and to examine his own conduct and reputation.
shots.B12C088S01H02: Yudhishthira asks how one man among equals in strength and skill rises above the rest and comes to rule them.
shots.B12C088S01H03: Bhishma says the strong prey on the weak in nature and among men, so the king must watch both subjects and foes, spare traders and farmers from heavy taxes, and remember that gifts sustain all beings.

B12C089.summary: Bhishma recounts the teaching that the sage Utathya gave to King Mandhatri, son of Yuvanaswa. Utathya says a king rules rightly only by upholding righteousness, that a king who does so is godlike, and that pride and unrighteousness bring ruin. He urges the king to honour Brahmanas and avoid vice, and warns that neglecting righteousness brings drought, floods, disorder and the collapse of property and worship.

scenes.B12C089S01: Bhishma introduces Utathya's teaching to Mandhatri, which sets out the king's duty to uphold righteousness, the dangers of pride, and the disasters that follow neglect.

shots.B12C089S01H01: Bhishma introduces the sage Utathya's teaching to King Mandhatri, son of Yuvanaswa.
shots.B12C089S01H02: Utathya says a king is made by righteousness and must uphold it, that neglecting it brings ruin, that Brahmanas must be honoured, and that pride and vice must be avoided, while the lack of restraint brings drought, floods, disorder and collapse of worship and property.

B12C090.summary: The sage Utathya tells Mandhatri that rain, prosperity and the four ages all depend on the king's conduct. A righteous king who corrects the orders is like a washerman who cleans cloth without stripping its colour, while a heedless king brings ruin on all creatures. Utathya lists the king's duties, including protecting the weak, punishing wrongdoers, honouring priests and avoiding pride, and Bhishma says Mandhatri obeyed and became lord of the whole earth.

scenes.B12C090S01: Utathya's long teaching sets out how the king shapes the age, the duties of kingship, and the dangers of weakness and pride, and Bhishma says Mandhatri followed it.

shots.B12C090S01H01: Utathya teaches that the king's conduct decides the state of the world and the four ages, compares a righteous king to a washerman who cleans the orders, and lists the king's duties of protecting the weak, punishing wrongdoers, honouring priests and avoiding pride.
shots.B12C090S01H02: Bhishma says Mandhatri followed this counsel, became lord of the whole earth, and urges Yudhishthira to act the same way.

B12C091.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king should behave. Bhishma tells how King Vasumanas asked the sage Vamadeva for counsel on keeping to his duties. Vamadeva says righteousness is the highest guide and that kings who follow it conquer the earth, while kings who rely on force, wicked ministers or caprice bring their own downfall.

scenes.B12C091S01: Vamadeva advises King Vasumanas to rule by righteousness, to avoid force, wicked ministers and caprice, and to be generous, honest and willing to take counsel.

shots.B12C091S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king should behave, and wants Bhishma's answer.
shots.B12C091S01H02: Bhishma tells how King Vasumanas, a man of knowledge and purity, asks the sage Vamadeva to teach him the conduct that keeps a king within his duties.
shots.B12C091S01H03: Vamadeva says righteousness is the surest guide, that kings who follow it conquer the earth, while force, wicked ministers and caprice lead to ruin, and he recommends generosity, honour to the worthy and seeking the counsel of teachers.

B12C092.summary: Vamadeva continues his counsel to Vasumanas. He warns that a king's conduct is copied by his people and kinsmen, so he must be honest, kind and fair, and must choose capable, loyal officers. He advises watching rival kings through secret agents, attacking only weaker neighbours, sharing the duties of state with trusted ministers, and never trusting those who wish him ill.

scenes.B12C092S01: Vamadeva gives a long list of advice on personal conduct, choosing officers, dealing with neighbours and rivals, and guarding against false friends.

shots.B12C092S01H01: Vamadeva continues that the king's conduct is copied by others, so he should be honest and kind, choose capable and loyal officers, watch rival kings through agents, attack only weaker neighbours, share state duties with trusted ministers, and never trust those who harbour ill will.

B12C093.summary: Vamadeva says a king should win victories without battle where he can, and should first make his own power secure before seeking new lands. A contented army, a loyal and compassionate people, and a king who controls his temper make his power sound. Bhishma says that King Vasumana followed this counsel and that Yudhishthira would likewise conquer both worlds.

scenes.B12C093S01: Vamadeva explains how a king's power is confirmed and why he should win by wisdom rather than battle, and Bhishma closes by applying the teaching to Yudhishthira.

shots.B12C093S01H01: Vamadeva says a king should win without battle where possible, first secure his own power, and keep contented soldiers, a loyal people and a temper under control.
shots.B12C093S01H02: Bhishma says King Vasumana followed these counsels, and that Yudhishthira would also conquer both worlds by doing the same.

B12C094.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a Kshatriya should act in seeking to conquer another Kshatriya. Bhishma says the invader should first call on the people to accept him and pay tribute, and fight only those who resist. He then sets out rules of fair combat between warriors, such as matching armour with armour and not striking the fallen, unarmed or wounded, and says a victory won by sinful means is no victory.

scenes.B12C094S01: Bhishma explains how a king should approach a conquest, and then gives the rules of fair combat between Kshatriyas and why righteous victory matters.

shots.B12C094S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a Kshatriya should act in victory when he seeks to subdue another Kshatriya in battle.
shots.B12C094S01H02: Bhishma says the invader should call on the people to accept him and pay tribute, and that fighting is needed only if they resist.
shots.B12C094S01H03: Yudhishthira asks how a Kshatriya king should conduct himself in battle against another king.
shots.B12C094S01H04: Bhishma sets rules of fair combat: match mail with mail and army with army, answer deceit with deceit, do not strike the fallen, wounded or unarmed, avoid poisoned arrows, and keep to righteousness, since a sinful victory brings ruin.

B12C095.summary: Bhishma says a king should never conquer by unrighteous means, since such victories bring no heaven and weaken both king and land. He sets out rules for dealing with the vanquished: spare the disarmed, keep a defeated king in one's palace for a year, return captured women after a year, give captured cattle to Brahmanas, and never harm a Brahmana who comes to make peace. He advises winning over conquered subjects with soothing words and gifts.

scenes.B12C095S01: Bhishma lays down the rules a victorious king should follow with the defeated, the captured and the conquered people, and gives examples of righteous kings.

shots.B12C095S01H01: Bhishma says a king should never conquer by unrighteous means, and lays out how to treat the vanquished: spare the disarmed, keep a defeated king in the palace for a year, return captured women, give cattle to Brahmanas, and win conquered subjects over with kindness and gifts.

B12C096.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a warrior-king can win heaven when Kshatriya practice involves so much slaughter. Bhishma says kings are cleansed by punishing the wicked, supporting the good, and offering sacrifices and gifts, and that protecting people from robbers is itself a great gift. He concludes that a hero who fights bravely and dies in battle wins heaven, while a coward who flees or dies at home without honour does not.

scenes.B12C096S01: Bhishma explains how a king is purified by righteous conduct, and describes the merit of bravery in battle and the shame of cowardice and an ignoble death.

shots.B12C096S01H01: Yudhishthira says Kshatriya practice seems very sinful, and asks by what acts a king wins regions of felicity.
shots.B12C096S01H02: Bhishma says kings are cleansed by punishing the wicked, supporting the good, and offering sacrifices and gifts, and that heroes who defend others and die in battle win heaven, while cowards and those who die at home without honour do not.

B12C097.summary: Yudhishthira asks what regions unreturning heroes win by dying in battle. Bhishma tells how King Amvarisha, in heaven, sees his former general Sudeva ranked above himself, though Sudeva had made fewer sacrifices to the gods. Indra explains that battle is itself a sacrifice, with warriors as priests and blood as the final libation, and that brave heroes who die fighting win the highest regions. Bhishma says Amvarisha accepted this teaching.

scenes.B12C097S01: Bhishma recounts how Amvarisha, in heaven, sees his former general Sudeva raised above him, and how he questions Indra about it.
scenes.B12C097S02: Indra describes the battle-sacrifice in full detail, with its priests, offerings and fees, and says heroes who die bravely win the highest regions while cowards sink to hell.

shots.B12C097S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what regions are won by heroes who die in battle without turning back.
shots.B12C097S01H02: Bhishma tells how King Amvarisha, son of Nabhaga, sees in heaven his former general Sudeva rising higher than himself.
shots.B12C097S01H03: Amvarisha recounts his own virtues, sacrifices and victories, and asks Indra why Sudeva has risen above him.
shots.B12C097S01H04: Indra answers that Sudeva often spread out the great sacrifice of battle, and that any warrior who advances in battle array takes part in it.
shots.B12C097S01H05: Amvarisha asks what the libations, offerings, fees and priests of that battle-sacrifice are.
shots.B12C097S02H01: Indra describes the battle as a sacrifice in full detail, with elephants as priests, weapons as ladles, blood as the final libation, and says brave heroes who die fighting win the highest regions while cowards sink to hell.
shots.B12C097S02H02: Bhishma says Amvarisha approved of Indra's words and understood how warriors win heaven through battle.

B12C098.summary: Bhishma tells how King Janaka of Mithila rallied his warriors before a battle with Pratardana. Janaka showed them the heaven awaiting brave men and the hell reserved for deserters, and then set out the battle order. He advised against over-pursuing a routed enemy and ended by praising heroism as the support of the world.

scenes.B12C098S01: Janaka rallies his troops with pictures of heaven and hell, sets their battle order, and warns against pursuing a routed enemy too far.

shots.B12C098S01H01: Bhishma tells how King Janaka of Mithila, before his battle with Pratardana, showed his warriors the heaven of brave men and the hell of deserters, then set out the battle order, advised against over-pursuit, and praised heroism.

B12C099.summary: Yudhishthira asks how kings should lead their troops into battle even if that means bending the rules of righteousness a little. Bhishma says a king may use crooked policy only to counter enemies, then gives a long set of military preparations: stocking arms, choosing the season and safe roads, picking camp sites, placing troops by wind and sun, sparing the helpless, and rewarding brave men. He ends by describing an oath of steadfastness and battle formations, including tricks to make a small force look larger.

scenes.B12C099S01: Bhishma sets out the king's military preparations, the rules for who may not be attacked, the rewards for courage, and the battle formations and deceptions used to win.

shots.B12C099S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how kings seeking victory should lead their troops into battle even if this means slightly offending against righteousness.
shots.B12C099S01H02: Bhishma says a king may use crooked policy only to counter enemies, then covers preparations: stocking arms, choosing the season and safe roads, camp sites, troop positions, sparing the helpless, rewarding brave men, and battle formations.
shots.B12C099S01H03: A heading marks the start of Section CI.

B12C100.summary: Yudhishthira asks what temperament, appearance, dress and arms make combatants fit for battle. Bhishma says each people should fight with the weapons it knows, and notes the fighting styles of various regions. He then lists bodily and temperamental marks of brave fighters, and says the fiercest tribes of the outlying districts make the best vanguard, though they turn angry if treated gently.

scenes.B12C100S01: Bhishma describes the fighting styles of different peoples and the physical and temperamental signs of courageous soldiers.

shots.B12C100S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what temperament, appearance, dress and arms make combatants fit for battle.
shots.B12C100S01H02: Bhishma says troops should fight with the weapons they know, notes the styles of different peoples, lists the bodily and temperamental marks of brave fighters, and says the fiercest outlying tribes make the best vanguard, though they turn wrathful if treated mildly.

B12C101.summary: Yudhishthira asks for the known signs that an army will succeed. Bhishma lists omens of success, such as cheerful troops, favourable winds, auspicious birds and animals, and bright sacrificial fires. He advises trying conciliation, division and gifts before fighting, and says victory in battle depends largely on fate. He ends by urging a mix of severity and mildness toward the defeated, with genuine grief for the slain.

scenes.B12C101S01: Bhishma lists the omens of an army's success, explains why battle should be avoided where possible, and advises a mixture of forgiveness and severity toward the enemy.

shots.B12C101S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what well-known signs predict the success of an army.
shots.B12C101S01H02: Bhishma lists omens of success such as cheerful troops, favourable winds, auspicious animals and birds and bright sacrificial fires, advises trying conciliation, division and gifts before fighting, and urges a mix of mildness and severity toward the defeated, with sorrow for the slain and honour for one's own brave men.

B12C102.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a king should treat a mild foe, a fierce foe and a foe with many allies. Bhishma tells how Vrihaspati advised Indra to avoid open quarrel, hide his feelings, speak sweetly while planning, strike at the right moment, and corrupt the enemy's forces by division and gifts. Vrihaspati then lists the marks of a wicked person, and Bhishma says Indra followed this teaching and subdued his foes.

scenes.B12C102S01: Vrihaspati advises Indra on dealing with foes: concealment, patience, sweet words while planning, timed strikes, and dividing and corrupting the enemy's forces.
scenes.B12C102S02: Vrihaspati lists the signs of a wicked person, and Indra acts on the teaching to subdue his enemies.

shots.B12C102S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a king should treat a mild foe, a fierce foe and a foe with many allies and a large force.
shots.B12C102S01H02: Bhishma introduces an old discourse between Vrihaspati and Indra, in which Indra approaches the sage with joined palms.
shots.B12C102S01H03: Indra asks how he can subdue his foes through policy without exterminating them, and how to keep his newly won prosperity.
shots.B12C102S01H04: Vrihaspati advises concealing one's feelings, speaking sweetly to foes while planning, waiting for the right moment, corrupting the enemy's forces by division, gifts and poison, and never sleeping at ease after victory.
shots.B12C102S01H05: Indra asks how he can recognise a wicked person.
shots.B12C102S02H01: Vrihaspati says a wicked person speaks ill of others behind their backs, envies their success, avoids praising them, breaks promises when unobserved, eats apart and sorrows at others' joys.
shots.B12C102S02H02: Bhishma says Indra acted on these instructions and reduced all his enemies to subjection.

B12C103.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king who has lost his officers, treasury and army can still find happiness. Bhishma tells of Kshemadarsin, the prince of Kosala, who fell into distress and went to the sage Kalakavrikshiya. The sage teaches that all things are impermanent and that grief for lost wealth is useless, and advises him to let go of craving, enjoy what he has, and perhaps retire to the forest.

scenes.B12C103S01: Kshemadarsin, ruined and distressed, asks the sage what to do, and the sage teaches detachment from wealth, the impermanence of things, and the advantage of a simple life.

shots.B12C103S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king who has lost his officers, treasury, army and wealth can seek happiness.
shots.B12C103S01H02: Bhishma tells of Kshemadarsin, who fell into great distress and approached the sage Kalakavrikshiya.
shots.B12C103S01H03: Kshemadarsin asks the sage what a ruined man can do, short of suicide, theft or begging, and asks for guidance toward happiness.
shots.B12C103S01H04: The sage says all things are impermanent and grief is pointless, and asks why the king should be unhappy with his lot, while the king replies that Time swept his kingdom away and he now lives on charity.
shots.B12C103S01H05: The sage advises him to stop craving, enjoy what he has, avoid envying others, and perhaps retire to the forest and live simply.

B12C104.summary: The sage Kalakavrikshiya tells King Kshemadarsin that, if he still has courage, he can recover his kingdom by a line of policy. He advises him to humble himself before Janaka, the ruler of Mithila, to earn that king's trust, and then to weaken his foes through division, luxury, a drained treasury and misdirected sacrifices. He ends by saying that poison and fraud can destroy a hostile kingdom.

scenes.B12C104S01: The sage offers a plan for recovering the kingdom by serving Janaka and then weakening enemies through division, luxury, depleted treasuries and deceit.

shots.B12C104S01H01: The sage says that if the king still has spirit he can recover his kingdom, and offers to set out a policy for doing so.
shots.B12C104S01H02: Kshemadarsin says he is willing to hear and act on the counsel, hoping the meeting will bear fruit.
shots.B12C104S01H03: The sage advises him to humble himself before his foes, serve Janaka of Mithila until he is trusted, then weaken his enemies through division, luxury, drained treasuries and misdirected sacrifices, even by poison and fraud.

B12C105.summary: Kshemadarsin refuses to win back his kingdom by fraud and says he will live only by honest means. The sage Kalakavrikshiya praises his righteousness and brings him to Janaka, the ruler of Videha, who recognises his worth. The two kings make peace and trust each other, and Janaka honours his guest with his own daughter and jewels, reasoning that peace is the high duty of kings.

scenes.B12C105S01: Kshemadarsin rejects deceit, the sage introduces him to Janaka, and the two kings make peace and exchange honours.

shots.B12C105S01H01: Kshemadarsin says he will not live by deceit or win wealth by unrighteous means, and that the sage's advice does not suit him.
shots.B12C105S01H02: The sage praises his righteous disposition, promises a lasting union with Janaka, and says a loyal, learned minister of noble birth is a rare prize.
shots.B12C105S01H03: The sage presents Kshemadarsin to Janaka as a man of pure heart and royal birth, Janaka welcomes him as an equal, and the two kings make peace, with Janaka giving his daughter and jewels, reasoning that peace is the king's high duty.

B12C106.summary: Yudhishthira recaps the earlier teachings and asks how a king should treat the many brave men around him so that they stay loyal and undivided. Bhishma says enmity between the king and the nobility arises from greed on the king's side and wrath on theirs. Nobles who stay united, honour their leaders and settle quarrels early prosper, while disunion and oppression drive them to the king's enemies.

scenes.B12C106S01: Bhishma explains how enmity grows between the king and the nobility, and how the king should consult their leaders and keep the nobles united.

shots.B12C106S01H01: Yudhishthira recaps the earlier topics and asks how a king should treat the many brave men around him, keeping them loyal and undivided.
shots.B12C106S01H02: Bhishma says enmity between king and nobility arises from greed in the king and wrath in the nobles, that united nobles prosper while disunion and oppression drive them to the enemy, and that the king should consult their leaders and settle quarrels early.

B12C107.summary: Yudhishthira asks which duties matter most for earning merit now and in the next world. Bhishma answers that honouring mother, father and teacher is the chief duty, and that they should be obeyed and served with humility. He says the teacher deserves the greatest reverence because he gives an immortal life, and that neglecting or injuring any of the three is a grave sin.

scenes.B12C107S01: Bhishma names the honour owed to parents and teachers as the highest duty, ranks the teacher above the parents, and describes the sins of neglecting them.

shots.B12C107S01H01: Yudhishthira asks which duties are most important for earning merit and fame here and hereafter.
shots.B12C107S01H02: Bhishma says honouring mother, father and preceptor is the chief duty, that they should be obeyed and served humbly, that the preceptor is worthy of the greatest reverence, and that injuring or neglecting them is a grave sin.

B12C108.summary: Yudhishthira asks how someone who wants to follow virtue should tell truth from falsehood, and what eternal virtue is. Bhishma says truth is generally right but must be withheld when it serves evil, and that a falsehood may be told to save a life or another's wealth or to escape sinful men. He concludes that righteousness is what upholds creatures and prevents their injury, so the honest should be met with honesty and the deceitful with deceit.

scenes.B12C108S01: Bhishma explains when truth and falsehood are proper, what righteousness is, and how to deal with the honest and the deceitful.

shots.B12C108S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a person who holds to virtue should decide between truth and falsehood, and what eternal virtue is.
shots.B12C108S01H02: Bhishma says truth is generally right but must be withheld when it serves evil, that a falsehood may save life or others' wealth, that righteousness is what upholds creatures and prevents their injury, and that the deceitful should be met with deceit and the honest with honesty.

B12C109.summary: Yudhishthira asks how creatures can overcome the many afflictions that beset them. Bhishma answers with a long list of people who overcome difficulties: those who keep to their duties, speak the truth, give without taking, honour guests and parents, and avoid harm and greed. He ends by identifying Krishna as Narayana, the Lord who protects those who seek his refuge, and says reciting these verses helps one overcome difficulties.

scenes.B12C109S01: Bhishma lists the kinds of people who overcome difficulties and identifies Krishna with Narayana, whose refuge protects those who seek it.

shots.B12C109S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how creatures, who are constantly afflicted in many ways, can overcome their difficulties.
shots.B12C109S01H02: Bhishma lists those who overcome difficulties, such as the upright, the truthful, the generous, the hospitable and the harmless, and says Krishna is Narayana, whose refuge protects those who seek it, and that reciting these verses also helps.

B12C110.summary: Yudhishthira asks how to tell people who are truly tranquil from those who only appear so. Bhishma tells of a cruel king, Paurika, reborn as a jackal who lives purely and refuses meat. A tiger takes the jackal as his minister, but envious old servants frame him for stealing the tiger's meat, and the jackal, though cleared, leaves the court and ends his life by fasting, going to heaven.

scenes.B12C110S01: Bhishma tells how the reborn jackal becomes the tiger's minister, is framed by envious courtiers, and leaves the court after being cleared and insulted.
scenes.B12C110S02: The jackal retires to the forest and ends his life by fasting, rejecting the tiger's pleas, and goes to heaven.

shots.B12C110S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how to tell people who are truly tranquil from those who only look tranquil.
shots.B12C110S01H02: Bhishma tells of King Paurika of Purika, cruel in life, who is reborn as a jackal, refuses meat, lives on fallen fruit, and speaks gently of virtue, so that a tiger takes him for a learned and righteous sage.
shots.B12C110S01H03: The tiger offers the jackal the post of minister and warns him of his own fierce nature.
shots.B12C110S01H04: The jackal accepts on conditions: he wants to be left free to live as he likes, to advise the tiger in private, and to be spared punishment for others' faults.
shots.B12C110S01H05: Envious old servants hide the tiger's meat in the jackal's den to frame him, the tiger's mother pleads for him, and a loyal agent exposes the plot, but the jackal, hurt by the insult, leaves the court and warns that such treatment breeds enemies and mistrust.
shots.B12C110S02H01: The jackal retires to the forest, rejects the tiger's entreaties, fasts to death and goes to heaven as a reward for his good deeds.

B12C111.summary: Yudhishthira asks what a king should do to be happy. Bhishma warns against the example of a camel of the Krita age, who won from Brahman a boon of a very long neck after great austerities. The camel grew idle, and while sheltering from a storm in a cave, a jackal and his wife ate his neck and killed him. Bhishma uses the tale to urge a king to avoid idleness and to act with intelligence, aided by wise counsel and allies.

scenes.B12C111S01: Bhishma tells of the idle camel that was killed after gaining a long neck by boon, and draws the lesson that a king should act with intelligence, avoid idleness and seek wise counsel.

shots.B12C111S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what a king should do to become happy, and asks for a full answer.
shots.B12C111S01H02: Bhishma warns a king against the example of a camel of the Krita age who, after great austerities, won a boon from Brahman for a very long neck.
shots.B12C111S01H03: The camel grew idle, and when a storm drove him into a cave, a jackal and his wife ate his stretched neck and killed him, which Bhishma uses to urge intelligence, careful action and wise counsel over idleness.

B12C112.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a king without the usual aids should behave toward a powerful foe. Bhishma tells of the Ocean asking the rivers why they never sweep away the canes on their banks, though they uproot great trees. Ganga explains that the cane bends with the current and survives, while rigid trees resist and are torn away, and Bhishma concludes that a wise man facing a stronger foe should yield like the cane.

scenes.B12C112S01: The Ocean and the rivers discuss why canes survive floods, and Bhishma draws the lesson that a wise man should yield to a stronger foe.

shots.B12C112S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a king without the usual aids should behave toward a powerful foe after winning a precious kingdom.
shots.B12C112S01H02: Bhishma introduces an old discourse between the Ocean, lord of rivers, and the rivers themselves.
shots.B12C112S01H03: The Ocean asks why the rivers sweep away great trees but never the canes on their banks.
shots.B12C112S01H04: Ganga explains that rigid trees resist the current and are uprooted, while the cane bends, knows the value of time and yielding, and rises again after the flood.
shots.B12C112S01H05: Bhishma says a man who resists a stronger foe able to destroy him will be ruined, and that a wise man who has weighed his strength against his foe's should act like the cane.

B12C113.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a learned, modest man should respond when an ignorant, conceited person abuses him in public. Bhishma advises patience: the man who does not answer anger takes the abuser's merit, and the abuser takes the patient man's demerit. The boasts and slanders of fools are empty, like a crow's cawing, and slanderers who speak ill of others behind their backs should be avoided, while one who endures their reproaches suffers no pain from speech.

scenes.B12C113S01: Bhishma explains why patience under abuse is wise, how the abuser's merit and sins pass between them, and why slanderers should be avoided.

shots.B12C113S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a learned, modest man should behave when an ignorant, conceited person heaps harsh insults on him in an assembly.
shots.B12C113S01H02: Bhishma advises patience: an abuser's merit passes to the patient man, the boasts and slanders of fools are empty, back-biters should be avoided, and one who endures such reproaches feels no pain from speech.

B12C114.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a king can keep his kingdom and royal line prosperous, and how he should choose servants, since a king who keeps company with wicked men loses his loyal servants. Bhishma answers that no king can rule alone and that he needs wise, honest and well-born ministers and officers. He adds that accounts and treasuries must be honestly supervised, justice fairly administered, and the subjects won over by kindness.

scenes.B12C114S01: Yudhishthira asks how a king should gratify his people and choose his servants, and Bhishma explains the qualities of the servants, ministers and officials a king needs.

shots.B12C114S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a king should keep his people content, which servants to choose, and how a king who keeps wicked companions loses the loyalty of good servants.
shots.B12C114S01H02: Bhishma says a king cannot rule alone, and that wise, loyal, honest and well-born ministers, supervisors of revenue and granaries, and fair judges bring a king prosperity, while the subjects should be won over by kindness.

B12C115.summary: Bhishma tells an old tale heard at the hermitage of Rama, son of Jamadagni. A sage in a forest is served by its beasts, and a devoted dog stays by him, but a leopard threatens the dog. The sage transforms the dog into a leopard to save it, and then, when a tiger comes, into a tiger, so that the beasts of the forest leave it alone.

scenes.B12C115S01: A forest sage, served by its animals, protects a devoted dog from a threatening leopard by transforming it, and then protects it again from a tiger.

shots.B12C115S01H01: Bhishma introduces the tale of a sage living in a forest, whose animals treat him as a master, and of a devoted dog who is threatened by a leopard and asks the sage for protection.
shots.B12C115S01H02: The sage transforms the dog into a golden leopard, then, when a hungry tiger approaches, into a tiger, and the transformed animal lives among the beasts as their king.

B12C117.summary: The dog, returned to its own form, is driven out of the hermitage. Bhishma draws the lesson for kings: examine servants carefully for truth, purity, learning, conduct, birth and self-control before employing them, and do not keep men of low birth. He describes the qualities of a good minister, the virtues of a righteous king, and the value of a loyal army, and says a king who wins the loyalty of his men can conquer the earth.

scenes.B12C117S01: Bhishma draws the lesson of the dog story for kings, describing how to choose ministers and servants, the virtues of a good king, and the value of a loyal army.

shots.B12C117S01H01: Bhishma says the dog, returned to its own form, is driven from the hermitage, and urges kings to examine servants for truth, learning, birth and self-control, to choose ministers of noble birth with many virtues, to cultivate kingly virtues and a loyal army, and to win every man's love so that he may conquer the earth.

B12C116.summary: The transformed dog, now a tiger, is threatened by an elephant and then a lion, and the sage changes it into each in turn. It is changed into a Sarabha to meet a fierce beast, and then grows ungrateful, planning to kill the sage. The sage reproves it, reminds it of its origin as a dog, and turns it back into a dog.

scenes.B12C116S01: The sage keeps transforming the dog into a larger beast whenever a stronger creature threatens it, until the animal turns ungrateful and plans to kill him, and the sage then recounts the transformations and returns it to dog form.

shots.B12C116S01H01: The transformed tiger is threatened by an elephant, which the sage changes it into, then by a lion, then by a Sarabha, and the creature finally grows ungrateful and plans to kill the sage.
shots.B12C116S01H02: The sage recounts how he transformed the dog from leopard to tiger, elephant, lion and Sarabha, reproves its ingratitude, and returns it to dog form.

B12C118.summary: Bhishma says that, taking the lesson of the dog story, a king should give each servant the office he is fit for and never raise a man above his station. He advises choosing honest, learned and well-born ministers, keeping the treasury and granaries in trustworthy hands, and caring for kinsmen and the city. He closes by asking Yudhishthira what further he would like to hear.

scenes.B12C118S01: Bhishma applies the dog story to the appointment of servants, counsels the king on ministers, treasury and kinsmen, and asks what more Yudhishthira wants to hear.

shots.B12C118S01H01: Bhishma says a king should give each servant the office he is fit for, choose honest, learned and well-born ministers, guard the treasury and granaries, care for kinsmen and the city, and asks what further Yudhishthira wishes to hear.

B12C119.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to restate the duties of kingship in a form that is easy to remember. Bhishma answers at length that protecting all creatures is the highest duty, and that a king should be like a peacock, varying his conduct to suit each purpose and keeping counsel secret. He should watch for danger, collect taxes gently as a bee gathers honey, appoint honest officers, avoid waste and greed, and act with intelligence and patience, so as to protect his people and earn the rewards of virtue.

scenes.B12C119S01: Bhishma gives a long, detailed summary of the king's duties, comparing the wise king to a peacock and setting out how to govern, tax, watch enemies and choose officers.

shots.B12C119S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to speak of the duties of kingship in a way that can be easily remembered.
shots.B12C119S01H02: Bhishma says protecting all creatures is the highest duty, and that a king should act like a peacock, varying his conduct to suit his aims, keeping counsel secret, watching for danger, taxing gently like a bee, appointing honest officers, avoiding waste and flattery, and protecting his people.

B12C120.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain Chastisement itself: its nature, form, origin and the power that keeps it watchful, since so much seems to depend on it. Bhishma says Chastisement is the principle by which righteousness is upheld and is also called Vyavahara, a term that Manu first declared. He describes its fearsome form and many names, and explains that legal procedure rests on Vedic and royal authority. He ends by saying that no one, not even a mother, father, brother, wife or priest, is exempt from the justice of a king who rules by duty.

scenes.B12C120S01: Yudhishthira asks what Chastisement is, and Bhishma explains its nature, names and forms, its roots in the Vedas and royal authority, and the king's duty to apply it to all alike.

shots.B12C120S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain what Chastisement is, what form and origin it has, and how it stays watchful over the world.
shots.B12C120S01H02: Bhishma explains that Chastisement upholds righteousness and is called Vyavahara, describes its fearsome form, many names and power over all things, traces its roots in the Vedas, and ends with the rule that no one is exempt from the king's justice, not even parents, brothers, wives or priests.

B12C121.summary: Bhishma tells how King Mandhatri visits the penitent king Vasuhoma and asks where Chastisement came from. Vasuhoma explains that Chastisement vanished during Brahman's sacrifice, causing disorder, until Vishnu created it anew and it was entrusted to the gods, sages and finally to Manu and his sons. Chastisement must be used with discrimination, and Bhishma says whoever heeds this teaching will gain the fulfilment of his wishes.

scenes.B12C121S01: Mandhatri asks Vasuhoma about the origin of Chastisement, Vasuhoma recounts how it arose and passed through the gods and sages to Manu, and Bhishma says the teaching brings its reward to those who follow it.

shots.B12C121S01H01: Bhishma introduces King Vasuhoma of the Angas, a penitent king of great piety, and his visit from the king Mandhatri, whom he receives with hospitality.
shots.B12C121S01H02: Mandhatri asks Vasuhoma where Chastisement came from, what was awake before it, what its end is, and how it came to depend on the Kshatriya.
shots.B12C121S01H03: Vasuhoma explains that Chastisement vanished during Brahman's sacrifice and disorder followed, until Vishnu created it anew, and that the rod was passed from the gods and sages down to Manu and his sons, to be used with discrimination.
shots.B12C121S01H04: Bhishma says whoever listens to Vasuhoma's teaching and acts on it will gain the fulfilment of his wishes.

B12C122.summary: Yudhishthira asks how Virtue, Wealth and Pleasure relate, and what their roots and fruits are. Bhishma says Wealth rests on Virtue, Pleasure is the fruit of Wealth, and all three aim at liberation, with the flaws of greed for reward and hoarding to be purged. He then tells how King Angaristha asks the sage Kamandaka how a king can undo sins committed through lust or ignorance, and Kamandaka prescribes Vedic study, respect for Brahmanas, banishing wicked men and seeking the company of the good.

scenes.B12C122S01: Bhishma explains how the three aims relate and how their flaws are purged, and then recounts Kamandaka's advice to King Angaristha on undoing sin.

shots.B12C122S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how Virtue, Wealth and Pleasure relate, what their roots and fruits are, and why they sometimes mingle and sometimes stand apart.
shots.B12C122S01H02: Bhishma explains that Wealth rests on Virtue and Pleasure is its fruit, that all three rest on will and aim at liberation, that their impurities are greed for reward and hoarding, and introduces King Angaristha's question to the sage Kamandaka on how to undo sins.
shots.B12C122S01H03: Kamandaka says a king who pursues only pleasure loses his wisdom and virtue, and prescribes Vedic study, respect for Brahmanas, banishing wicked men, seeking the company of the good, and speaking kindly to all.

B12C123.summary: Yudhishthira asks how virtuous behaviour is acquired. Bhishma recounts how Duryodhana, grieved at Yudhishthira's splendour at Indraprastha, asked his father Dhritarashtra the same question, and Dhritarashtra answered that good conduct wins the earth. He then tells the tale of Prahlada, who lost his sovereignty to Indra when a Brahmana disciple drew away his conduct and with it righteousness, truth, good deeds, might and prosperity. Dhritarashtra concludes that abstaining from injury, compassion and charity build good conduct, and that wicked men who prosper do not keep their fortune long.

scenes.B12C123S01: Bhishma introduces the exchange between Duryodhana and Dhritarashtra, in which Duryodhana laments Yudhishthira's wealth and his father urges him toward good conduct.
scenes.B12C123S02: Duryodhana asks how such conduct is acquired, and Dhritarashtra tells the tale of Prahlada, who lost his sovereignty to Indra when his conduct and other virtues departed from him.
scenes.B12C123S03: The goddess Prosperity explains that Indra took Prahlada's sovereignty by taking his conduct, and Dhritarashtra then explains how conduct is built and urges Duryodhana to follow it.

shots.B12C123S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how virtuous behaviour is acquired and what its characteristics are.
shots.B12C123S01H02: Bhishma says that Duryodhana, grieved at Yudhishthira's splendour at Indraprastha and mocked for his own errors, asked his father Dhritarashtra the same question.
shots.B12C123S01H03: Dhritarashtra asks Duryodhana why he is pale and emaciated when he has wealth, obedient brothers, fine robes and fine food.
shots.B12C123S01H04: Duryodhana replies that thousands of Brahmanas eat daily from gold plates at Yudhishthira's palace, and that his enemy's splendour burns him.
shots.B12C123S01H05: Dhritarashtra says that good conduct can win any prosperity, and cites Mandhatri, Janamejaya and Nabhaga, who won the earth by virtue.
shots.B12C123S02H01: Duryodhana asks how that conduct, which won the earth so quickly, can be acquired.
shots.B12C123S02H02: Dhritarashtra tells how Prahlada took Indra's sovereignty through his conduct, and how Indra first asked Vrihaspati for the source of happiness.
shots.B12C123S02H03: Vrihaspati sends Indra to Usanas, who sends him to Prahlada, and Indra comes to Prahlada disguised as a Brahmana disciple.
shots.B12C123S02H04: Prahlada says he rules by following the counsel of Brahmanas and Sukra, serving elders, controlling wrath and bearing no malice, and that this is the best good for a man.
shots.B12C123S02H05: The disguised Brahmana asks Prahlada for his conduct as a boon, and Prahlada's Behaviour, Righteousness, Truth, Good deeds, Might and Prosperity leave him one by one.
shots.B12C123S03H01: The goddess Prosperity explains that the Brahmana was Indra, who took Prahlada's sovereignty by taking his conduct, and that all virtues rest on conduct.
shots.B12C123S03H02: Bhishma says the goddess and the others departed, and that Duryodhana then asked his father how conduct is acquired.
shots.B12C123S03H03: Dhritarashtra says conduct is built by abstaining from injury in act, thought and word, by compassion and giving, and that wicked men who prosper do not keep their fortune long.
shots.B12C123S03H04: Dhritarashtra urges Duryodhana to be of good conduct if he wants greater prosperity than Yudhishthira's.
shots.B12C123S03H05: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that Dhritarashtra spoke these words, and that he should act on them.

B12C124.summary: Yudhishthira asks what Hope is and where it comes from, lamenting that Duryodhana's obstinacy destroyed the hope he had cherished of peace. Bhishma introduces the discourse between Sumitra and Rishabha and tells how King Sumitra of the Haihayas chases a wounded deer far through forests and across rivers without giving up.

scenes.B12C124S01: Yudhishthira asks about the nature of Hope, and Bhishma introduces the tale of King Sumitra, who chases a wounded deer deep into the forest.

shots.B12C124S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what Hope is, where it arises, and laments that Duryodhana's obstinacy destroyed the hope he had cherished of peace.
shots.B12C124S01H02: Bhishma introduces the discourse between Sumitra and Rishabha, and tells how King Sumitra of the Haihayas chases a wounded deer through forests and across rivers, never giving up.

B12C125.summary: King Sumitra, worn out by the hunt, arrives at a hermitage, where the ascetics honour him and ask why he has come. He tells them he is of the Haihaya race, has lost his deer, and is left disappointed in his hope. He then asks which is vaster, hope or the firmament, and says he wishes to hear the answer only if it is proper for the sages to give it.

scenes.B12C125S01: Sumitra introduces himself to the ascetics at the hermitage, explains his loss and his disappointed hope, and asks which is vaster, hope or the sky.

shots.B12C125S01H01: Sumitra arrives at a hermitage weary and hungry, is honoured by the ascetics, and tells them of his family, his hunt, his lost deer and his disappointed hope, asking which is vaster, hope or the sky.

B12C126.summary: The sage Rishabha, asked by Sumitra, recalls meeting the emaciated sage Tanu near the hermitage of Nara and Narayana. There King Viradyumna came searching for his lost son Bhuridyumna and asked Tanu what is greater than hope. Tanu explains that Bhuridyumna had insulted a holy sage by refusing him a golden jar and vegetable bark, leaving the sage disappointed, and the sages gather around the king to ask what brought him there.

scenes.B12C126S01: Rishabha recounts his meeting with Tanu, who was approached by King Viradyumna searching for his lost son, and Tanu's first answer about a sage's disappointment, after which the sages question the king.

shots.B12C126S01H01: Rishabha recounts how, on pilgrimage, he met the emaciated sage Tanu near the hermitage of Nara and Narayana, and how King Viradyumna, searching for his lost son Bhuridyumna, asked Tanu what is greater than hope.
shots.B12C126S01H02: Tanu says Bhuridyumna insulted a holy sage by refusing him a golden jar and vegetable bark, and the king honours Tanu, after which the sages gather around him and ask why he has come.

B12C127.summary: King Viradyumna asks Tanu what is exceedingly hard to obtain, and Tanu says that hope is the most slender thing of all. He lists the hopes that are slenderer still, such as hope placed in a giver who never gives, or in a father who longs to see his lost son again. The king is moved, Tanu produces the lost prince and reveals himself as the god of righteousness, and Sumitra then casts off his own hope. Bhishma urges Yudhishthira to be calm and collected like Himavat.

scenes.B12C127S01: Viradyumna explains his search for his lost son, and Tanu, long slighted by the king, answers that hope is the most slender thing.
scenes.B12C127S02: Tanu lists the hopes that are slenderer than his own body, the king accepts his teaching, Tanu restores the prince and reveals himself, and Bhishma applies the lesson to Yudhishthira.

shots.B12C127S01H01: Viradyumna explains that he is a king whose only young son, Bhuridyumna, is lost, and that he is searching the forest for him.
shots.B12C127S01H02: Rishabha explains that Tanu, once slighted by the king, had resolved to drive hope from his mind, and so he remains silent.
shots.B12C127S01H03: Viradyumna asks what is the measure of hope's slenderness, and what is most difficult to acquire.
shots.B12C127S01H04: Rishabha says Tanu, recalling the king's past disregard, now speaks to him.
shots.B12C127S01H05: Tanu says nothing is as slender as hope, and that the images hope places before the mind are the hardest of all to win.
shots.B12C127S02H01: The king says he understands, and asks what is more slender than Tanu's own body.
shots.B12C127S02H02: Tanu names hopes more slender than his body, such as hope placed in a giver who never gives, in an ungrateful or cruel man, in a father longing for a lost son, in an old woman hoping for children, and in a maiden hoping for marriage.
shots.B12C127S02H03: The king asks for Tanu's grace, says his words are true, and wishes to be reunited with his child.
shots.B12C127S02H04: Tanu brings the prince to the spot, rebukes the king, reveals himself as the god of righteousness, and tells the king to drive off even the slenderest hope.
shots.B12C127S02H05: Bhishma says that Sumitra then gave up his hope, and urges Yudhishthira to be calm and collected like Himavat.

B12C128.summary: Yudhishthira says he is never satiated with Bhishma's teaching on morality. Bhishma tells of the sage Gotama, who spent sixty thousand years in austerity on the Paripatra hills and was visited by Yama, the regent of the dead. Gotama asks how one can clear the debt owed to one's parents and win pure regions of bliss, and Yama answers that devotion to truth, purity, penance and reverence for one's parents, together with generous horse-sacrifices, win many regions.

scenes.B12C128S01: Yudhishthira asks for more, and Bhishma tells of Gotama's meeting with Yama, in which Yama explains how to honour one's parents and win heaven.

shots.B12C128S01H01: Yudhishthira says he is never satiated with Bhishma's teaching on morality and asks him to discourse further.
shots.B12C128S01H02: Bhishma tells of the sage Gotama, who lived for sixty thousand years in austerity on the Paripatra hills, and of Yama's visit to him.
shots.B12C128S01H03: Gotama asks how one can free oneself from the debt owed to mother and father, and how to win pure and difficult regions of bliss.
shots.B12C128S01H04: Yama says one should devote oneself to truth, purity and penance, worship one's mother and father without ceasing, and perform horse-sacrifices with generous gifts to Brahmanas.

B12C129.summary: Yudhishthira asks what a weak king should do when he is surrounded by enemies and treacherous ministers, with an empty treasury and no army, and whether he should seek wealth by evil means or give up his life. Bhishma says the question is subtle and that a king in extreme distress may take wealth from anyone except ascetics and Brahmanas, since treasury, army and people depend on one another. He insists that the treasury should be filled by righteous means where possible, and warns that filling it by oppression leads to ruin.

scenes.B12C129S01: Yudhishthira poses a dilemma about a besieged, weak king, and Bhishma answers that in great distress a king may gather wealth from others, but that righteous means are better and that the treasury, army and people sustain one another.

shots.B12C129S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what a king should do when he has few friends, many enemies, an empty treasury, no troops and treacherous ministers, and whether he should seek wealth by evil means or die without it.
shots.B12C129S01H02: Bhishma says the question is subtle, that a king in extreme distress may take wealth from anyone but ascetics and Brahmanas, that treasury, army and people depend on one another, and that the treasury should be filled by righteous means, not by oppression.

B12C130.summary: Yudhishthira asks what a weak, besieged king should do when his land is lost, his treasury is empty and his councils have leaked. Bhishma advises peace with an honest invader, and giving up land or even the capital to a treacherous one to save his life. If peace fails, the king should fight bravely, because a warrior who dies in battle goes to heaven.

scenes.B12C130S01: Yudhishthira asks about a king in ruin, and Bhishma answers with advice on peace, retreat and courageous fighting.

shots.B12C130S01H02: Yudhishthira asks what a weak king should do when his lands are taken, his wealth is gone and his allies cannot be supported.
shots.B12C130S01H03: Bhishma says an honest invader should be met with peace and the lost land restored, while a treacherous one may be bought off with land or even the capital.
shots.B12C130S01H04: Yudhishthira asks what a king should do when his own people turn against him, his treasury is empty and his counsels are leaked.
shots.B12C130S01H05: Bhishma advises peace with a righteous enemy and bold fighting against a wicked one, and says even a small loyal army can win or die honourably.

B12C131.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a Brahmana can make a living when proper rule has collapsed, robbers control the means of life, and he cannot abandon his family. Bhishma says he should live by his learning, and that in hard times a king may take wealth from the wicked and give it to the good. Even then the king must not oppress priests or Brahmanas, and he should not believe slander.

scenes.B12C131S01: Yudhishthira's question about a Brahmana's livelihood in a time of disorder, and Bhishma's long answer on conduct in distress.

shots.B12C131S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a Brahmana should support his family when righteous rule has broken down and robbers hold the means of living.
shots.B12C131S01H02: Bhishma says the Brahmana should live by knowledge, and that a king may seize wealth from the wicked for the good without provoking revolt, though he must never oppress Brahmanas, must not believe slander, and should bear his burdens steadily.

B12C132.summary: Bhishma explains that a king must keep his treasury full, drawing on his own realm and his enemies' lands by a middle course. He argues that a weak king with an empty purse loses respect and power, so he must not bend before enemies. On robbers, he advises bringing them under control rather than destroying them outright, since those who exterminate them live in fear.

scenes.B12C132S01: Bhishma's advice on filling the treasury, keeping a firm hand on the kingdom, and handling robbers.

shots.B12C132S01H01: Bhishma says a king must keep his treasury full, since a king without wealth loses respect, and he must deal firmly with robbers by bringing them under his rule rather than destroying them.

B12C133.summary: Bhishma says a Kshatriya's clear duties are religious merit and wealth, and that endless debate about the unseen future should not stop him from them. He argues that power is the foundation of righteousness and that the powerful can do much that the weak cannot. He then lists the penances by which a man who has fallen into sin can cleanse himself and win back respect.

scenes.B12C133S01: Bhishma on a Kshatriya's duties, the primacy of power over abstract righteousness, and the penance for one who has sinned.

shots.B12C133S01H01: Bhishma says a Kshatriya should pursue merit and wealth and seek power, since power sustains righteousness, and he lists the penances that cleanse a sinner.

B12C134.summary: Bhishma tells the story of Kayavya, a robber of mixed birth who was devout, protected Brahmanas and ascetics, and cared for his blind parents. When thousands of robbers choose him as their leader, he sets rules: spare women, children, ascetics and Brahmanas, and plunder only where it is due. Bhishma says that robbers who keep these rules win a good afterlife, and that hearing the tale brings safety from fear.

scenes.B12C134S01: The story of the robber Kayavya, his election as leader, the rules he sets, and the lesson Bhishma draws from it.

shots.B12C134S01H01: Bhishma introduces Kayavya, a skilled and devout robber who honours Brahmanas and his blind parents, and whom many robbers then wish to make their leader.
shots.B12C134S01H02: The robbers ask Kayavya to lead them and protect them the way a father or mother would.
shots.B12C134S01H03: Kayavya lays down rules: never kill women or non-combatants, spare Brahmanas, keep truth, and tax only those who refuse their dues.
shots.B12C134S01H04: Bhishma says the robbers obeyed Kayavya, prospered by giving up sin, and that hearing his story brings freedom from fear.

B12C135.summary: Bhishma quotes verses attributed to Brahman on how a king should fill his treasury. The wealth of sacrificers and of the gods must not be taken, but wealth of those who neglect sacrifice may be taken for the army and for worship, and the king should pass it on to good people rather than hoard it. He ends by comparing moral questions to dust that grows finer the more it is ground.

scenes.B12C135S01: Bhishma quotes Brahman's verses on which wealth a king may take, and closes with a comparison about moral questions.

shots.B12C135S01H01: Bhishma quotes verses of Brahman that allow a king to take wealth from those who neglect sacrifice but protect the wealth of sacrificers and temples, and says that moral questions grow finer the more they are discussed.

B12C136.summary: Bhishma tells a fable of three Sakula fish in a lake that fishermen are draining. One fish sees the danger and leaves early, another escapes by biting the string when caught, and the slow one is caught and dies. Bhishma's lesson is that foresight and quick thinking bring success, procrastination brings ruin, and well-timed action gets the best results.

scenes.B12C136S01: Bhishma's fable of the three fish and the lesson on acting in time.

shots.B12C136S01H01: Bhishma tells how three fish face draining water: the far-sighted one leaves early, the quick-witted one escapes by feigning capture, and the slow one is caught and dies.
shots.B12C136S01H02: Bhishma draws the lesson that procrastinators are destroyed, that foresight and presence of mind bring happiness, and that acting with regard to time and place wins the best results.

B12C137.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a weak king surrounded by many foes should choose friends and enemies, and when to make war or peace. Bhishma answers with the fable of a mouse and a cat caught in the same hunter's net, in which the mouse makes a timely alliance with the cat, frees him, and then refuses his later offer of friendship. The moral is that alliances rest on self-interest, so a ruler should seem trusting while staying wary, and should act at the right time.

scenes.B12C137S01: Yudhishthira's question about a besieged king, and the fable of the mouse Palita and the cat Lomasa, which ends with the mouse rejecting the cat's offer of friendship.
scenes.B12C137S02: The cat, shamed, pleads for renewed friendship, and the mouse answers with advice to keep a steady distrust of everyone.

shots.B12C137S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a weak king under attack from many powerful foes can choose friends and enemies and decide when to fight or make peace.
shots.B12C137S01H02: Bhishma replies that friends can turn into foes and back, so a king should sometimes make peace with enemies, and he introduces the tale of a cat and a mouse under a banyan tree.
shots.B12C137S01H03: The mouse Palita lives beneath a banyan where the cat Lomasa hunts birds, and the cat is caught in a hunter's net; seeing a mongoose and an owl waiting for himself, the mouse decides to strike a deal with the cat.
shots.B12C137S01H04: The grateful cat agrees to serve the mouse and accept the alliance, and the mouse says he will cut the net if the cat spares his life.
shots.B12C137S01H05: The mouse cuts the net slowly, then flees when the hunter arrives, and when the cat later asks for friendship the mouse refuses, arguing that all bonds rest on self-interest.
shots.B12C137S02H01: The cat, rebuked, is ashamed and speaks up.
shots.B12C137S02H02: The cat protests his loyalty and asks the mouse to renew their friendship, but the mouse refuses, advises constant mistrust, and slips into another hole.
shots.B12C137S02H03: Bhishma draws the morals: appear fearless while distrusting others, make peace with foes when it suits, and honour Brahmanas, and he urges Yudhishthira to act with the same wisdom.

B12C138.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a king can rule if he trusts no one, and Bhishma answers with the tale of the bird Pujani and King Brahmadatta. After the prince kills her chick, Pujani blinds him in revenge, and the two then argue over whether an injury can ever be forgiven. Brahmadatta appeals to Time and to reconciliation, while Pujani holds that enmity between injurer and injured never truly ends, so she leaves; the tale closes with advice that a king should protect his subjects and never provoke a stronger foe.

scenes.B12C138S01: Yudhishthira's doubt about mistrust, and the story of the prince who kills Pujani's chick and her revenge on him, which ends with an argument over whether the score is settled.
scenes.B12C138S02: The two argue over whether a wronged party can ever trust the one who wronged them, and whether living together softens hostility.
scenes.B12C138S03: Brahmadatta blames Time for all acts, Pujani answers with a long case for exertion and good rule, and she takes her leave.

shots.B12C138S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a king can rule and fight his foes if he may trust no one.
shots.B12C138S01H02: Bhishma introduces the bird Pujani, who lived at King Brahmadatta's palace and fed her chick and the prince on fruit, until the prince killed her chick and she blinded him in revenge.
shots.B12C138S01H03: Brahmadatta says the injury has been repaid and the account is squared, and he asks Pujani to stay.
shots.B12C138S01H04: Pujani says that a wrongdoer should leave the wronged party, that soothing words should not be trusted, and that enmity passes down to descendants.
shots.B12C138S01H05: Brahmadatta insists that avenging an injury is no offence and again asks her to stay.
shots.B12C138S02H01: Pujani says that friendship cannot be rebuilt once one side has injured the other and the other has struck back.
shots.B12C138S02H02: Brahmadatta argues that injurer and avenger should unite, since mutual hatred has been seen to cool that way.
shots.B12C138S02H03: Pujani replies that enmity never dies, and that insincere conciliation can subdue even the strong.
shots.B12C138S02H04: Brahmadatta says that living together softens hostility, citing the Chandala and the dog, and that animosity fades quickly.
shots.B12C138S02H05: Pujani lists five causes of hostility, says the fire of enmity burns until one party is destroyed, and says she cannot trust him again.
shots.B12C138S03H01: Brahmadatta says Time causes all acts and deaths, so no one is truly to blame, and he asks her to forgive and stay.
shots.B12C138S03H02: Pujani challenges his view by asking why people avenge, why physicians treat the sick and why rites matter if Time rules all, then describes the miseries of life and warns against trusting a wronged foe.
shots.B12C138S03H03: Brahmadatta replies that withholding trust wins no object and that fear makes a man as good as dead.
shots.B12C138S03H04: Pujani argues that exertion matters more than fate, lists the marks of wisdom, and says she will leave a bad king's realm; she then describes a just king who protects his subjects and a tyrant who brings ruin on himself.
shots.B12C138S03H05: Bhishma closes that Pujani has taken her leave and gone away, and asks Yudhishthira what else he would like to hear.

B12C139.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a king should act when righteousness and people have declined and robbers plague the land. Bhishma tells how Satrunjaya, king of the Sauviras, asked the sage Bharadwaja how to gain, grow, guard and use wealth. Bharadwaja replies that a ruler must rely on firm punishment, cut the roots of his foes, and mix sternness, mildness and deceit as the moment requires, and the king prospers by following this advice.
