shots.B12C261S01H02: Jajali asks how a seller of scents and herbs has gained such firm understanding and where his knowledge came from.
shots.B12C261S01H03: Bhishma introduces Tuladhara, a Vaisya, who explains the ways of morality to the ascetic Jajali.
shots.B12C261S01H04: Tuladhara explains that morality is universal friendliness and harmlessness, describes his honest trade and even-minded way of living, argues that harmlessness is the highest duty, criticizes cruel treatment of animals and people, retells how Nahusha's sin was spread among creatures, and says he treats his praisers and his injurers alike.

B12C262.summary: Jajali objects that Tuladhara's doctrine of harmlessness would end farming, food, and sacrifice, and so end the world. Tuladhara replies that he does not reject sacrifice, only the greedy and violent kinds, and that offerings made with faith and without desire of fruit lead to Brahma. He says harmless offerings of plants, herbs and clarified butter are proper, and that the Soul is itself a sacred place. Bhishma says the wise applauded these duties.

scenes.B12C262S01: Jajali objects to Tuladhara's teaching, Tuladhara explains that sacrifice should be done with faith and without animal slaughter, and Jajali asks for more, which Tuladhara gives before Bhishma closes the passage.

shots.B12C262S01H01: Jajali objects that Tuladhara's doctrine would close heaven, end farming and food, and bring sacrifice to an end.
shots.B12C262S01H02: Tuladhara replies that he does not reject sacrifice, only greedy and violent ritual, and says sacrifices made with faith and without desire of fruit lead to Brahma. He allows that a man of cleansed soul may even offer a cow, but tells others to offer plants and herbs.
shots.B12C262S01H03: Jajali says he has never heard these teachings of the mental sacrifice before and asks Tuladhara to explain them.
shots.B12C262S01H04: Tuladhara says faithless sacrifices are not true sacrifices, names clarified butter and a rice-ball as proper offerings, and says the Soul is a sacred place, so there is no need to wander to holy sites.
shots.B12C262S01H05: Bhishma says Tuladhara's duties were applauded because they agree with reason and are kept by the good and wise.

B12C263.summary: Tuladhara asks Jajali to call back the birds that once nested on his head, to see who truly follows the duty of harmlessness. The birds answer that acts done without harm bring good results, while acts that injure others destroy faith. Bhishma says Tuladhara and Jajali both went on to heaven, and that Jajali became calm after hearing these teachings.

scenes.B12C263S01: Tuladhara asks Jajali to summon the birds, the birds speak about faith and harmless acts, and Bhishma reports that Tuladhara and Jajali both went to heaven.

shots.B12C263S01H01: Tuladhara asks Jajali to watch the birds that once nested on his head, now flying home, and to call them to show who truly follows the path of duty.
shots.B12C263S01H02: The birds answer that harmless acts bring benefit both here and hereafter, that acts that hurt others destroy faith, and that faith and self-restraint make sacrifice fruitful. They end by praising faith and urging Jajali to follow his own path with faith.
shots.B12C263S01H03: Bhishma says Tuladhara and Jajali both went to heaven, and that Jajali, having heard these teachings, grew calm. He asks Yudhishthira what other truths he wants to hear.

B12C264.summary: Bhishma tells of King Vichakhy, who pitied the animals at a cow-slaughter sacrifice and blessed the kine. Vichakhy condemns animal slaughter in sacrifice, saying harmlessness is the highest duty and that only the greedy or foolish praise it. Yudhishthira asks how a man who avoids all harm can keep his body alive, and Bhishma says one should acquire merit so the body does not suffer and death does not come early.

scenes.B12C264S01: Bhishma recounts King Vichakhy's protest at a sacrifice of slaughter, and Yudhishthira asks how a man who avoids harm can keep his body, with Bhishma's short reply.

shots.B12C264S01H01: Bhishma tells of King Vichakhy, who saw a bull mangled and heard the cries of kine at a cow-slaughter sacrifice, and blessed all kine, condemning animal sacrifice and calling harmlessness the highest duty.
shots.B12C264S01H02: Yudhishthira asks how a man who wants to do no harm can keep his body alive when the body and dangers are always at odds.
shots.B12C264S01H03: Bhishma says one should gain merit where one can, so the body does not languish and death does not come early.

B12C265.summary: Yudhishthira asks whether a hard duty should be judged quickly or after delay. Bhishma tells of Chirakarin, son of Gautama, who was ordered in anger to kill his mother and who took a long time to decide, weighing the duty to his father against the duty to his mother. When Gautama returned and repented, he learned that Indra had tempted the wife, so she was innocent, and he praised his son for his delay. The chapter closes with the lesson that one should reflect long before acting, especially when violence is at stake.

scenes.B12C265S01: Yudhishthira asks how to judge hard acts, and Bhishma tells the story of Chirakarin, whose long deliberation saved his mother, ending with Gautama's praise of reflection.

shots.B12C265S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how a person should judge hard acts he is bound to do or to refrain from, and whether such judgment should be quick or slow.
shots.B12C265S01H02: Bhishma tells the story of Chirakarin, nicknamed for his long reflection, who was ordered by his father to kill his mother and deliberated for a long time, then concluded that she was innocent and that the father should be obeyed as well. When Gautama returned, he repented, told how Indra had come in disguise, and praised his son for his delay. The chapter closes with verses praising long reflection before acting on anger or violence.

B12C266.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a king can protect his subjects without harming anyone. Bhishma tells of the debate between King Dyumatsena and his son Satyavat, where Satyavat says killing can never be righteous and Dyumatsena argues that unpunished crime would destroy all distinctions. Satyavat proposes that Brahmanas guide the other orders, that offenders be punished gently, and that killing be avoided. Dyumatsena answers that punishment has grown harsher as righteousness has declined through the ages, and the chapter ends with Satyavat's advice on the ages and the role of Manu.

scenes.B12C266S01: Yudhishthira asks how a king can protect subjects without harm, and Bhishma recounts the debate between Dyumatsena and Satyavat about capital punishment, mercy, and the ages.

shots.B12C266S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a king can protect his subjects without harming anyone.
shots.B12C266S01H02: Bhishma recounts the case of Dyumatsena and his son Satyavat, where prisoners were led out for execution, and Satyavat declared that killing can never be a righteous act.
shots.B12C266S01H03: Dyumatsena argues that sparing the guilty would blur right and wrong and bring about a breakdown of the world, and asks Satyavat to explain how society could go on without punishment.
shots.B12C266S01H04: Satyavat proposes that Brahmanas guide the other orders and that offenders be corrected gently and not killed, and Dyumatsena answers that punishment has grown harsher as men have declined from the earlier ages.
shots.B12C266S01H05: Satyavat advises that sacrifice and a king's good example can restrain wrongdoers, and recounts that Manu and the Creator set out how punishment should change as righteousness fades from age to age.

B12C267.summary: Yudhishthira asks which is better, the duties of the householder or the duties of yoga, since both lead to the same end. Bhishma tells the story of the sage Kapila, who protests when King Nahusha is about to kill a cow for a guest. A sage named Syumarasmi, speaking through the cow, argues that the Vedas authorise sacrifice with animals and that sacrifice upholds the world. The passage ends with the claim that those who do not sacrifice have neither this world nor the next.

scenes.B12C267S01: Yudhishthira asks which path is higher, Bhishma tells of Kapila and the cow, and the cow's voice, speaking for Syumarasmi, defends sacrifice and the authority of the Vedas.

shots.B12C267S01H01: Yudhishthira asks which is superior, the duties of the householder or the duties of yoga, since both lead to enjoyment and liberation.
shots.B12C267S01H02: Bhishma says both paths are good, and tells how King Nahusha was about to slaughter a cow for a guest, and how the sage Kapila cried out in dismay at the sight.
shots.B12C267S01H03: Kapila says he does not blame the Vedas, that all four stages of life lead to the same end, and asks whether there is a higher duty than harmlessness.
shots.B12C267S01H04: The cow, speaking through the sage Syumarasmi, defends sacrifice as the root of the world. It names the animals and offerings used, says sacrifice must be done without desire for reward, and states that those who do not sacrifice have neither this world nor the next.

B12C268.summary: Kapila argues that ascetics who renounce action reach Brahma and so have no need of household life. Syumarasmi answers that the householder supports every other stage of life, and that Vedic rites are needed for the dead and for sacrifice. Kapila then describes the self-control of the four doors of the body, and Syumarasmi asks how the Vedas can both urge and forbid acts. Syumarasmi finally asks to be taught about Emancipation, and Kapila says that knowledge of the one Soul is the way across the river of life.

scenes.B12C268S01: Kapila praises renunciation and Syumarasmi defends the householder life, with Kapila describing self-control of the four doors and Syumarasmi asking how the Vedas can both urge and forbid acts.
scenes.B12C268S02: Syumarasmi introduces himself and asks what visible fruit the yogis gain, Kapila explains that knowledge and self-control lead to liberation, and Syumarasmi asks to be taught about Emancipation.

shots.B12C268S01H01: Kapila says the Yatis gain Brahma through knowledge and self-restraint, so the householder's duties are not needed by those who have reached that end.
shots.B12C268S01H02: Syumarasmi argues that the householder life supports all the other stages, and that Vedic rites and mantras are needed for births, deaths, and offerings to the Pitris.
shots.B12C268S01H03: Kapila says that the sacrifices are difficult and their fruits are temporary, and he describes the four doors of the body and how self-control should guard speech, food, sexual conduct and anger.
shots.B12C268S01H04: Syumarasmi asks how the Vedas can both enjoin and forbid acts, and why renunciation is praised if acts are necessary.
shots.B12C268S01H05: Kapila asks what visible results come from the acts that men of action pursue, compared with the yogi's path.
shots.B12C268S02H01: Syumarasmi introduces himself as a seeker of knowledge, says he knows the Vedas and the logic that explains them, and asks what visible fruit yoga gives, as no one is free from grief or desire.
shots.B12C268S02H02: Kapila says that knowledge helps people cross the river of life and death, and warns that proud men who lack understanding fall into the darkness of tamas and its vices.
shots.B12C268S02H03: Syumarasmi agrees the scriptures teach that equity is right and grief follows unrighteousness, says that few can renounce action, and asks Kapila to teach him about Emancipation without delay.

B12C269.summary: Kapila says the Vedas are authoritative, and that rites purify the body so a twice-born man can receive knowledge of Brahma. He recalls men of old, such as King Janaka and the Brahmana Yajnavalkya, who lived by duty, were free from expiation, and attained Brahma. Syumarasmi asks who reaches the highest place in heaven, and Kapila replies that householders are blessed but cannot enjoy the joy of renunciation. Kapila ends by saying that acts only cleanse the body, while knowledge is the highest end.

scenes.B12C269S01: Kapila praises the purity and self-discipline of men of old and describes renunciation as the highest end, and Syumarasmi and Kapila then debate whether householders or renouncers reach the higher place.

shots.B12C269S01H01: Kapila says the Vedas are authoritative, rites cleanse the body so the twice-born can receive knowledge of Brahma, and men of old who lived by duty and self-discipline never needed expiation.
shots.B12C269S01H02: Syumarasmi asks which people, among those who give gifts, study, or renounce after enjoying wealth, reach the highest place in heaven.
shots.B12C269S01H03: Kapila says householders are auspicious and gain many blessings, but cannot enjoy the happiness that comes with renunciation.
shots.B12C269S01H04: Syumarasmi says both paths depend on a means, knowledge for renunciation and acts for householders, but both aim at Emancipation, so he asks for the truth about their relative worth.
shots.B12C269S01H05: Kapila says acts only cleanse the body, knowledge is the highest end, and he lists the qualities such as forgiveness, truthfulness and renunciation that lead to Brahma.

B12C270.summary: Yudhishthira asks which of religion, profit and pleasure is the highest, and Bhishma tells of a poor Brahmana who prayed to the cloud Kundadhara for wealth. Kundadhara asks the gods to make the Brahmana virtuous instead, and they grant it. The Brahmana goes to the forest, gains spiritual power, and boasts that his word can bestow kingdoms, so Kundadhara shows him kings suffering in hell. Kundadhara rebukes his greed, the Brahmana repents and is forgiven, and the story teaches that virtue brings more lasting happiness than wealth.

scenes.B12C270S01: Bhishma tells how a poor Brahmana sought wealth from the cloud Kundadhara, how the gods granted him virtue instead, and how he rose to spiritual power and was shown kings in hell.
scenes.B12C270S02: Kundadhara rebukes the Brahmana for his greed and points out the vices that enchain men, and the Brahmana repents and is forgiven, with the lesson that virtue outweighs wealth.

shots.B12C270S01H01: Yudhishthira asks which of religion, profit, and pleasure is the highest aim.
shots.B12C270S01H02: Bhishma begins the story of a poor Brahmana who wanted wealth for sacrifice, and who prayed to the cloud Kundadhara after his penances failed.
shots.B12C270S01H03: Kundadhara grants the Brahmana his prayer for virtue rather than wealth, and the gods agree, while the Brahmana cares nothing for costly cloth.
shots.B12C270S01H04: The Brahmana resolves that if no one values good deeds, he will go to the forest and live righteously.
shots.B12C270S01H05: The Brahmana does great penances, gains spiritual vision, and boasts that his word can bestow sovereignty, so Kundadhara shows him kings sunk in hell.
shots.B12C270S02H01: Kundadhara rebukes the Brahmana for his greed and asks him to look at the carnal desires that shut men out of heaven.
shots.B12C270S02H02: Bhishma says the Brahmana then sees many men enslaved by lust, wrath, greed, fear, pride, sleep, procrastination and idleness.
shots.B12C270S02H03: Kundadhara explains that these vices enchain men, that no one becomes virtuous without the gods' leave, and that the Brahmana's power comes from virtue.
shots.B12C270S02H04: The Brahmana bows and repents, Kundadhara forgives him and disappears, and Bhishma concludes that virtue, not wealth, brings the greater happiness.

B12C271.summary: Yudhishthira asks which sacrifice is performed for virtue alone, not for heaven or wealth. Bhishma passes on Narada's story of Satya, a Brahmana who lived on gleanings and worshipped Vishnu, and of his wife Pushkaradharini, who disapproved of his cruel rites. When a deer asks to be sacrificed, Satya is tempted to slay it, but Dharma, who had taken the form of a deer, stops him, saying that killing is no part of sacrifice. Narada concludes that abstaining from injury brings the fullest reward.

scenes.B12C271S01: Yudhishthira asks which sacrifice is for virtue alone, and Bhishma passes on Narada's story of Satya, the deer, and Dharma, which ends with the teaching that harmlessness is the highest religion.

shots.B12C271S01H01: Yudhishthira asks which sacrifice is ordained for virtue alone, not for heaven or wealth.
shots.B12C271S01H02: Bhishma says he will relate the story Narada once told of a Brahmana who lived on gleanings and performed sacrifices.
shots.B12C271S01H03: Narada tells of the Brahmana Satya and his wife Pushkaradharini, who disapproves of his cruel rites. A deer asks to be sacrificed, the goddess Savitri urges Satya to do what the deer asks, but he refuses, and when the deer presses him Satya is tempted to slay the deer until Dharma, who had taken the deer's form, stops him, saying killing is no part of sacrifice. Narada closes by saying that abstaining from injury is the religion with the fullest reward.

B12C272.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a man becomes sinful or virtuous, and how he reaches renunciation and liberation. Bhishma explains that desire follows the senses, that attachment and greed then lead to hypocrisy and sin, and that the righteous man, guided by the wise, turns to virtue and knowledge. Such a man eventually gives up even the rewards of virtue and reaches liberation.

scenes.B12C272S01: Yudhishthira asks how sin, virtue, renunciation and liberation come about, and Bhishma traces the path of the sinful man and the righteous man, ending with an exhortation to adhere to virtue.

shots.B12C272S01H01: Yudhishthira asks by what means a man becomes sinful or virtuous, and how he attains renunciation and liberation.
shots.B12C272S01H02: Bhishma says desire follows the senses, then attachment and greed lead to hypocrisy and sin, while the righteous man turns to knowledge, gives up even the rewards of virtue, and reaches liberation, and he ends by urging Yudhishthira to hold to virtue.

B12C273.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for the means by which liberation is won. Bhishma says there is only one path to liberation, and lists the remedies that go with it: forgiveness against anger, patience against lust, study against error, and contentment against greed. He says the soul must finally be controlled by the soul, and that giving up desire in speech, body and mind is the path of liberation.

scenes.B12C273S01: Yudhishthira asks for the means to liberation, and Bhishma gives the single path, with its remedies for anger, desire, fear, greed and ignorance, and the control of the soul by the soul.

shots.B12C273S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the means by which liberation is won.
shots.B12C273S01H02: Bhishma praises the question and gives the single path to liberation, with remedies for each fault: forgiveness against anger, patience against desire, knowledge against ignorance, contentment against greed, and self-control against sleep and fear, ending with the restraint of speech, body and mind without desire.

B12C274.summary: Narada asks the sage Asita-Devala how the universe was created and how it is destroyed. Asita names five primal essences, water, space, earth, wind and heat, with Time as the sixth, and says that these together with ignorance and past acts cause creation and destruction. He describes the senses, the mind and understanding, sleep and dreams, and the Jiva that passes from body to body until knowledge frees it to reach Brahma.

scenes.B12C274S01: Narada asks about creation and destruction, and Asita-Devala answers with the five essences, the organs of knowledge and action, the states of sleep and dream, and the migration of the Jiva to Brahma.

shots.B12C274S01H01: Bhishma introduces the talk between Narada and the sage Asita-Devala, who sat at ease, when Narada asked him about the origin and dissolution of creatures.
shots.B12C274S01H02: Narada asks where the universe came from and where it all goes at the great dissolution.
shots.B12C274S01H03: Asita names the five essences, adds Time, Ignorance and past acts as causes, and describes how the senses, mind and understanding work, how sleep and dreams arise, and how the Jiva migrates until knowledge frees it to reach Brahma.

B12C275.summary: Yudhishthira laments that he and his people have killed kin and friends in pursuit of wealth, and asks how to end this thirst. Bhishma tells of the king of Videha, who has nothing yet is happy because he does not cling to possessions, and who advises that desire grows like a cow's horns and that giving it up brings the highest happiness. The sage Mandavya is pleased with this teaching and turns to the path of liberation.

scenes.B12C275S01: Yudhishthira laments the killing and asks how to end greed, and Bhishma tells of the king of Videha's teaching to the sage Mandavya, who turns to liberation.

shots.B12C275S01H01: Yudhishthira laments that he and his people have killed brothers, kin, friends and sons in their thirst for wealth, and asks how that thirst can be ended.
shots.B12C275S01H02: Bhishma tells of the king of Videha, who says he has nothing yet lives happily, that desire grows as wealth grows, and that giving up desire brings the highest happiness, and Mandavya, pleased, turns to liberation.

B12C276.summary: Yudhishthira asks what good a man should seek while time runs swiftly. Bhishma tells of a learned son, Medhavin, who asks his Vedic father what to do, and the father advises study, household life, sacrifice, and then forest life. The son answers that Death and old age are always near, so one should practise truth, give up desire, and seek inner knowledge rather than offspring or ritual killing. The father follows the son's advice, and Bhishma urges Yudhishthira to do the same.

scenes.B12C276S01: Yudhishthira asks what good to seek, and Bhishma tells how the learned son Medhavin asks his father what to do, and the father gives the conventional four-stage advice.
scenes.B12C276S02: The son answers that Death and decrepitude are always near, urges truth, sacrifice of the self, and renunciation, and the father follows him.

shots.B12C276S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what good he should seek, since time is running swiftly and brings terror to all creatures.
shots.B12C276S01H02: Bhishma introduces the story of Medhavin, a learned son of a Vedic father, who asks his father how to use his short life.
shots.B12C276S01H03: Medhavin asks what a wise man should do while life runs quickly, so that he may pursue virtue under his father's guidance.
shots.B12C276S01H04: The father advises study of the Vedas, household life with offspring to rescue his ancestors, sacrifice, and then life in the forest as a sage.
shots.B12C276S01H05: The son asks how his father can speak so calmly when the world is under siege by such bolts of time.
shots.B12C276S02H01: The father asks what besieges the world and what the falling bolts are, and whether his son is trying to frighten him.
shots.B12C276S02H02: The son answers that Death and decrepitude beset the world, that day and night wear away life, and that Death takes everyone without warning, so virtue should be practised now. He urges truth, a sacrifice of the self in place of ritual killing, and renunciation, and asks how his father can rest at ease.
shots.B12C276S02H03: Bhishma says the father acted as his son advised, and urges Yudhishthira to do the same, devoted to truth.

B12C277.summary: Yudhishthira asks what conduct, knowledge and practice lead to Brahma. Bhishma describes the renouncer who is frugal, calm, and free from attachment, who does no harm, who does not speak ill of others, and who begs only what he needs. He lives alone in quiet places, takes praise and blame alike, and wanders without a home. Bhishma says the sage Harita taught this path, which leads to bright and lasting regions.

scenes.B12C277S01: Yudhishthira asks which conduct leads to Brahma, and Bhishma describes the life of the renouncer and the path that the sage Harita taught.

shots.B12C277S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what conduct, knowledge and devotion lead to the unchanging place of Brahma beyond Prakriti.
shots.B12C277S01H02: Bhishma describes the renouncer's life of frugality, self-control, harmlessness, and detachment, from begging and dwelling to food, praise and blame, and ends by saying the sage Harita taught this path to lasting bright regions.

B12C278.summary: Yudhishthira laments that even kings born of the gods suffer, and asks when he can renounce. Bhishma replies that nothing lasts, that rebirth has an end, and that the soul is darkened by ignorance until knowledge removes it. He then tells how the Daitya Vritra, deprived of his kingdom, showed no grief and spoke of the cycle of rebirth, and asked the preceptor Usanas how to reach high Brahma. The chapter ends by pointing to Usanas's answer, which Bhishma is about to recount.

scenes.B12C278S01: Yudhishthira laments his sorrow and asks when he will renounce, Bhishma says nothing is permanent and explains ignorance, and Vritra speaks to his preceptor Usanas about rebirth and asks how to reach Brahma.

shots.B12C278S01H01: Yudhishthira says that he and his brothers, though born of the gods, have endured much sorrow, and asks when he can give up sovereignty for renunciation.
shots.B12C278S01H02: Bhishma says everything has an end, even rebirth, that the soul is clouded by ignorance and desire, and introduces Vritra, who after his defeat was unmoved by grief, and whom his preceptor Usanas questions.
shots.B12C278S01H03: Vritra says he understands the coming and going of creatures, who sink into hell or rise to heaven and are reborn according to their acts, and Usanas calls his words foolish.
shots.B12C278S01H04: Vritra recalls his old penances and his battle with Indra, where he saw Narayana, and asks Usanas how high prosperity arises, how it falls away, and how a creature can attain eternal Brahma.
shots.B12C278S01H05: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira and his brothers to listen as he recounts what the sage Usanas said in reply to the Danava prince.

B12C279.summary: The sage Sanatkumara comes to Usanas and Vritra and teaches them the greatness of Vishnu, saying that the universe rests in him and that he is reached by restraint of the senses and purification of the heart. He describes the cycles of creation, the colours of beings that follow from the three qualities, and the stages by which a soul moves through rebirths until it attains Brahma. Vritra is comforted and gives up his life-breath in yoga, and Yudhishthira then asks whether Krishna is that same Lord, which Bhishma affirms and ends by reassuring the Pandavas.

scenes.B12C279S01: Usanas and Vritra hear Sanatkumara's long teaching on Vishnu's greatness, the cycles of creation and the stages of the soul, and Vritra's peaceful death in yoga.
scenes.B12C279S02: Yudhishthira asks whether Krishna is the Lord Sanatkumara described, Bhishma identifies Kesava as a portion of the Supreme, and he reassures the Pandavas about their future.

shots.B12C279S01H01: Usanas bows to the Lord who holds the earth and sky, and promises to speak of the greatness of Vishnu, whose head is the place of final liberation.
shots.B12C279S01H02: Sanatkumara arrives, is honoured, and at Usanas's request begins to teach Vritra about Vishnu's greatness.
shots.B12C279S01H03: Sanatkumara says the universe rests on Vishnu, who creates and withdraws all things, and that he is reached through restraint of the senses. He describes purification through many lives, the cycles of creation, the six colours that come from the three qualities, and the stages by which a soul rises and falls until it reaches Brahma.
shots.B12C279S01H04: Vritra says the teaching agrees with the truth, that his sorrow and sin are gone, and that Vishnu, who is the Supreme Soul, holds the universe.
shots.B12C279S01H05: Bhishma says Vritra then gave up his breath, joining his soul to the Supreme Soul in yoga, and so reached the highest state.
shots.B12C279S02H01: Yudhishthira asks whether Janardana (Krishna) is the illustrious Lord that Sanatkumara spoke of to Vritra.
shots.B12C279S02H02: Bhishma says the highest Deity creates all things, and that Kesava is a portion of that Supreme Lord, who is the Creator of pure soul and rests in the waters at universal dissolution.
shots.B12C279S02H03: Yudhishthira says Vritra must have foreseen his end and so was not grieved, and he asks whether he and his brothers will reach a white, pure state or a lower one.
shots.B12C279S02H04: Bhishma tells the Pandavas that they are born of a pure race and will rise to the gods' regions, then be numbered among the Siddhas, and urges them to have no fear.

B12C280.summary: Yudhishthira asks how Vritra, a devoted and learned Asura, could be defeated by Indra. Bhishma describes the great battle, in which the huge Vritra overwhelms Indra with rocks and illusions, and Indra is stupefied until the sage Vasishtha revives him. Mahadeva sends a fever into Vritra, Vishnu enters Indra's thunderbolt, and Indra vows to slay the Asura. The Asuras lose their memory and their illusions vanish, and Indra's appearance is so awe-inspiring that no one can look at it.

scenes.B12C280S01: Yudhishthira asks how Vritra was defeated, Bhishma describes the battle, Vasishtha revives Indra, and Mahadeva and Vishnu give their help to Indra.
scenes.B12C280S02: Indra vows to slay Vritra, the Asuras are confused by Mahadeva's fever, and Indra's form on his car is so awe-inspiring that no one can look at it.

shots.B12C280S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how the devoted and learned Vritra could be overcome by Indra, and asks for an account of the battle.
shots.B12C280S01H02: Bhishma describes Vritra's huge size and fearsome look, the terror of Indra's army, and the battle, in which Vritra's rocks and illusions stupefy Indra until Vasishtha restores him.
shots.B12C280S01H03: Vasishtha urges Indra not to yield to weakness, reminding him that the gods, Vishnu, and Siva are watching, and to slay his foe.
shots.B12C280S01H04: Indra is strengthened and uses yoga to dispel Vritra's illusions. Mahadeva's energy becomes a fever in Vritra's body, and Vishnu enters Indra's thunderbolt at the urging of the sages.
shots.B12C280S01H05: Mahesvara tells Indra that Vritra is hard to defeat, that Brahman granted him great powers after long penances, and that he should now slay him with the thunderbolt.
shots.B12C280S02H01: Indra vows to slay the son of Diti with his thunderbolt before the eyes of the god who gave him strength.
shots.B12C280S02H02: Bhishma says the Asuras lose their memory and their illusions vanish, the gods and sages rejoice, and Indra's form on his car is so awe-inspiring that no one can look at it.

B12C281.summary: Bhishma describes Vritra's fever and death at Indra's thunderbolt, and the sin of Brahmanicide, a fierce woman, which comes out of Vritra and seizes Indra. Brahma divides that sin among Agni, the trees and herbs, the Apsaras and the Waters, each with a condition on how it may pass to men. Indra is cleansed by a horse sacrifice, and Bhishma says the cocks born of Vritra's blood are unclean food for the twice-born, and that reciting this tale on Parva days removes sin.

scenes.B12C281S01: Vritra's fever and death at Indra's thunderbolt, the sin of Brahmanicide seizing Indra, and Brahma's search for a way to free him.
scenes.B12C281S02: Brahma gives Agni, the trees and herbs, and the Apsaras each a portion of the sin, with a condition for each.
scenes.B12C281S03: Brahma gives the Waters a portion of the sin, with a condition on how it passes to men.
scenes.B12C281S04: Indra is cleansed by a horse sacrifice, the origin of the unclean cocks is explained, and Bhishma says the tale brings freedom from sin.

shots.B12C281S01H01: Bhishma describes Vritra's symptoms under the fever, then Indra's thunderbolt kills him, and the sin of Brahmanicide, a fierce woman, comes out of his body and seizes Indra, who then hides in a lotus stalk.
shots.B12C281S01H02: Brahmanicide, seeing Brahma pleased, asks only for a dwelling place once she leaves Indra.
shots.B12C281S01H03: Brahma agrees, and calls on Agni, who appears and asks what he should do.
shots.B12C281S01H04: Brahma says he will divide the sin and asks Agni to take a fourth part of it to free Indra.
shots.B12C281S01H05: Agni asks how he himself will be freed from the sin.
shots.B12C281S02H01: Brahma tells Agni that the sin will pass to any man who, in a dull mood, refuses to make offerings to him.
shots.B12C281S02H02: Agni accepts, and Brahma summons the trees, herbs and grasses, who ask how they can be freed from the sin.
shots.B12C281S02H03: Brahma tells the trees that the sin will pass to any man who cuts or tears them on Parva days.
shots.B12C281S02H04: Brahma summons the Apsaras and asks them to take a portion of the sin for Indra's sake.
shots.B12C281S02H05: The Apsaras agree but ask how they will be freed from the bargain.
shots.B12C281S03H01: Brahma says the sin will leave them and pass to any man who has intercourse with women during their menstrual time.
shots.B12C281S03H02: The Waters come to Brahma at his summons and ask what he wants.
shots.B12C281S03H03: Brahma gives the Waters a fourth part of the sin, which came upon Indra after he slew Vritra.
shots.B12C281S03H04: The Waters ask how they may be freed, and say that Brahma is their only refuge.
shots.B12C281S03H05: Brahma says the sin will pass to any man who fouls the waters with phlegm, urine and dung.
shots.B12C281S04H01: Bhishma says Brahmanicide left Indra, who performed a horse sacrifice and was cleansed, that the cocks born of Vritra's blood are unclean food for the twice-born, and that reciting this tale on Parva days removes sin.

B12C282.summary: Yudhishthira asks how the fever arose before Vritra was slain. Bhishma tells how Mahadeva sat on Mount Meru with a great court, and how the god Daksha held a horse sacrifice without giving Mahadeva a share. Uma is grieved, and Mahadeva sends his followers to wreck the sacrifice, and a fierce being born from his sweat burns it. Brahma makes peace, Mahadeva accepts a share, and Fever is spread among many creatures. Bhishma adds that Vritra was first struck by Fever, and that reading this tale brings freedom from disease.

scenes.B12C282S01: Yudhishthira asks where Fever came from, and Bhishma describes Mahadeva's court on Mount Meru, Daksha's sacrifice, and Uma's question about why Mahadeva does not attend.
scenes.B12C282S02: Mahadeva explains that he has no share of the sacrifices, Uma grieves, Mahadeva's followers destroy the sacrifice, Brahma makes peace, and Fever is spread among creatures, with Bhishma's closing words.

shots.B12C282S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how Fever arose, since Vritra was first stupefied by Fever and then slain by Indra's thunderbolt.
shots.B12C282S01H02: Bhishma describes Mount Savitri on Meru and Mahadeva seated there with Uma, attended by the gods, sages, Ganga, and the followers of Nandi.
shots.B12C282S01H03: Daksha begins a sacrifice, the gods set out for it, and Uma asks Mahadeva why they are going.
shots.B12C282S01H04: Mahadeva says that Daksha is holding a horse sacrifice and that the gods are going to it.
shots.B12C282S01H05: Uma asks why Mahadeva does not go to the sacrifice himself.
shots.B12C282S02H01: Uma repeats her question and asks what stops him from going to that place.
shots.B12C282S02H02: Mahadeva explains that the gods had agreed that he would receive no share of any sacrifice, and so they give him none.
shots.B12C282S02H03: Uma tells him he is the greatest of beings yet is denied a share, and she is filled with grief.
shots.B12C282S02H04: Mahadeva sends his followers, who destroy the sacrifice, and he chases the sacrifice in the form of a deer, and from the sweat on his brow a fierce being rises who burns it, and Brahma appears to make peace.
shots.B12C282S02H05: Brahma tells Mahadeva that he will receive a share, and that Fever should be spread among many creatures, and Mahadeva agrees and distributes Fever, and Bhishma closes by saying Vritra was first struck by it and that reading this story brings freedom from disease.

B12C283.summary: Janamejaya asks how Daksha's horse sacrifice was destroyed and how its divided parts were made whole again. Vaisampayana tells how Daksha held the sacrifice on Himavat without inviting Shiva, how the sage Dadhichi warned that it would be ruined, and how Uma asked Shiva to win a share. Shiva creates the fierce Virabhadra, who with Mahakali and a host of spirits wrecks the sacrifice, and Daksha, who is then humbled, asks Shiva to make the wrecked offerings useful to him. Shiva agrees, and Daksha praises him with his thousand and eight names.

scenes.B12C283S01: Janamejaya asks about the destruction of Daksha's sacrifice, and Vaisampayana describes the gathering on Himavat, Dadhichi's warning, and Daksha's refusal to honour Shiva.
scenes.B12C283S02: Uma asks Shiva how he may win a share, Shiva answers with pride and creates a fierce being, and Virabhadra and the spirits wreck the sacrifice.
scenes.B12C283S03: Virabhadra says he came to destroy the sacrifice, Daksha praises Shiva, and Shiva grants Daksha's request that the wrecked offerings be made useful to him.

shots.B12C283S01H01: Janamejaya asks how Daksha's horse sacrifice was destroyed in the age of Vaivaswata Manu, and how Daksha reunited the divided parts of the sacrifice after Uma's grief and Mahadeva's wrath.
shots.B12C283S01H02: Vaisampayana describes Daksha's sacrifice on the breast of Himavat, to which gods, demons, spirits and sages come, and Dadhichi warns that the sacrifice is ruined because Rudra is not worshipped in it.
shots.B12C283S01H03: Daksha says he knows the eleven Rudras but does not know who this Maheswara is.
shots.B12C283S01H04: Dadhichi says that since no god is greater than Maheswara, the sacrifice will surely be ruined.
shots.B12C283S01H05: Daksha says he will offer the sacrifice to Vishnu, the Lord of all sacrifices, rather than Rudra.
shots.B12C283S02H01: Vaisampayana says that Uma, seated with her lord, then spoke.
shots.B12C283S02H02: Uma asks what gifts or penances might win Shiva a share of the offerings, and Shiva replies that she does not know him and that all sacrifices are dedicated to him.
shots.B12C283S02H03: Uma says even ordinary men praise themselves in front of their wives.
shots.B12C283S02H04: Shiva says he does not praise himself, and that he will create a being to destroy the sacrifice that has displeased her.
shots.B12C283S02H05: Shiva creates Virabhadra, who sets out with Mahakali and a host of spirits, and they wreck the sacrifice with fire, destruction and uproar, until the gods ask who he is.
shots.B12C283S03H01: Virabhadra says he is not Rudra and came only to destroy the sacrifice, sent by Rudra, with his companion who sprang from Uma's wrath. Daksha bows to Maheswara and sings his praises, and Shiva appears from the sacrificial pit and asks Daksha what he wants. The text notes that the five and a half verses of the hymn appear to be later interpolations.
shots.B12C283S03H02: Daksha asks that the wrecked and polluted offerings be made useful to him, and Shiva grants his wish, and Daksha praises him by his thousand and eight names.

B12C284.summary: Yudhishthira asks for the names by which Daksha praised the great god. Bhishma gives Daksha's long hymn, which lists Shiva's many names and forms, ends by asking forgiveness for leaving him out of the sacrifice, and is answered with Shiva's grace and a share of the sacrificial fruit. Shiva then teaches Daksha the Pasupata religion, which is open to all, and disappears with Uma and his followers. Bhishma says that anyone who hears or recites the hymn is freed from fear, disease and sin, and gains success.

scenes.B12C284S01: Yudhishthira asks for Daksha's names of the god, Bhishma gives the long hymn, a heading marks the next section, and Shiva accepts Daksha's praise and promises him the fruit of many sacrifices.
scenes.B12C284S02: Shiva consoles Daksha, teaches him the Pasupata religion, and disappears, and Bhishma explains the power of the hymn to protect and to bring success.

shots.B12C284S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to recite the names by which Daksha praised the great god.
shots.B12C284S01H02: Bhishma says he will recite the names, both secret and open, of the god of gods.
shots.B12C284S01H03: Daksha's long hymn praises Shiva in many names and forms, calling him the lord of all, the destroyer of Andhaka, the three-eyed, the source of all gods, and the one who destroyed the sacrifice in the form of a deer, and it ends with Daksha asking forgiveness for not inviting him.
shots.B12C284S01H04: A heading marks the start of the next section, CCCII.
shots.B12C284S01H05: Shiva, pleased with the praise, tells Daksha he needs no more praise, and promises him the fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices and a hundred Vajapeyas for this incomplete sacrifice.
shots.B12C284S02H01: Shiva consoles Daksha, says this is not the first time he has destroyed Daksha's sacrifice, and teaches him the Pasupata religion, which leads to liberation and is open to all who practise self-control. He then disappears with Uma and his followers, and Bhishma explains that the hymn brings success, long life, protection from spirits, freedom from fear, and a place among Shiva's attendants.

B12C285.summary: Yudhishthira asks what Adhyatma is and where it comes from. Bhishma explains that the five great essences, earth, wind, space, water and light, form all bodies, and that the understanding creates the senses and the three qualities, while the Soul is only a witness. He says the understanding and the Soul are joined eternally, and that knowledge carries one across the river of delusion.

scenes.B12C285S01: Yudhishthira asks about Adhyatma, and Bhishma explains the five essences, the senses, the understanding, the three qualities, and the difference between the understanding and the Soul.

shots.B12C285S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain what Adhyatma is with respect to man and where it arises.
shots.B12C285S01H02: Bhishma says Adhyatma explains everything, names the five great essences that create and dissolve all creatures, and explains how the senses, mind, understanding, and the three qualities arise from them, with the understanding creating the attributes while the Soul only watches. He ends by saying knowledge carries one across the flood of delusion and ends sorrow and wrongdoing.

B12C286.summary: Yudhishthira asks how sorrow and death can be kept away from living creatures. Bhishma tells of the sage Samanga, whom Narada finds always cheerful and free of anxiety. Samanga explains that he knows past, present and future, that all creatures live by the fruits of past acts, and that the wise are those whose senses are free of error. He has conquered desire through penance, so grief cannot trouble him.

scenes.B12C286S01: Yudhishthira asks how to escape sorrow and death, and Bhishma tells of the sage Samanga, whose calm Narada admires, and whose explanation of past acts and freedom from desire shows why grief cannot touch him.

shots.B12C286S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how sorrow and death can be prevented for living creatures.
shots.B12C286S01H02: Bhishma says he will tell the old discourse between Narada and Samanga.
shots.B12C286S01H03: Narada sees Samanga bow low to his superiors, always cheerful and untroubled, and asks how he is so free of anxiety.
shots.B12C286S01H04: Samanga says he knows the past, present and future, that all creatures live by the fruits of past acts, that wisdom comes from freedom of the senses from error, and that by long penance he has overcome desire, so grief cannot afflict him.

B12C287.summary: Yudhishthira asks what is beneficial for a man who doubts the scriptures and lacks self-restraint. Bhishma recommends honouring teachers and hearing the scriptures, and tells how Galava asks Narada which course is beneficial when the scriptures disagree. Narada says the four stages of life each have their proper duties, that true excellence lies in friendship, truth, mildness, contentment and study, and that boasting and idleness should be avoided. He also advises where to live and under which kings, and says that the highest good is hard to describe.

scenes.B12C287S01: Yudhishthira asks what benefits a doubting man, and Bhishma tells of Galava's question to Narada about the good among differing scriptural paths, with Narada's long reply on virtue, places to live, and the rule of kings.

shots.B12C287S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what is beneficial for a man who does not know the scriptures, is always in doubt, and lacks self-restraint.
shots.B12C287S01H02: Bhishma says that serving the teacher, honouring the elders, and listening to the scriptures are of supreme benefit, and tells how Galava asks Narada which course is beneficial, since the scriptures differ.
shots.B12C287S01H03: Narada says the four stages of life each have their own duties, that true excellence lies in friendship, truth, mildness, and study, that boasting and idleness are faults, and that a man should live among righteous people, under a just king, and away from places of sin, and that the highest good is hard to state.

B12C288.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a king should behave and what makes a man free of attachment. Bhishma recounts how the sage Arishtanemi taught King Sagara that the true happiness is liberation, and that attachment to children, wealth and a wife is the trap. Arishtanemi says each creature lives and suffers by its own acts, and lists the marks of a freed man, including contentment, equal regard for all, and awareness of death and disease. Sagara follows this teaching and rules his subjects well.

scenes.B12C288S01: Yudhishthira asks how a king should live, Bhishma introduces Arishtanemi's teaching to Sagara, Sagara asks for the good, and Arishtanemi describes the way to freedom from attachment.

shots.B12C288S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a king should behave, keeping the highest aim in view, and what qualities keep him free from attachment.
shots.B12C288S01H02: Bhishma says he will recite the old teaching that Arishtanemi gave to Sagara when Sagara asked for his counsel.
shots.B12C288S01H03: Sagara asks what good will bring happiness here and how one can avoid grief and agitation.
shots.B12C288S01H04: Arishtanemi says liberation is true happiness, which ignorant men who cling to children, animals and wealth cannot see. He advises raising children, enjoying the senses in measure, and letting go of attachments, since each creature lives and suffers by its own acts. He then lists the marks of the freed man: contentment, equal regard for all, awareness of death and disease, and detachment from pleasure and pain. Sagara follows this teaching and rules well.

B12C289.summary: Yudhishthira asks why the sage Usanas, called Kavi and Sukra, sided with the Asuras, and how he gained his name and why he cannot reach the middle of the sky. Bhishma explains that Usanas used yoga to enter the god Kubera and rob him of his wealth. When Kubera complained to Shiva, Shiva raised his lance, Usanas sat on its tip, and Shiva bent the lance into his bow Pinaka and swallowed him. Usanas wandered inside Shiva until Shiva told him to leave by the urethra, and Uma then saved him from Shiva's anger and made him her son.

scenes.B12C289S01: Yudhishthira asks about Usanas's alliance with the Asuras and his name, and Bhishma tells how Usanas robbed Kubera, was swallowed by Shiva, and got out through the urethra, with Uma saving him.
scenes.B12C289S02: Shiva lets Usanas go, and Bhishma ends the story of the Bhargava.

shots.B12C289S01H01: Yudhishthira asks why Usanas sided with the Asuras against the gods, how he got the name Sukra, and why he cannot reach the middle of the sky.
shots.B12C289S01H02: Bhishma says Usanas robbed Kubera of his wealth by entering him through yoga, and that when Kubera complained to Shiva, Shiva raised his lance, Usanas sat on its tip, Shiva bent the lance into his bow Pinaka, and swallowed Usanas.
shots.B12C289S01H03: Yudhishthira asks how Usanas could move about inside Shiva's stomach, and what Shiva did while he was there.
shots.B12C289S01H04: Bhishma says Shiva sat in meditation in the waters for ages, then Brahma came to ask after him. Inside, Usanas kept praying for a way out, and Shiva told him to leave by the urethra, and he came out shining and was named Sukra.
shots.B12C289S01H05: Uma tells Shiva that the Brahmana has become her son and that one who comes out of his stomach should not be slain.
shots.B12C289S02H01: Shiva, calmed by Uma, lets Usanas go, and Bhishma says he has told the story of the Bhargava as Yudhishthira asked.

B12C290.summary: Yudhishthira asks what good acts lead to benefit in this world and the next. Bhishma tells how King Janaka asked the sage Parasara what is beneficial for all creatures. Parasara says that righteousness through right action is the highest good, that the four classes each have their duties, and that acts and their fruits belong to each person, refuting the sceptic who denies this. He ends by saying that a man should not do what he would condemn in others.

scenes.B12C290S01: Yudhishthira asks what good acts to do, Bhishma tells of Janaka's question to Parasara, and Parasara explains righteousness, the duties of the classes, the fruits of acts, and the rule against doing what one would condemn in others.

shots.B12C290S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what good acts a man should do to gain benefit in this world and the next, saying he never tires of Bhishma's words.
shots.B12C290S01H02: Bhishma says King Janaka asked the sage Parasara what is beneficial for all creatures, and Parasara answered to please the king.
shots.B12C290S01H03: Parasara says that righteousness through right action is the highest good, that the four classes each have their duties, and that every creature takes its fate from its own past acts. He answers the sceptic who denies this, says the acts of eye, mind, tongue and limbs bear fruit, and lists the virtues that bring happiness. He ends by saying that a man must not do what he would censure in others, and that those who fail in their duties deserve pity.

B12C291.summary: Parasara continues his teaching to Janaka. He compares the body to a chariot that the mind must steer with the reins of knowledge, and he says that wrongs done knowingly bring sorrow while wrongs done in ignorance can be expiated. Acts done with judgment increase merit, and kings should protect their subjects, while devotees should later retire to the forest and treat all creatures as their own selves.

scenes.B12C291S01: Parasara explains how to steer the body and senses with knowledge, the difference between knowing and unknowing wrongdoing, the value of judgment in acts, and the duties of kings and of those who retire to the forest.

shots.B12C291S01H01: Parasara says the wise man steers his body and senses with the reins of knowledge, that sins done knowingly bring sorrow while those done in ignorance can be expiated, that deliberate acts increase merit, and that kings should protect their subjects, while those in later life should retire to the forest and treat all creatures as themselves.

B12C292.summary: Parasara says that people mostly act for themselves, so gifts and debts matter greatly. He says that wealth must be earned by fair means and never at others' expense, and that a man owes debts to the Rishis, the gods, the Pitris, his fellow men, his servants and himself, each of which can be paid in a set way. He cites examples of sages who won success through devotion and says that parents, the sacred fire and the teacher must be honoured.

scenes.B12C292S01: Parasara discusses self-interest, fair wealth, the debts a man owes, and the honour due to parents, the sacred fire, and teachers.

shots.B12C292S01H01: Parasara says that people mostly act for themselves, that gifts and fair wealth bring merit, that a man owes debts to the Rishis, gods, Pitris, fellow men, servants and himself, and that parents, the sacred fire and the teacher must be honoured.

B12C293.summary: Parasara explains the duties of the four classes. The Sudra should serve the higher classes and keep company with good people, the Vaishya should farm and tend cattle, the Kshatriya should protect, and the Brahmana should study and enjoy. Each class that keeps to its own duty helps keep righteousness whole, and gifts made with respect bring the greatest merit.

scenes.B12C293S01: Parasara sets out the duties of each class, the value of keeping to one's own duty, and the best way to make gifts.

shots.B12C293S01H01: Parasara explains that the Sudra should serve the higher classes and keep company with good people, that the Vaishya farms and tends cattle, the Kshatriya protects, the Brahmana studies, and each class gains respect by keeping to its duty, and he explains that gifts made with respect bring the greatest merit.

B12C294.summary: Parasara says that wealth earned by each class's proper means is praised, and that a Brahmana may take up another class's work in need but must not fall to the lowest order's tasks. He traces how pride, wrath and desire, the Asuras, spread among men, and how Shiva destroyed the Asura chiefs with his arrow and lance. The seven Rishis then set up Indra and the kings, and some kings took to Asura ways, so Parasara urges avoiding harm and seeking knowledge of the Soul.

scenes.B12C294S01: Parasara explains the lawful means of livelihood for each class, traces the rise of pride and desire among men, the defeat of the Asuras by Shiva, and the rule that followed, and urges avoiding injury and seeking knowledge of the Soul.

shots.B12C294S01H01: Parasara explains the lawful livelihoods of each class, warns against trades that are censured, tells how men's pride, wrath and desire grew until Shiva destroyed the three Asura chiefs, and then how the seven Rishis appointed Indra and kings, and urges avoiding harm and seeking knowledge of the Soul.

B12C295.summary: Parasara moves on to penance. He says that householders grow attached to wealth, kin and pleasure, and that despair, awakening, study and penance follow from this, so penance is open to all classes. He warns that penance done for reward brings misery, that the pleasures of the senses are short-lived, and that householders should enjoy wealth honestly while doing their duties. He ends by saying that the householder is the refuge of all other orders.

scenes.B12C295S01: Parasara describes how attachment to household life leads to despair, study and penance, warns against penance done for reward, and tells householders to do their duties with honest effort.

shots.B12C295S01H01: Parasara explains that householders grow attached to wealth and kin, that despair leads to awakening, study and penance, that penance is open to all, that penance done for fruit brings misery, and that householders should do their duties with effort, since they are the refuge of all other orders.

B12C296.summary: Janaka asks why men of different classes differ in colour when all are said to have sprung from Brahmanas. Parasara explains that the classes arose when penance declined, that the four classes came from the Lord's mouth, arms, thighs and feet, and that mixed castes arose from their intermixture. He adds that sages born of mixed wombs became Rishis through penance, and he sets out the special and common duties of the classes, with the rule that a man is stained more by his acts than by his birth.

scenes.B12C296S01: Janaka asks why the classes differ, and Parasara explains the four classes, the mixed castes, the sages born of mixed wombs, and the Gotras, then Janaka asks for the duties.
scenes.B12C296S02: Parasara sets out the special and common duties of the classes, and answers Janaka that acts stain a man more than birth, and that the way of acts free from harm leads to Yoga and liberation.

shots.B12C296S01H01: Janaka asks why men of different classes differ in colour, since the Srutis say all offspring are the father himself and all men sprang from Brahmanas.
shots.B12C296S01H02: Parasara says the classes arose when penance declined, that the Lord created the four classes from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet, and that mixed castes arose from their intermixture.
shots.B12C296S01H03: Janaka asks how men of mixed birth came to be Brahmanas, if all were of one origin.
shots.B12C296S01H04: Parasara says sages born of mixed wombs became Rishis through penance, names several such sages, and says the Gotras were founded by the penances of their founders.
shots.B12C296S01H05: Janaka asks Parasara to tell him the special duties of each class and their common duties.
shots.B12C296S02H01: Parasara lists the special duties: Brahmanas accept gifts, sacrifice and teach, Kshatriyas protect, Vaishyas farm, rear cattle and trade, and Sudras serve the higher classes. He then lists common duties such as compassion, truthfulness, hospitality and self-restraint, and says even a virtuous Sudra is to be honoured.
shots.B12C296S02H02: Janaka asks whether a man is stained by his acts or by the class in which he is born.
shots.B12C296S02H03: Parasara says both can stain a man, but acts stain him more than birth does.
shots.B12C296S02H04: Janaka asks which acts are righteous and do no harm to other creatures.
shots.B12C296S02H05: Parasara says that those who give up domestic fire and attachment, and climb the path of yoga, reach liberation, and that all classes gain heaven by truthful and righteous conduct.

B12C297.summary: Parasara speaks at length on devotion to elders, the rules of battle for Kshatriyas, and the course of death and rebirth. He says that the body dissolves into its elements, that the soul roves for a time before taking a new body, and that the righteous die well while ignorance is the chief foe. He urges the four stages of life, rates human birth as the best, and recommends sacred places, cremation rites, and the Vedas for those without stain. Bhishma says the sage taught all this to the king of Videha.

scenes.B12C297S01: Parasara discusses devotion to elders, rules of battle, the dissolution of the body, rebirth, the good death, the four stages of life, and the duties to the dead, and Bhishma closes by naming the king of Videha as the listener.

shots.B12C297S01H01: Parasara speaks at length on devotion to elders, the rules of battle for Kshatriyas, the dissolution of the body and the roving soul's rebirth, the righteous and sinful deaths, ignorance as the chief foe, the four stages of life, the value of human birth, kindness to all creatures, sacred places, cremation rites, and the Vedas being for the stainless.
shots.B12C297S01H02: Bhishma says the high-souled sage spoke all this to the ruler of the Videhas in days of old for his benefit.

B12C298.summary: King Janaka asks the sage Parasara what is good, what the best path is, what cannot be destroyed, and where one need not return from. Parasara answers that detachment and knowledge are the highest good, that harmlessness is the greatest gift, and that sin clings only to the attached. He adds that family and wealth cannot help after death, and that each creature bears the fruit of its past acts. Janaka hears the teaching and is greatly pleased.

scenes.B12C298S01: Bhishma introduces Janaka's question, Janaka asks about the best path, Parasara answers at length on detachment, knowledge, harmlessness and past acts, and Janaka is pleased.
scenes.B12C298S02: Janaka hears the sage's words and is made very happy.

shots.B12C298S01H01: Bhishma says Janaka, king of Mithila, again questioned the sage Parasara about all duties.
shots.B12C298S01H02: Janaka asks what is good, what is the best path for living creatures, what is never destroyed, and where one need not return.
shots.B12C298S01H03: Parasara answers that detachment and knowledge are the highest good, that harmlessness is the greatest gift, that sin clings only to the attached, that family and wealth cannot help after death, and that each creature bears the fruit of its past acts.
shots.B12C298S01H04: Bhishma says Janaka received the sage's teaching in the way the sage gave it.
shots.B12C298S01H05: Janaka, the foremost of the righteous, hears everything the Rishi says.
shots.B12C298S02H01: Janaka hears the sage's words and gains great happiness from them.

B12C299.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what he thinks of truth, self-restraint, forgiveness and wisdom. Bhishma tells of Brahma appearing as a golden swan before the Sadhyas, who ask the swan about the highest good. The swan teaches restraint of speech and wrath, forgiveness, truth and self-control, and says that truth is the only way to heaven. The Sadhyas then ask what covers the world and what makes a Brahmana divine, and the swan answers that ignorance and attachment cover the world and that study, vows, and wisdom mark the true Brahmana.

scenes.B12C299S01: Yudhishthira asks about the virtues, Bhishma introduces the golden swan and the Sadhyas, and the swan answers the first question with a long teaching on restraint, forgiveness and truth.
scenes.B12C299S02: The Sadhyas ask the swan about what covers the world, who is truly happy among Brahmanas, and what makes a Brahmana divine or impure, and the swan answers each question.
scenes.B12C299S03: Bhishma ends the discourse by saying that the body is the seat of acts and the Jiva is truth.

shots.B12C299S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what he thinks of truth, self-restraint, forgiveness and wisdom, which learned men praise.
shots.B12C299S01H02: Bhishma says Brahma, the unborn Lord, took the form of a golden swan and wandered the three worlds until he came upon the Sadhyas.
shots.B12C299S01H03: The Sadhyas call themselves deities, say they have heard that the swan is learned, and ask what is the highest object and the one act that frees one from bonds.
shots.B12C299S01H04: The swan says one should practise austerity, self-restraint, truth and mental control, avoid wounding others with cruel words, meet insults with forgiveness, hold forgiveness and truth as the highest virtues, and treat truth as the only way to heaven.
shots.B12C299S01H05: The Sadhyas ask what covers the world, why people fail to shine, why they cast off friends, and why they fail to reach heaven.
shots.B12C299S02H01: The swan says ignorance covers the world, malice keeps men from shining, covetousness makes them abandon friends, and attachment keeps them from heaven.
shots.B12C299S02H02: The Sadhyas ask who among Brahmanas is always happy, who keeps silence amid many, who is strong though weak, and who avoids quarrels.
shots.B12C299S02H03: The swan answers that the wise man among Brahmanas is each of these.
shots.B12C299S02H04: The Sadhyas ask where the divinity, purity, impurity and humanity of Brahmanas lie.
shots.B12C299S02H05: The swan answers that divinity lies in Vedic study, purity in vows and observances, impurity in reproach, and humanity in death.
shots.B12C299S03H01: Bhishma ends the discourse by saying that the body is the seat of acts and that the Jiva is truth.

B12C300.summary: Yudhishthira asks how the Sankhya and Yoga systems differ. Bhishma says that each school praises itself and gives its reasons, but that both are approved and both require purity, compassion and vows, differing mainly in the scriptures they follow. He describes how the strong Yogin breaks the bonds of the world and gains great powers while the weak are lost, and sets out meditation, diet, the difficult path of Yoga, and its highest fruit of union with Brahma. The chapter closes the second part of the Shanti Parva.

scenes.B12C300S01: Yudhishthira asks about the two systems, Bhishma compares the schools and their reasons, explains the strength a Yogin needs, and describes the meditation that brings liberation.
scenes.B12C300S02: Bhishma lists the diets and restraints that build a Yogin's power, describes the hard path of Yoga and its highest fruit, and closes the section.

shots.B12C300S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the difference between the Sankhya and Yoga systems of philosophy.
shots.B12C300S01H02: Bhishma says each school praises its own view and gives reasons for it, that the Yogins hold that one who denies God cannot be freed, and that both systems are approved, both require purity, compassion and vows, and they differ mainly in the scriptures they follow.
shots.B12C300S01H03: Yudhishthira asks why, if the vows, purity and fruits are the same, the scriptures of the two systems differ.
shots.B12C300S01H04: Bhishma says that the Yogin who casts off five faults breaks free, that the strong Yogin escapes the world's nets as a large fish or bird does while the weak are caught, that a strong Yogin can create many bodies, and that meditation like a bowman's aim, a boatman's steady hand, or a charioteer's control brings liberation, with the Jiva joined to the subtle Soul at parts of the body.
shots.B12C300S01H05: Yudhishthira asks what diet and what conquests give a Yogin his power.
shots.B12C300S02H01: Bhishma lists diets, from broken rice and barley to water and milk taken at longer and longer intervals and abstention from meat, and the mastery of desire, anger, fear and sleep that Yoga needs. He describes the Yoga path as a dangerous road that few can walk, and says its highest fruit is union with Brahma, through which the Yogin can enter the gods, the elements and all creatures.
shots.B12C300S02H02: Closing line: the second part of the Santi Parva ends here.

B12C301.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to set out the Sankhya philosophy. Bhishma presents its view of the world, the elements and qualities that make up the body and cosmos, the faults of the body, and the path by which the wise rise through the qualities to liberation. Yudhishthira then asks whether a liberated person keeps consciousness, a question he says bears on which way of life is superior.

scenes.B12C301S01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the Sankhya principles, and Bhishma describes the doctrine's view of the world, the body's faults and the way of liberation. Yudhishthira then raises the question of whether consciousness survives liberation.
scenes.B12C301S02: Bhishma answers that the senses serve the soul, that a freed soul merges into Brahma, and that Sankhya knowledge is the source of other learning. He ends by describing Narayana as the one who creates and withdraws the universe.

shots.B12C301S01H01: Yudhishthira praises the account of Yoga he has heard and asks Bhishma to now explain the Sankhya principles.
shots.B12C301S01H02: Bhishma calls the Sankhya doctrine faultless and lists the wise who hold it, then describes their knowledge of the world's faults, the three qualities and the chain of elements leading up to Narayana.
shots.B12C301S01H03: Yudhishthira asks what faults Bhishma sees in the body and asks for a full and true answer.
shots.B12C301S01H04: Bhishma names five bodily faults, explains how each is overcome, and describes the ocean of life that the wise cross to reach the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C301S01H05: Yudhishthira asks whether the liberated keep memory and consciousness, noting that the answer bears on the two ways of life and on what deep sleep is.
shots.B12C301S02H01: Bhishma calls the question proper but hard, explains that the senses serve the soul and rest in sleep, and says a freed soul merges into Brahma and does not return.
shots.B12C301S02H02: Bhishma says Sankhya knowledge feeds all other learning, that its adherents rise to godly status or to Brahma, and that the wise man who masters it becomes like Narayana, who creates and reabsorbs the universe in cycles.

B12C302.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the difference between the Deteriorating and the Undeteriorating, and Bhishma answers with an old teaching of Vasishtha to king Karala of Janaka's race. Vasishtha describes the cycles of creation and destruction, the sequence of elements and senses that make up every embodied being, and a twenty-fifth principle that lies beyond them. He explains that union with Prakriti makes the Indestructible seem destructible, and that knowledge reveals its true nature.

scenes.B12C302S01: Vasishtha teaches king Karala about the Destructible and the Indestructible, covering the cosmic cycles, the twenty-four principles and the twenty-fifth beyond them.

shots.B12C302S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what the Undeteriorating and the Deteriorating are, and says he wants to hear it all from Bhishma while Bhishma still has time to teach.
shots.B12C302S01H02: Bhishma tells the old story of Vasishtha and king Karala, who asks Vasishtha about the supreme Brahma and what the universe returns to at its destruction.
shots.B12C302S01H03: Vasishtha describes the measure of the cosmic days, the creation of Hiranyagarbha, and the elements and senses that make up every living body, all of which he calls destructible.
shots.B12C302S01H04: Vasishtha names Vishnu as the twenty-fifth principle beyond the twenty-four, and explains how the soul, joined to Prakriti, takes on the three qualities and so falls into different destinies.

B12C303.summary: Vasishtha continues by explaining how the soul, forgetting its true nature, falls under ignorance and is reborn again and again among gods, men and lower beings. He lists the many bodily ailments, ascetic practices, rites and worldly roles the soul takes on while it believes itself bound by them. He says Prakriti drives the cycle of birth, death and acts, and that the soul, though free of all attributes, imagines it has them.

scenes.B12C303S01: Vasishtha describes the endless births and sufferings of the forgetful soul, the bodies and practices it takes on, and the cycle of acts driven by Prakriti.

shots.B12C303S01H01: Vasishtha describes the forgetful soul's endless births and sufferings, the many ascetic and worldly roles it takes on, and the cycle of acts driven by Prakriti.

B12C304.summary: Vasishtha closes the teaching by comparing the soul to the moon, which waxes and wanes while one of its sixteen portions stays constant. Under ignorance the soul is repeatedly reborn, and its pure nature becomes tied to the three qualities of Prakriti. Emancipation is described as release from that union.

scenes.B12C304S01: Vasishtha compares the soul to the moon's sixteen portions, explains how ignorance keeps Jiva in repeated births, and defines emancipation as freedom from Prakriti.

shots.B12C304S01H01: Vasishtha compares Jiva to the moon's sixteen portions, fifteen subject to change and one pure, and says emancipation means release from union with Prakriti.

B12C305.summary: King Janaka asks Vasishtha how Emancipation can exist if Purusha and Prakriti are always joined, as male and female are in creation, and he asks for direct evidence of it. Vasishtha answers that memorized texts without understanding are of no use. He explains that Sankhya and Yoga teach the same truth, that the Supreme Soul is beyond all attributes, and that unity marks the Indestructible while multiplicity marks the destructible.

scenes.B12C305S01: Janaka asks how Emancipation can exist given the constant union of Purusha and Prakriti, and Vasishtha answers that texts must be understood, then explains the Supreme Soul and the difference between unity and multiplicity.

shots.B12C305S01H01: Janaka compares the union of male and female to that of Purusha and Prakriti, asks how Emancipation can then exist, and asks for direct evidence of it.
shots.B12C305S01H02: Vasishtha says memorized texts without understanding are of no use, then argues that Sankhya and Yoga teach the same truth, that the Supreme Soul is beyond attributes, and that unity and multiplicity mark the two kinds of being.

B12C306.summary: Janaka says he is still confused about unity and multiplicity, and asks Vasishtha to explain again the knower, Jiva, knowledge, ignorance, and both the Sankhya and Yoga systems. Vasishtha describes the Yoga practice of contemplation, breath control and stillness, and the vision of the Supreme Soul it brings. He then sets out the Sankhya chain of principles, how they dissolve back in reverse order, and how the Soul is the true knower freed from returning to the world.

scenes.B12C306S01: Janaka asks for a fuller account of unity and multiplicity; Vasishtha explains the Yoga practice of contemplation, then the Sankhya principles and how the Soul is known as the true knower.

shots.B12C306S01H01: Janaka admits he has not grasped unity and multiplicity and asks Vasishtha to explain again the knower, Jiva, knowledge, ignorance, and the Sankhya and Yoga systems in detail.
shots.B12C306S01H02: Vasishtha describes Yoga as contemplation through concentration and breath control, the stillness it demands, and the Supreme Soul that the Yogin sees shining in the heart.
shots.B12C306S01H03: Vasishtha sets out the Sankhya principles from Prakriti down to the senses, their dissolution in reverse order, and the distinction between Kshetra, Kshetrajna and Purusha, and says that one who knows the Soul does not return to the world.

B12C307.summary: Vasishtha defines knowledge (Vidya) and ignorance (Avidya) in terms of the Sankhya principles, with Prakriti as ignorance and the Purusha beyond the twenty-four as knowledge. He explains why both Prakriti and the Jiva can be called indestructible or destructible. He then gives the Jiva's lament at being caught in Prakriti like a fish in a net, and its resolve to turn to the Supreme Soul, before noting that Sankhya and Yoga teach the same knowledge.

scenes.B12C307S01: Vasishtha defines knowledge and ignorance through the Sankhya principles, gives the Jiva's lament at its bondage to Prakriti and its resolve to turn to the Supreme Soul, and notes that Sankhya and Yoga agree.

shots.B12C307S01H01: Vasishtha defines knowledge and ignorance through the principles, explains why both Prakriti and the Jiva are called indestructible and destructible, and gives the Jiva's lament at its bondage to Prakriti.
shots.B12C307S01H02: Vasishtha says Sankhya and Yoga teach the same knowledge, that it can awaken any listener, and that Yoga speaks of Brahma and the Jiva as two only because of ignorance.

B12C308.summary: Vasishtha contrasts the Supreme Soul with the Jiva, which takes on the qualities of Prakriti through ignorance and is freed only by recognizing itself as distinct from her. He says the teaching must be given only to worthy and humble disciples, never to deceitful or unworthy ones. Bhishma closes the whole discourse by tracing its line of transmission from Hiranyagarbha through Vasishtha and Narada to himself, and by assuring the king that knowledge frees him from ignorance.

scenes.B12C308S01: Vasishtha contrasts the Supreme Soul with the Jiva, explains how the Jiva is freed, and says who may receive the teaching. Bhishma then closes the discourse with its line of transmission and an assurance to the king.

shots.B12C308S01H01: Vasishtha contrasts the Supreme Soul with the Jiva, explains how the Jiva is freed by recognizing itself as distinct from Prakriti, and says that a soul takes on the qualities of whatever it unites with.
shots.B12C308S01H02: Vasishtha lists the kinds of people who may and may not receive this knowledge, calls on Karala to be fearless, and says he received the teaching from Hiranyagarbha.
shots.B12C308S01H03: Bhishma closes by tracing the teaching from Hiranyagarbha through Vasishtha and Narada to himself, and tells the king that knowledge of Kshara and Akshara frees him from ignorance.

B12C309.summary: A king of Janaka's race, Vasuman, meets a Rishi of Bhrigu's line while hunting and asks what brings lasting benefit to a man whose body is unstable and whose desires are strong. The Rishi advises restraint, righteous conduct, generous gifts from honestly earned wealth, firmness, and the company of virtuous people. The king accepts the counsel and turns his mind to righteousness.

scenes.B12C309S01: King Vasuman asks a Bhrigu-line Rishi how to gain lasting good, and the Rishi advises righteousness, gifts, firmness and the company of the virtuous. The king takes this advice to heart.

shots.B12C309S01H01: King Vasuman, of Janaka's race, meets a Rishi of Bhrigu's line in the forest and asks what benefits a man with an unstable body and strong desires.
shots.B12C309S01H02: The Rishi advises restraint, righteous conduct, honest gifts, purity, patience and firmness, and keeping company with the virtuous.
shots.B12C309S01H03: Vasuman accepts the counsel and sets his mind on righteousness.
shots.B12C309S01H04: A section heading marking the start of Section CCCXI.

B12C310.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for teaching on what is free from duty, doubt, birth and death. Bhishma offers an old dialogue in which king Daivarati of Janaka's race questions the Rishi Yajnavalkya about the senses, Prakriti, Brahma and the limits of life. Yajnavalkya begins his answer with the list of principles and the stages of creation.

scenes.B12C310S01: Yudhishthira asks for teaching on the eternal and indestructible, and Bhishma introduces a dialogue in which Janaka questions Yajnavalkya, who begins by listing the principles and the stages of creation.

shots.B12C310S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to teach him about what is beyond duty, doubt, birth and death, and is eternal and free from effort.
shots.B12C310S01H02: Bhishma introduces an old dialogue between Yajnavalkya and king Daivarati of Janaka's race, who asks the Rishi a question.
shots.B12C310S01H03: The king asks how many kinds of senses and Prakriti there are, what the Unmanifest and highest Brahma are, and what birth, death and the limits of age mean.
shots.B12C310S01H04: Yajnavalkya names the eight Prakriti principles and sixteen modifications, then gives the stages of creation that make up the twenty-four principles.

B12C311.summary: Yajnavalkya measures the length of Brahma's day and night and describes how Brahman, born from a golden egg, creates the earth and sky. He then traces the creation of the five elements, their qualities, and the senses. He ends by saying the mind rules the senses, so the senses act only through it.

scenes.B12C311S01: Yajnavalkya describes Brahma's day and night, his emergence from a golden egg, the creation of the elements and senses, and the mind's rule over them.

shots.B12C311S01H01: Yajnavalkya gives the length of Brahma's day and night, describes his emergence from a golden egg, the creation of the elements and the qualities of sound and touch, and says the mind directs the senses.

B12C312.summary: Yajnavalkya explains how creation is dissolved at the end of Brahman's day. Maharudra, urged by the Unmanifest, burns all living things, and then fire, water, wind, space, mind, consciousness and Mahat are each absorbed in turn into Sambhu. He then announces that he will turn to the three frames of teaching, Adhyatma, Adhibhuta and Adhidaivata.

scenes.B12C312S01: Yajnavalkya describes the dissolution of creation at the end of Brahma's day, from Maharudra's fire to the absorption of all into Sambhu, and introduces the three frames of teaching.

shots.B12C312S01H01: Yajnavalkya describes the dissolution of creation, from Maharudra's fire through the absorption of each element into Sambhu, and then announces the three frames of teaching.

B12C313.summary: Yajnavalkya pairs each sense and faculty with three aspects: its inner organ (Adhyatma), its outer object (Adhibhuta), and its presiding deity (Adhidaivata). He then explains that Prakriti multiplies the three qualities into countless forms, and he lists the qualities that belong to Sattwa, Rajas and Tamas.
