shots.B12C362S01H01: The Brahmin thanks the Naga for his teaching, says he is satisfied, and asks to be remembered and sent for now and then.
shots.B12C362S01H02: The Naga asks what business brought the Brahmin, says he should stay, since he and the Brahmin are now friends.
shots.B12C362S01H03: The Brahmin agrees that the Naga is equal to the gods in wisdom, says his doubt is resolved through the Unccha vow, and takes his leave.
shots.B12C362S01H04: Bhishma says the Brahmin went to the sage Chyavana to be initiated into the Unccha life, and traces the story through Janaka, Narada, Indra, and the Vasus to himself.
shots.B12C362S01H05: Closing line: the end of the Santi Parva.
shots.B12C362S02H02: Note 1: a period of impurity after a death, which the Sraddha rite ends.
shots.B12C362S02H03: Note 2: the phrase literally means the thing will not appear by inward light.
shots.B12C362S02H04: Note 3: the weapon will leave the man's memory near death, though he may command it at other times.
shots.B12C362S02H05: Note 4: the Kurus who fell in battle have gone to heaven, and grief is now the lot of the living.
shots.B12C362S03H01: Note 5: the reading Sanjata Valaratnesu is the true one.
shots.B12C362S03H02: Note 6: the Bombay reading Jayaphalam is correct, though the Bengal reading is not meaningless.
shots.B12C362S03H03: Note 7: Yudhishthira argues that the slain warriors did not reach heaven, since men of wrath cannot.
shots.B12C362S03H04: Note 8: pairs of opposites such as heat and cold, joy and grief.
shots.B12C362S03H05: Note 9: wealth lets its owner perform religious rites.
shots.B12C362S04H01: Note 10: if one does not wrong forest dwellers, there is less chance of wronging townsmen.
shots.B12C362S04H02: Note 11: recluses who take fallen fruit as the tree's alms, treating the tree as a guest.
shots.B12C362S04H03: Note 12: possessions and kinsfolk depend on past acts, and also shape later lives.
shots.B12C362S04H04: Note 13: those for whom one acts do not take on the results of one's acts.
shots.B12C362S04H05: Note 14: Nilakantha's gloss on one word, as the lordship of heaven.
shots.B12C362S05H01: Note 15: since the Ordainer cannot be blamed, the duties he gave Kshatriyas cannot be blamed either.
shots.B12C362S05H02: Note 16: those who sacrifice and eat the offering acquire merit no other act can match.
shots.B12C362S05H03: Note 17: a grammar note; one who firmly regards himself as Siva gains success like that deity's, as the Srutis say.
shots.B12C362S05H04: Note 18: those who die in the bright fortnight of summer reach the sun, those in the dark fortnight of winter the moon, and the detached reach Brahma's realm.
shots.B12C362S05H05: Note 19: without gods, Pitris, or Brahma, souls sink and become worms and vermin.
shots.B12C362S06H01: Note 20: the gods themselves became gods through action.
shots.B12C362S06H02: Note 21: the first word is a compound of a negative and the word for believer.
shots.B12C362S06H03: Note 22: the path of the gods is the strict observance of the Vedic rites.
shots.B12C362S06H04: Note 23: the renouncer is one who wastes his body by fasting, so in effect he denies himself.
shots.B12C362S06H05: Note 24: such a person is not a true renouncer, and for a Kshatriya such a life would be sinful.
shots.B12C362S07H01: Note 25: Nilakantha says this life suits a Brahmin, not a Kshatriya, so Yudhishthira would sin by leaving the rule to a brother.
shots.B12C362S07H02: Note 26: acts done from vanity, claiming to be the doer, differ from acts done in renunciation, without hope of fruit.
shots.B12C362S07H03: Note 27: the threefold aims of life are religion, pleasure, and profit.
shots.B12C362S07H04: Note 28: Nilakantha's explanation of the word antarala.
shots.B12C362S07H05: Note 29: the word for the inner self is set against the outer, and explained as encased in the body, that is the mind.
shots.B12C362S08H01: Note 30: Sahadeva's point is that selfish action brings death, while the opposite attitude leads to Brahma.
shots.B12C362S08H02: Note 31: the sense depends on one word, and a variant would leave the sense unchanged.
shots.B12C362S08H03: Note 32: the three kinds of strength are the master's power, good counsel, and one's own courage and perseverance.
shots.B12C362S08H04: Note 33: a literal rendering: crushed with the rod of chastisement.
shots.B12C362S08H05: Note 34: punishments by class: censure for a Brahmin, loss of property for a Kshatriya, forfeiture for a Vaisya, and little or none for a Sudra.
shots.B12C362S09H01: Note 35: a fisherman who would not kill fish would go without food.
shots.B12C362S09H02: Note 36: killing these creatures to support life is no sin.
shots.B12C362S09H03: Note 37: Nilakantha glosses the word for enjoyment as a boundary or limit.
shots.B12C362S09H04: Note 38: the cow gives milk, and maidens marry, only out of fear of punishment.
shots.B12C362S09H05: Note 39: fear of being thought a fool induces a learner to study, though it is not as harsh as the saying about the rod.
shots.B12C362S10H01: Note 40: killing a tiger that attacks the herd is better than standing by, since passive witnessing is itself a sin.
shots.B12C362S10H02: Note 41: the three humours are phlegm, bile, and wind.
shots.B12C362S10H03: Note 42: the speaker was always above joy and grief, and never swayed by either.
shots.B12C362S10H04: Note 43: the argument is that the insult to his wife should stir Arjuna's wrath, which justifies the slaying of his foes.
shots.B12C362S10H05: Note 44: having given up prosperity and kingship, Yudhishthira must be reborn and fight his doubts again.
shots.B12C362S11H01: Note 45: a difficult verse, which Nilakantha reads as a call to conquer the mind, the foe of the unmanifest self.
shots.B12C362S11H02: Note 46: Draupadi's locks, which were unbound after Duhsasana seized her, are restored after the slaughter.
shots.B12C362S11H03: Note 47: the Bengal tiger acts as a fisher, and the translator has seen its catch with claw-marks sold in a village market.
shots.B12C362S11H04: Note 48: kings cannot escape hell without penances, which are hard to perform amid luxury, so taking wealth and not using it is impractical.
shots.B12C362S11H05: Note 49: a sign that one is not free from desire.
shots.B12C362S12H01: Note 50: false speech here means claiming detachment while enjoying wealth and power.
shots.B12C362S12H02: Note 51: the path of the Pitris is Vedic ritual for future bliss, and the path of the gods is contemplation without rites.
shots.B12C362S12H03: Note 52: unity with the Supreme Soul is attaining Brahma, and selfishness, the root of sin, then disappears.
shots.B12C362S12H04: Note 53: the word refers to sacrifice.
shots.B12C362S12H05: Note 54: a literal rendering: your resolve is of one kind, while your acts are of another.
shots.B12C362S13H01: Note 55: Nilakantha reads the word as dependent on destiny, though the simpler sense is dependent on action.
shots.B12C362S13H02: Note 56: a wedded wife is a companion in one's religious acts.
shots.B12C362S13H03: Note 57: one should therefore not give up action.
shots.B12C362S13H04: Note 58: a true renouncer stands alone, so Janaka's giving up wife and kingdom does not fit perfect renunciation, and he could have enjoyed them without attachment.
shots.B12C362S13H05: Note 59: such libations work only when poured on fires kindled with mantras.
shots.B12C362S14H01: Note 60: Janaka should resume his kingdom and give alms, or else mendicants would be ruined.
shots.B12C362S14H02: Note 61: a man could rule a kingdom and still be a mendicant, if he rules without attachment.
shots.B12C362S14H03: Note 62: refers to the Nyaya definition of the soul by desire, aversion, will, pleasure, pain, and the faculties of knowing.
shots.B12C362S14H04: Note 63: the soul, though without attributes, passes from body to body through ignorance, and once freed from ignorance it ceases to act.
shots.B12C362S14H05: Note 64: the three phrases mean learned in reasoning, firmly convinced from a past life, and hard to understand.
shots.B12C362S15H01: Note 65: it is better to give up sacrifices that cannot be done without wealth.
shots.B12C362S15H02: Note 66: the word for self here means wealth, and misusing wealth is a kind of killing of oneself and a sin like killing a foetus.
shots.B12C362S15H03: Note 67: the Srutis say that whoever frightens others is frightened himself, so Yudhishthira is urged to take the throne.
shots.B12C362S15H04: Note 68: Nilakantha's reading of a phrase, meaning that some do praise contemplation.
shots.B12C362S15H05: Note 69: a literal rendering: lack of contentment with present prosperity.
shots.B12C362S16H01: Note 70: the word means a robber who takes property by force, and some texts read a different word.
shots.B12C362S16H02: Note 71: Manu also gives the king a sixth of the produce.
shots.B12C362S16H03: Note 72: Nilakantha explains the word as meaning one without pride.
shots.B12C362S16H04: Note 73: yoga here means vigour in action, and nyasa means giving up pride.
shots.B12C362S16H05: Note 74: those who by dying have escaped all grief.
shots.B12C362S17H01: Note 75: Nilakantha glosses one word as meaning increased.
shots.B12C362S17H02: Note 76: true knowledge is knowledge of Brahma, and conduct should follow the view of those who have it.
shots.B12C362S17H03: Note 77: it is better not to covet wealth for sacrifice, and a poor man does better to skip sacrifice than to use ill-gotten wealth.
shots.B12C362S17H04: Note 78: the speaker undertakes severe penance so as not to be reborn as a lower animal.
shots.B12C362S17H05: Note 79: 'even such' means arising from such causes.
shots.B12C362S18H01: Note 80: man seeks freedom from decay and immortality, but on earth gets decay and death instead.
shots.B12C362S18H02: Note 81: these things appear and disappear in the course of time.
shots.B12C362S18H03: Note 82: a literal rendering: the science of life.
shots.B12C362S18H04: Note 83: this inevitable path is the path of life, since every creature is subject to birth.
shots.B12C362S18H05: Note 84: a disputed point, whether the body can exist apart from life; the subtle body persists as the cause for the unborn soul.
shots.B12C362S19H01: Note 85: the word param means Paramatma, and to pay court means to seek and enjoy.
shots.B12C362S19H02: Note 86: this sacrifice is one in which the performer gives away all his wealth.
shots.B12C362S19H03: Note 87: the word Vasumati means possessed of wealth.
shots.B12C362S19H04: Note 88: the Bengal reading is preferred over the Bombay one, which Nilakantha explains as become conscious.
shots.B12C362S19H05: Note 89: the seven sacrifices are named, each requiring the consecration of the Soma.
shots.B12C362S20H01: Note 90: only kings could have a single umbrella held over their heads.
shots.B12C362S20H02: Note 91: Kanwa raised Sakuntala, Bharata's mother, and Bharata was born in Kanwa's retreat.
shots.B12C362S20H03: Note 92: Nilakantha glosses one word as praising, and it may also mean with triple gifts.
shots.B12C362S20H04: Note 93: the legend of the Ganga, which was held in Brahma's pot and brought down by Bhagiratha to save his ancestors; Urvasi's literal meaning is given.
shots.B12C362S20H05: Note 94: the Ganga is triple-coursed, flowing in heaven, on earth, and in the nether regions.
shots.B12C362S21H01: Note 95: Dilipa was so rich that his gold-decked elephants were not kept in guarded pens.
shots.B12C362S21H02: Note 96: Nilakantha explains the name Satadhanwan as one whose bow can bear a hundred Anantas.
shots.B12C362S21H03: Note 97: a literal rendering of a phrase: me he shall suck.
shots.B12C362S21H04: Note 98: the translators differ on whether Asita and Gaya, or Anga and Vrihadratha, are one or two persons, and both readings are wrong.
shots.B12C362S21H05: Note 99: Yayati hurled a piece of wood and raised an altar where it fell, going on to the sea shore.
shots.B12C362S22H01: Note 100: the word is explained as men possessed of Dakshya, or liberal-minded men.
shots.B12C362S22H02: Note 101: literally, only one umbrella was open on the earth in his time.
shots.B12C362S22H03: Note 102: the word nala is probably used for rhythm, and the correct word means a distance of four hundred cubits.
shots.B12C362S22H04: Note 103: a literal rendering: one whose excreta are gold.
shots.B12C362S22H05: Note 104: a Kshatriya protects Brahmins' penances and Vaisyas' duties, and must clear obstacles in their way.
shots.B12C362S23H01: Note 105: the results of all acts attach to the Supreme Being, who urges every creature to act.
shots.B12C362S23H02: Note 106: the phrase means there is no Supreme Being and no next world.
shots.B12C362S23H03: Note 107: since no one is free in this life, and all acts stem from past acts, no one is responsible for present deeds.
shots.B12C362S23H04: Note 108: the battle shows design, not chance, and the correct reading of one word is hatham.
shots.B12C362S23H05: Note 109: Nilakantha reads the phrase as meaning through their own faults.
shots.B12C362S24H01: Note 110: a performer of a hundred sacrifices.
shots.B12C362S24H02: Note 111: a teacher who charges his pupils a fee for the scriptures.
shots.B12C362S24H03: Note 112: meaning not in a sacrifice.
shots.B12C362S24H04: Note 113: the word means one who intends to slay.
shots.B12C362S24H05: Note 114: one who knows that the Soma is offered to gratify the gods.
shots.B12C362S25H01: Note 115: the Krischara vow sets out a six-year fast with a fixed pattern of eating, to cleanse the sin of killing a Brahmin.
shots.B12C362S25H02: Note 116: a harder rule of fasting and limited eating over a longer cycle.
shots.B12C362S25H03: Note 117: the five products of the cow, besides earth, water, ashes, acid, and fire.
shots.B12C362S25H04: Note 118: examples of appropriation, untruth, and killing that are allowed to a king or a loyal servant.
shots.B12C362S25H05: Note 119: reciters of scripture were a profession, much like the rhapsodists of ancient Greece.
shots.B12C362S26H01: Note 120: a person who knows the Vedas.
shots.B12C362S26H02: Note 121: this verse, and the half of the next, appear with slight changes in Manu.
shots.B12C362S26H03: Note 122: Nilakantha's gloss is fanciful, and the plain meaning is that the speaker is about to lay down his life.
shots.B12C362S26H04: Note 123: the priest of the Kauravas.
shots.B12C362S26H05: Note 124: identifies the plants sami, pippala, palasa, and udumvara.
shots.B12C362S27H01: Note 125: the six expedients are peace, war, marching, halting, sowing dissension, and defence by alliances and forts.
shots.B12C362S27H02: Note 126: acting otherwise would have made the king ungrateful.
shots.B12C362S27H03: Note 127: the literal meaning of Purusha as applied to the Supreme Being is one that pervades all forms.
shots.B12C362S27H04: Note 128: Aditi, and her self as born in different shapes at different times.
shots.B12C362S27H05: Note 129: Yugas may mean the three ages or three pairs of virtues.
shots.B12C362S28H01: Note 130: a Virat is above an emperor and a Swarat above a Virat.
shots.B12C362S28H02: Note 131: Vishnu as a dwarf tricked the Asura Vali into giving up three worlds, which he then restored to Indra.
shots.B12C362S28H03: Note 132: the son of Uttanapada, who adored Vishnu from a young age in the Krita age and won valuable boons.
shots.B12C362S28H04: Note 133: Sudharman was the Kurus' priest, and the note asks how Dhaumya, the Pandavas' priest, had a home in the Kuru capital.
shots.B12C362S28H05: Note 134: the allusion is to Krishna's three strides, which covered the three worlds and deprived Vali of sovereignty.
shots.B12C362S29H01: Note 135: ordinary men have three states of consciousness, and the fourth, Turiya, is reached only by Yogins.
shots.B12C362S29H02: Note 136: mind is the seat of the senses and feelings, and the Bombay reading is correct here.
shots.B12C362S29H03: Note 137: the Supreme Being is called Hansa, the swan, and That, as in the Vedic formula, beyond words.
shots.B12C362S29H04: Note 138: Brahma has no attributes we can name.
shots.B12C362S29H05: Note 139: the Vaks are mantras, the Anuvaks are Brahmanas, the Nishads lead to knowledge of the gods, and the Upanishads deal with knowledge of the Soul.

B12C363.summary: This last section of the chapter has no narrative of its own in this file. It is a run of Ganguli's translator notes, numbered from 594 on, that explain Sanskrit words, variant readings, and the doctrine of Bhishma's teaching on the mind, the soul, yoga, the three qualities, and the illusion of the world. The notes also compare the teaching with Sankhya, Vedanta, Buddhist, and sceptical views of rebirth. They matter as the translator's guide to how the difficult closing doctrine should be read.

shots.B12C363S01H01: Note 594: the sacred thread is wound round the thumb, as the Grihyasutras prescribe.
shots.B12C363S01H02: Note 595: the recipient's formulas of satisfaction, and a note on krisara, a dish of rice and pulses.
shots.B12C363S01H03: Note 596: the polite form of address, bhavan, uses the third person, since the second person is too direct.
shots.B12C363S01H04: Note 597: the recollection of sins makes the sinner miserable, though the text does not say how sins reach him.
shots.B12C363S01H05: Note 598: merit and sin depend on the mind, so even mental harm to others is condemned.
shots.B12C363S02H01: Note 599: if the mind is sinful, no associate can help, since the mind alone is the cause of virtue.
shots.B12C363S02H02: Note 600: adhyatma covers whatever depends on the mind, including the yoga of the mind.
shots.B12C363S02H03: Note 601: the question seems a repetition, but it follows Bhishma's claim that righteousness belongs to the mind.
shots.B12C363S02H04: Note 602: the Sanskrit word vijnanani is better rendered as cognitions.
shots.B12C363S02H05: Note 603: the mind, understanding, and soul are distinguished, with the soul as a portion of the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C363S03H01: Note 604: Goodness covers high moral qualities, Passion covers love and worldly emotions, and Darkness covers anger and lust.
shots.B12C363S03H02: Note 605: the translator follows Nilakantha's grammar but finds the verse unclear, and asks whether Bhishma teaches idealism.
shots.B12C363S03H03: Note 606: followers of Reid, the note says, treated perceptions as modifications of the mind and denied the outside world.
shots.B12C363S03H04: Note 607: the ocean simile illustrates the rare feat of transcending the three attributes through yoga power.
shots.B12C363S03H05: Note 608: one should trace a harmful thought to its cause, which is Passion, and dispel it.
shots.B12C363S04H01: Note 609: the first two words of the second line repeat verse 5 of the earlier section.
shots.B12C363S04H02: Note 610: Nilakantha explains one word as due to great ill-luck.
shots.B12C363S04H03: Note 611: the translator does not follow Nilakantha in rendering this verse.
shots.B12C363S04H04: Note 612: the soul is a witness, not an actor, and the note compares this to the conscience as an impartial judge.
shots.B12C363S04H05: Note 613: such a person transcends the three qualities, instead of being carried along by them.
shots.B12C363S05H01: Note 614: Nilakantha treats the third line as elliptical and supplies a verb.
shots.B12C363S05H02: Note 615: explains several words, and gives the commentator's view that acts are a hindrance to liberation.
shots.B12C363S05H03: Note 616: explains words for lust and wrath, and says sinful acts bring fear both here and hereafter.
shots.B12C363S05H04: Note 617: Bhishma prefers the yoga that trains mind and understanding to Vedic rites, for quicker liberation.
shots.B12C363S05H05: Note 618: the soul-state is one of purity, lost through worldly attachment and regained by yoga.
shots.B12C363S06H01: Note 619: vichara, viveka, and vitarka are technical terms for stages of progress in yoga.
shots.B12C363S06H02: Note 620: all attainments come from exertion or destiny, and yoga felicity is reached by neither.
shots.B12C363S06H03: Note 621: the commentator takes Sankhya here to mean Vedanta inquiry.
shots.B12C363S06H04: Note 622: according to Sankhya, silent recitation of mantras is not needed, and mental meditation can lead to Brahma.
shots.B12C363S06H05: Note 623: silent recitation of Om may continue only until one sees one's own soul.
shots.B12C363S07H01: Note 624: the two paths are action, called pravritti, and abstention, called nivritti; the first gives rise to sacrifice.
shots.B12C363S07H02: Note 625: one must first cleanse the heart through the virtues already listed.
shots.B12C363S07H03: Note 626: samadhi is meditation with the senses drawn into the mind, fixed on Brahma alone.
shots.B12C363S07H04: Note 627: the goal of yoga is freedom from decay and death, a death at will, or absorption into Brahma.
shots.B12C363S07H05: Note 628: hell here means the opposite of liberation, since heaven still brings rebirth.
shots.B12C363S08H01: Note 629: even this is a kind of hell, since rebirth follows it.
shots.B12C363S08H02: Note 630: godlike powers such as becoming tiny or huge are below the goal of absorption into the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C363S08H03: Note 631: a faulty line in the Bengal texts is omitted in the Bombay text, which makes verses 10 and 11 couplets.
shots.B12C363S08H04: Note 632: the phrase is explained as giving up enjoyments without really being detached.
shots.B12C363S08H05: Note 633: in that state there are no forms to be objects, so all is pure knowledge.
shots.B12C363S09H01: Note 634: lists the six Angas of the Vedas: pronunciation, ritual, grammar, etymology, metre, and astronomy.
shots.B12C363S09H02: Note 635: an insight gained by intuition and not in the ordinary way.
shots.B12C363S09H03: Note 636: K.P. Singha mistranslates sadhaye, which means I go, and the Burdwan rendering is correct.
shots.B12C363S09H04: Note 637: work and abstention from work are the two courses of duty.
shots.B12C363S09H05: Note 638: Vikrita gave away a cow and transferred the merit of that gift to Virupa.
shots.B12C363S10H01: Note 639: a gleaner picks up single grains from the crevices of harvested fields.
shots.B12C363S10H02: Note 640: Virupa returns the merit of one cow, and Vikrita offers in return the merit of two cows he has given.
shots.B12C363S10H03: Note 641: the king says the dispute has come before him, and he must judge fairly without taking gifts as a Brahmin would.
shots.B12C363S10H04: Note 642: the king feels drawn to accept the gift, but kingly rules restrain him, so he offers his own merit in return.
shots.B12C363S10H05: Note 643: this is not liberation, only terminable felicity.
shots.B12C363S11H01: Note 644: the phrase means attaining emancipation or absorption into the essence of Brahma.
shots.B12C363S11H02: Note 645: the four means of knowledge are direct perception, revelation, inference, and intuition.
shots.B12C363S11H03: Note 646: six states of suffering, hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, disease, and death, and sixteen parts, the breaths, senses, and mind.
shots.B12C363S11H04: Note 647: K.P. Singha misunderstands three ends: absorption, terminable pleasure, and the happiness of freedom from desire.
shots.B12C363S11H05: Note 648: the king asks the Brahmin to share with him the rewards he has won.
shots.B12C363S12H01: Note 649: yogins attain Brahma even in this life, while reciters attain him only after death.
shots.B12C363S12H02: Note 650: the speaker professes to worship a god he does not know, which Vrihaspati calls false, and asks how to be rescued from such falsehood.
shots.B12C363S12H03: Note 651: explains the six Vedangas, covering prosody, astronomy, etymology, rites, and pronunciation.
shots.B12C363S12H04: Note 652: those who think happiness is not eternal drop pious acts and seek knowledge and liberation.
shots.B12C363S12H05: Note 653: the meaning of hell in such passages was explained earlier.
shots.B12C363S13H01: Note 654: Vrihaspati means by acts sacrifices and other observances, which he says are needed to secure the aims of life.
shots.B12C363S13H02: Note 655: one should practise acts as a preparation and then give them up for the higher end, so they help toward Brahma indirectly.
shots.B12C363S13H03: Note 656: mind and acts create all things, and both are good paths if the fruits of acts are mentally abandoned.
shots.B12C363S13H04: Note 657: Nilakantha reads the grammar of the first line differently, and the translator proposes a better construction.
shots.B12C363S13H05: Note 658: acts have three kinds of attributes, good, passionate, and dark, and the mind determines the kind of fruit.
shots.B12C363S14H01: Note 659: this is a cruce, and Nilakantha's reading is correct; the words are taken as unconnected.
shots.B12C363S14H02: Note 660: acts done by the body lead to heaven, while liberation must be sought through the mind.
shots.B12C363S14H03: Note 661: liberation needs freedom from all acts, including recitation and meditation, since these are acts too.
shots.B12C363S14H04: Note 662: the note explains the words as referring to taste and the other senses.
shots.B12C363S14H05: Note 663: existent is the atom, non-existent is space, and existent-and-non-existent is Maya or illusion.
shots.B12C363S15H01: Note 664: the commentator explains the phrase as lacking any notion of a knower.
shots.B12C363S15H02: Note 665: one sees one's own soul.
shots.B12C363S15H03: Note 666: the soul divides into a thousand forms, like the moon's image in agitated water.
shots.B12C363S15H04: Note 667: good and evil fruits dwell together, and knowledge resides in the material body, which is the analogy.
shots.B12C363S15H05: Note 668: the translator cannot see why the image of lamps set on trees is introduced.
shots.B12C363S16H01: Note 669: fire, wind, sunlight, and rivers all return after they seem to die, which shows the body changes form without being destroyed.
shots.B12C363S16H02: Note 670: the soul exists in its own nature, unaffected by qualities and accidents.
shots.B12C363S16H03: Note 671: the correct readings are samanah and sabuddhih, and the Bombay edition has a misprint.
shots.B12C363S16H04: Note 672: the translators misread linga in verses 14 and 15, which here means the gross body.
shots.B12C363S16H05: Note 673: the commentator cites a parallel passage in the Gita about the senses above the body.
shots.B12C363S17H01: Note 674: the verse suggests the Rishis knew spectacles or a microscope, which the commentator calls upanetra.
shots.B12C363S17H02: Note 675: explains the phrase by death on sleep.
shots.B12C363S17H03: Note 676: explains words such as simultaneous and independent, and says a dreaming soul is distinct from senses and body.
shots.B12C363S17H04: Note 677: the soul knows pleasures and pains that arise from the three attributes, but does not enjoy them and is a silent witness.
shots.B12C363S17H05: Note 678: as wind is separate from the fire in a stick, so the soul is separate from the senses.
shots.B12C363S18H01: Note 679: the Bengal reading indriyanam is adopted, and the Bombay reading is set aside.
shots.B12C363S18H02: Note 680: a tree is not before birth and not after destruction, so its form is only an interim state.
shots.B12C363S18H03: Note 681: the translators misrender the second line, and the words jneyam and jnanabhisamhitam name Brahma.
shots.B12C363S18H04: Note 682: tamas is Rahu, and the moon's waxing and waning serves as the simile for the approach of darkness.
shots.B12C363S18H05: Note 683: in dream and deep sleep the subtle form is detached from the body, which shows emancipation is possible.
shots.B12C363S19H01: Note 684: the form caswasasya is explained as naming the main attribute that goes with an object.
shots.B12C363S19H02: Note 685: the word indriyarupani means forms perceived through the senses.
shots.B12C363S19H03: Note 686: the objects to be abandoned are those the senses grasp and the subtle forms of primordial matter.
shots.B12C363S19H04: Note 687: the phrase means that one regains one's real nature.
shots.B12C363S19H05: Note 688: the Bombay reading aptavan is adopted, and pravritti dharma is the religion of action.
shots.B12C363S20H01: Note 689: abstaining from objects conquers desire only in part, and desire is suppressed only when one sees one's soul.
shots.B12C363S20H02: Note 690: the first clause denies an objective world, so objects have only a subjective existence, which the note compares with European views of matter.
shots.B12C363S20H03: Note 691: te is explained as Brahmabhigatah, and K.P. Singha's last foot is wrong.
shots.B12C363S20H04: Note 692: te in the first line means tava, your.
shots.B12C363S20H05: Note 693: the words jnanam and jneyam are used inconsistently in the original.
shots.B12C363S21H01: Note 694: ordinary men treat attributes as separate from substances, but the first step is to see them as one, a view close to European idealism, and then contemplation annihilates attributes to reach Brahma.
shots.B12C363S21H02: Note 695: antaratmanudarsini means that which has the inner self as witness, and the Burdwan rendering of the second line is wrong.
shots.B12C363S21H03: Note 696: the first knowledge is of the true link between soul and not-soul, and fruits are the bodies gained in rebirth.
shots.B12C363S21H04: Note 697: sorrow comes from the relation of knower and known, and whatever depends on that relation is transitory.
shots.B12C363S21H05: Note 698: the translator takes the plain meaning rather than Nilakantha's learned explanation.
shots.B12C363S22H01: Note 699: yogins lured by the wish for extraordinary powers and the bliss of highest heaven do not behold the Supreme.
shots.B12C363S22H02: Note 700: the word gunam means attributes, so the phrase means objects possessed of attributes.
shots.B12C363S22H03: Note 701: the so-called external world has no objective existence, so the mind sees and hears itself.
shots.B12C363S22H04: Note 702: a cruce; the note reads gunadana as the withdrawal of the senses into the mind and then into understanding, which yields the powers of yogins.
shots.B12C363S22H05: Note 703: happiness and sorrow have an end, and the soul will reach its final resting place, which the note links to a doctrine of endless spiritual improvement.
shots.B12C363S23H01: Note 704: rishavam sarvattwam means the bull of the Sattwatas, and here it refers to righteous persons who prize Goodness.
shots.B12C363S23H02: Note 705: Prajapati means lord of creatures, a name for sons of Brahman who begot children.
shots.B12C363S23H03: Note 706: Samavartin is another name for Yama, the punisher of the wicked.
shots.B12C363S23H04: Note 707: nirapekshan is explained as gazing only toward hell, and the Burdwan idea of nomads is unsupported.
shots.B12C363S23H05: Note 708: K.P. Singha takes Naravara as a tribe, which the translator calls a careless blunder.
shots.B12C363S24H01: Note 709: the sandhyakala is the junction of the Treta and Dwapara ages, a time of terrible famine when Viswamitra ate a dog's haunch.
shots.B12C363S24H02: Note 710: the correct reading is mahatmana, which points to Krishna, and the Burdwan translator misrenders it.
shots.B12C363S24H03: Note 711: the verse shows a dispute over Krishna's supremacy, since Sisupala and Jarasandha refused to accept his divinity.
shots.B12C363S24H04: Note 712: the etymology of Sanatana given here is fanciful, since the word normally means eternal.
shots.B12C363S24H05: Note 713: atma atmanah is explained as the true nature of the living soul.
shots.B12C363S25H01: Note 714: the word swamatmanam is explained as the true identity of the self.
shots.B12C363S25H02: Note 715: if all men share one material cause, why do the Srutis and Smritis differ about their duties?
shots.B12C363S25H03: Note 716: at the start of each age the rules of conduct and marriage arise anew, and knowledge of duty grows with the human race until the Creator withdraws all.
shots.B12C363S25H04: Note 717: the word here means the body.
shots.B12C363S25H05: Note 718: a river cannot exist without water, and the soul cannot exist without a body, except when yoga separates them.
shots.B12C363S26H01: Note 719: the mind has no existence apart from the soul, like the second moon seen in water.
shots.B12C363S26H02: Note 720: swabhavahetuja bhava means the virtuous and vicious propensities from past acts, while all else comes from Avidya or Maya.
shots.B12C363S26H03: Note 721: verses 3 and 4 are linked; propensities born of ignorance are the same as the lower propensities, while higher aspirations come from Brahma direct.
shots.B12C363S26H04: Note 722: before creation there was only the soul with knowledge, and its connection with the world is neither necessary nor eternal.
shots.B12C363S26H05: Note 723: the soul's sense that it is a man or an animal is like dreaming that one is a king, and the origin of this delusion cannot be traced.
shots.B12C363S27H01: Note 724: desires lead the soul into a form, acts lead to new desires, and the circle of existence has no beginning or end.
shots.B12C363S27H02: Note 725: the cause is ignorance and the effect is the body and senses, and the acts done through them become causes of new states.
shots.B12C363S27H03: Note 726: as wind stays pure while bearing dust, the soul remains unattached to body and senses.
shots.B12C363S27H04: Note 727: the Vedas urge both action and abstention, action as a step toward abstention, and few understand this.
shots.B12C363S27H05: Note 728: deha-yapanam means severing the body's bond, and acts should be done only to purify, not for the fruit of heaven.
shots.B12C363S28H01: Note 729: vipakram is explained as unripe, and apakvakashayakhya as the teaching given to one whose passions are not matured.
shots.B12C363S28H02: Note 730: anuplavan means following, and akramya means crushing.
shots.B12C363S28H03: Note 731: vijnana here means the loss or absence of knowledge.
shots.B12C363S28H04: Note 732: yathartham means for the true aims of life, acting righteously and gaining liberation.
shots.B12C363S28H05: Note 733: the soul was once pure knowledge, and union with ignorance created the universe, so consciousness is the root of all sorrow.
shots.B12C363S29H01: Note 734: if all rests on consciousness, why are waking perceptions uniform unlike the irregular dreams, and the answer is that past acts produce this uniformity, as time produces the seasons.
shots.B12C363S29H02: Note 735: the last line is expanded to make the sense of nasyati clear, following Nilakantha's simile.
shots.B12C363S29H03: Note 736: the Srutis say Brahma has knowledge, ignorance, and Maya, and it is Maya that binds the living souls to worldly things.
shots.B12C363S29H04: Note 737: mana is worship of one's own self, darpa is freedom from restraint, and ahankara is disregard of others, and ahankara is not consciousness.
shots.B12C363S29H05: Note 738: kritalakshanah is explained as kritaswikarah, meaning that which is accepted or made.
shots.B12C363S30H01: Note 739: Prakriti binds the soul and causes its birth, women are Prakriti and men are souls, so men should avoid women; the note notes the popularity of this doctrine in Indian languages.
shots.B12C363S30H02: Note 740: kritya is the power of Atharvan rites, and women are as dangerous as such rites, sunk so deeply in Rajas as to be invisible.
shots.B12C363S30H03: Note 741: vermin spring from sweat and filth, and children from the seed, so one's offspring are like vermin on the body, and wisdom teaches indifference to both.
shots.B12C363S30H04: Note 742: Rajas causes the impulse to act, Sattwa leads to Brahma, and both rest on Tamas.
shots.B12C363S30H05: Note 743: knowledge overspread by darkness is the seed of the body, and the Burdwan and K.P. Singha versions misread the second line.
shots.B12C363S31H01: Note 744: in the womb the soul remembers past acts, and these shape the senses and the character of the new life.
shots.B12C363S31H02: Note 745: the translator disagrees with Nilakantha's grammar, since tebhyah tyagat is not a violation, and the ablative is not rare here.
shots.B12C363S31H03: Note 746: the senses come from Rajas, so the conquest of Rajas, with sharpened vision from scripture, is needed.
shots.B12C363S31H04: Note 747: the note explains that the two classes of senses, of knowledge and of action, are escaped from rebirth in liberation.
shots.B12C363S31H05: Note 748: arthasamanyam is explained as the highest liberation, and the Pravritti religion cannot reach it, though its followers gain good qualities.
shots.B12C363S32H01: Note 749: the Krichchra vow is a set of fasts, including three days standing in water up to the chin.
shots.B12C363S32H02: Note 750: the three Riks begin with ritam and satyam, and every Brahmin who knows his prayers knows them well.
shots.B12C363S32H03: Note 751: the verse describes yoga, sending the breaths up the Sushumna duct and reducing the attributes to the state beyond the senses.
shots.B12C363S32H04: Note 752: the knowledge beyond the senses is real, and a sage who has it sees the world as mind, and such a mind is eternal, free of passion, and luminous; this is liberation in life.
shots.B12C363S32H05: Note 753: the phrase means freeing oneself from Passion and Darkness by practising abstention from acts.
shots.B12C363S33H01: Note 754: adatte comes from a root meaning to cut, and manasam volam means desires, so a man of ripe understanding gains knowledge that does not decay with age.
shots.B12C363S33H02: Note 755: compassion can lead to excess attachment, as with Bharata and his deer, who was reborn as a deer for thinking of one at death.
shots.B12C363S33H03: Note 756: K.P. Singha translates this verse wrongly, and the Burdwan rendering is correct.
shots.B12C363S33H04: Note 757: the buddhi here is intelligence cleansed by scripture, and samahitam manak means mind freed from anger and malice.
shots.B12C363S33H05: Note 758: one should not covet kingdoms or thrones, and the non-existent objects are sons and wives who are dead, unborn, or unwed.
shots.B12C363S34H01: Note 759: samsara means this world and the next, and words spoken are never destroyed, affecting speaker and listener over countless lives, which the note compares to Babbage's view of indestructible energy.
shots.B12C363S34H02: Note 760: confession of one's acts destroys their effects and stops them recurring.
shots.B12C363S34H03: Note 761: robbers laden with booty are always at risk, and unintelligent men bearing life's burdens are likewise liable to destruction.
shots.B12C363S34H05: Note 763: the reading prakasela is adopted, with Nilakantha's interpretation.
shots.B12C363S35H01: Note 764: kulmasha is ripe grain or seeds, pinyaka is an oil cake of sesame or mustard, and yavaka is unripe barley boiled in hot water.
shots.B12C363S35H02: Note 765: before creation the soul had only knowledge, and ignorance from Brahma made it an ordinary creature, so it took its own products for things independent of itself.
shots.B12C363S35H03: Note 766: the correct reading is upagatasprihah, and the first verse is for yogins, the second for yogins and others alike.
shots.B12C363S35H04: Note 767: dreams come from impressions of this life and of past lives, which the Soul keeps and calls up, a view the note links to Avicenna's theory.
shots.B12C363S35H05: Note 768: one of the three attributes, brought to the mind by past acts, makes the subtle elements produce images that match it.
shots.B12C363S36H01: Note 769: only yoga can destroy these images, since they spring from desires generated by past acts.
shots.B12C363S36H02: Note 770: the Bombay reading Manohrishyan is better.
shots.B12C363S36H03: Note 771: the external and inner worlds both come from consciousness, which comes from delusion affecting the soul, so the soul knowing itself gains omniscience.
shots.B12C363S36H04: Note 772: the body is the door of dreams because it comes from past acts, and in dreamless sleep the senses sink into the mind and the mind into the soul.
shots.B12C363S36H05: Note 773: a purified mind gains omniscience and omnipotence.
shots.B12C363S37H01: Note 774: the Burdwan translator jumbles Nilakantha's gloss and makes nonsense of both text and gloss.
shots.B12C363S37H02: Note 775: Brahma cannot be seized like a creature; it is understood only by reason and analogy, through withdrawal of the senses.
shots.B12C363S37H03: Note 776: the commentator takes the Rishi to be Narayana, friend of Nara, whose retreat at Vadari Vyasa later used.
shots.B12C363S37H04: Note 777: the Pravritti religion of acts cannot free from rebirth, while the Nivritti religion of abstention leads to Brahma.
shots.B12C363S37H05: Note 778: nidarsarkah is explained as wishing to see.
shots.B12C363S38H01: Note 779: the unmanifest is primordial matter, and beyond both matter and Purusha is the Supreme Soul, Brahma.
shots.B12C363S38H02: Note 780: Purusha is non-creating and beyond the three attributes, as the commentator explains.
shots.B12C363S38H03: Note 781: asamhatau means utterly separate, and the two Purushas are the chit-soul and the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C363S38H04: Note 782: four topics are set out: how Prakriti and Purusha resemble and differ, and how Purusha and Iswara do; the four grounds are no beginning or end, consciousness, distinction, and activity.
shots.B12C363S38H05: Note 783: the note says the common saying about yogins beholding the Lord is the praise of yoga.
shots.B12C363S39H01: Note 784: the commentator says the verse means dying at a sacred place such as Kasi, where Siva himself guides the dying man to liberation.
shots.B12C363S39H02: Note 785: divested of Rajas means freed from the senses and their pleasures.
shots.B12C363S39H03: Note 786: the destruction of the gross body means escape from rebirth, and the karana body is a subtler form than the linga-sarira.
shots.B12C363S39H04: Note 787: when knowledge of Brahma arises, the mistaken who take the body for the self are caught in endless births and deaths without liberation.
shots.B12C363S39H05: Note 788: the commentator takes patience as staying in yoga posture and adoring the senses as Prana and the Indriyas; the translator doubts this leads to Brahma.
shots.B12C363S40H01: Note 789: the stages from the Gita are senses, objects, mind, understanding, soul, Unmanifest, and Purusha, and nothing is above Purusha.
shots.B12C363S40H02: Note 790: a flash of lightning seen again and again becomes a mass of blazing light, which may be the speaker's meaning.
shots.B12C363S40H03: Note 791: the Bengal texts make verse 28 a triplet, and the correct word is dehantam.
shots.B12C363S40H04: Note 792: the three are Mara, meaning the effects, Prakriti, their material cause, and Purusha, the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C363S40H05: Note 793: another reading names censurers of the various Lokayatika sects.
shots.B12C363S41H01: Note 794: the mind is described as having five currents.
shots.B12C363S41H02: Note 795: the five sheaths are food, breath, mind, knowledge, and bliss, and the note refers the reader to Wilson's dictionary.
shots.B12C363S41H03: Note 796: the verb nyavedayat means started for discourse, and the Burdwan rendering of it is incorrect.
shots.B12C363S41H04: Note 797: the Burdwan version wrongly says Asuri learned from his disciple's questions, while samprishtah means carefully asked.
shots.B12C363S41H05: Note 798: kutumvini means a matron or a householder's wife.
shots.B12C363S42H01: Note 799: the speaker is either Markandeya or Sanatkumara, according to the commentator.
shots.B12C363S42H02: Note 800: the Sankhya view is that every state of life brings sorrow, and the goal of that philosophy is the permanent end of sorrow.
shots.B12C363S42H03: Note 801: these are the marks of the delusion under which man is born and lives until he conquers sorrow.
shots.B12C363S42H04: Note 802: the death of the soul is its extinction, the verse gives the sceptics' opinion, and K.P. Singha's rendering is wrong.
shots.B12C363S42H05: Note 803: this and the following verses are the sceptics' arguments.
shots.B12C363S43H01: Note 804: verse 29 is very terse and lists the heads of sceptical arguments that nothing exists beyond the seen and felt body.
shots.B12C363S43H02: Note 805: the translator uses more words than the Sanskrit, and calls these verses cruces meant to stagger Ganesa.
shots.B12C363S43H03: Note 806: the commentator calls the rebirth theory in verse 34 Buddhist, and verse 35 refutes it, since Buddhists deny an indestructible soul.
shots.B12C363S43H04: Note 807: the acts of one person do not affect another, so no proof exists that acts in one life carry over to a different being, using the example of Chaitra and Maitra.
shots.B12C363S43H05: Note 808: the translator's literal rendering of the second line would be unintelligible, so a fuller version is given.
shots.B12C363S44H01: Note 809: if Consciousness is destroyed and reborn, Buddhist Nirvana cannot be the final liberation of the Brahmanical texts.
shots.B12C363S44H02: Note 810: the Buddhists gain nothing by a permanent soul, since the Brahmanical soul has no attributes and a soul with attributes would be destructible.
shots.B12C363S44H03: Note 811: the senses merge into their causes, and the speaker argues that a substance also perishes with its attributes, so the analogy fails.
shots.B12C363S44H04: Note 812: here the speaker attacks the orthodox Brahmanical doctrine of the soul.
shots.B12C363S44H05: Note 813: this is perhaps because such doctrines are based on Revelation.
shots.B12C363S45H01: Note 814: the first five are effects of intelligence, the breaths come from wind, and the juices and humours from digestive heat.
shots.B12C363S45H02: Note 815: intelligence is called avyaya and mahat because it leads to the eternal Brahma, and tattwanischaya is the seed of liberation.
shots.B12C363S45H03: Note 816: the path meant is yoga.
shots.B12C363S45H04: Note 817: casting off the mind casts off the five organs of action, and casting off the understanding casts off the organs of knowledge.
shots.B12C363S45H05: Note 818: in each of these operations three causes must exist together.
shots.B12C363S46H01: Note 819: the note infers that when functions are destroyed the organs and the mind are destroyed too.
shots.B12C363S46H02: Note 820: the note explains na in the verse as the nominative of nri, meaning the dreamer, and praises Nilakantha's ingenuity.
shots.B12C363S46H03: Note 821: dreamless sleep is a temporary dissociation of soul from mind and senses caused by Tamas, and differs from the eternal felicity of liberation.
shots.B12C363S46H04: Note 822: liberation is untouched by darkness, though it may seem like dreamless sleep, and the verse says no trace of sorrow is seen in it.
shots.B12C363S46H05: Note 823: in both sleep and liberation the qualities are discarded, and swakarmapratyayah refers to rebirth from past acts.
shots.B12C363S47H01: Note 824: creatures exist through Avidya, desire, and acts, and the note asks how the eternal soul could be called destructible, which it treats as an unanswerable question.
shots.B12C363S47H02: Note 825: the gross body dissolves into the subtle, the subtle into the potential form, and that into the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C363S47H03: Note 826: merit and sin are destroyed when one is unattached and practises abstention, and the phrase refers to Saguna Brahma.
shots.B12C363S47H04: Note 827: urnanabha means a worm that spins thread, here a silk-worm, which completes the analogy.
shots.B12C363S47H05: Note 828: the Burdwan rendering of nipatyasaktah is wrong, and K.P. Singha gives the sense but changes another word.
shots.B12C363S48H01: Note 829: samudayah is explained as hetu, cause.
shots.B12C363S48H02: Note 830: the verse refers to giving food and clothes to the poor and needy in times of scarcity.
shots.B12C363S48H03: Note 831: the reading vrataluvdhah is preferred, and the Bengal reading would mean that men are deceived by their vows.
shots.B12C363S48H04: Note 832: Bhishma's two answers show that giving pain to others, such as sacrificing animals, and giving pain to oneself are both censurable.
shots.B12C363S48H05: Note 833: existence and non-existence both come into being and cease, meaning all phenomena appear and disappear.
shots.B12C363S49H01: Note 834: this refers to the theory that the soul is really inactive amid its seeming activity.
shots.B12C363S49H02: Note 835: the Burdwan rendering of the second line is wrong, since it has Gandharvas dance before thee.
shots.B12C363S49H03: Note 836: both vernacular translators misread the verse; Vali circled the earth hurling a wooden samya, marking out sacrificial spaces.
shots.B12C363S49H04: Note 837: pravyaharaya is explained as meaning at a great distance.
shots.B12C363S49H05: Note 838: he who regards himself as the slayer is steeped in ignorance, as the soul never acts, which the note compares with the Gita.
shots.B12C363S50H01: Note 839: the note compares this with the saying usually credited to Napoleon that St Helena was written in the book of Fate.
shots.B12C363S50H02: Note 840: a literal rendering would be that Time cooks everything.
shots.B12C363S50H03: Note 841: bhujyante is explained as meaning are consumed or gathered in.
shots.B12C363S50H04: Note 842: Brahma is indestructible as the living soul, and destructible as it appears in the form of the not-Self.
shots.B12C363S50H05: Note 843: the translator expands verse 50, since a literal version would be unintelligible.
shots.B12C363S51H01: Note 844: a thing that is borne with great difficulty.
shots.B12C363S51H02: Note 845: literally a desire for action, meaning abundance produced by labour.
shots.B12C363S51H03: Note 846: all the names given imply plenty and prosperity.
shots.B12C363S51H04: Note 847: a person whose hands are not washed after rising from or during his meals.
shots.B12C363S51H05: Note 848: the Puranic view is that the world stands around Meru, and that in the Savarnika Manwantara darkness will surround all but the top of Meru.
shots.B12C363S52H01: Note 849: all things are destructible instead of being eternal.
shots.B12C363S52H02: Note 850: hridyam means the true nature, and kalyanam means liberation.
shots.B12C363S52H03: Note 851: one who strives for liberation through yoga gains wonderful powers, and his objects follow without his seeking them.
shots.B12C363S52H04: Note 852: a wise man never regards himself as the actor and so feels no sorrow, while a fool who thinks himself the actor cannot bear sorrow calmly.
shots.B12C363S52H05: Note 853: the verse says right conclusions about duties are very rare.
shots.B12C363S53H01: Note 854: the speaker is said to resemble Gautama, who was calm after Indra violated Ahalya, not the passion-ruled Indra, and so Namuchi was master of his senses.
shots.B12C363S53H02: Note 855: the we is a pronoun of dignity that refers to the speaker alone.
shots.B12C363S53H03: Note 856: the sentence is a question, and K.P. Singha is right where the Burdwan translator is wrong.
shots.B12C363S53H04: Note 857: the Asuras had long stopped sacrifices, and with Indra's victory the sacrifices and universal peace returned.
shots.B12C363S53H05: Note 858: dhruvadwarabhavam is probably a Himalayan pass, though the vernacular translators took it as the Pole-star region, and the Puranic river from Vishnu's foot is mentioned.
shots.B12C363S54H01: Note 859: the note recalls the discourse between Mejnour and a neophyte in Lord Lytton's Zanoni on the Apennine ridges.
shots.B12C363S54H02: Note 860: K.P. Singha translates this verse wrongly.
shots.B12C363S54H03: Note 861: explains uchchhishta, meaning the hand or leftover food made unclean by eating, which is a particular Hindu notion.
shots.B12C363S54H05: Note 863: explains payasa as rice in sugared milk, krisara as milk, sesame, and rice, and sashkuli as a pie of rice or barley.
shots.B12C363S55H01: Note 864: no merit attaches to feeding an unlettered person.
shots.B12C363S55H02: Note 865: the correct reading is vyabhajat, since the Bengal reading would repeat the first line.
shots.B12C363S55H03: Note 866: everything except the Supreme Soul can be affected by Prakriti, which is why Brahma is said to be above Prakriti.
shots.B12C363S55H04: Note 867: the verb nihnuvanti means conceal, that is, do not brag of, and both vernacular translators misrender this verse.
shots.B12C363S55H05: Note 868: K.P. Singha mistranslates this verse.
shots.B12C363S56H01: Note 869: the Burdwan translator misunderstands anavajnata, and K.P. Singha skips it.
shots.B12C363S56H02: Note 870: a householder who is truly unattached to wife, children, and possessions is compared to a lotus leaf that water does not soak, which is more meritorious than fleeing from desire.
shots.B12C363S56H03: Note 871: the words kalajnanena nishthitam set limits to the periods of creation and dissolution, as the days and nights of Brahman.
shots.B12C363S56H04: Note 872: agre is explained as before creation.
shots.B12C363S56H05: Note 873: the Krita age lasts 4,800 years, the Treta 3,600, the Dwapara 2,400, and the Kali 1,200, in years of the deities, and verses 15 to 17 and 20 to 21 occur in Manusmriti.
shots.B12C363S57H01: Note 874: this verse occurs in Manusmriti with a slightly different reading, and the translator follows Medhatithi's gloss.
shots.B12C363S57H02: Note 875: the total of 12,000 years makes a Devayuga, and a thousand Devayugas make a day of Brahman.
shots.B12C363S57H03: Note 876: the external world is nothing but Mind transformed, which is why Mind is called Vyaktatmaka, and the note records a difference in how some texts divide the section.
shots.B12C363S57H04: Note 877: tejomayam is explained as having the principle of desire within it, without which creation could not happen.
shots.B12C363S57H05: Note 878: Mahat means pure or subtle intelligence, from which the manifest world starts.
shots.B12C363S58H01: Note 879: the seven great entities are Mahat, Mind, and the five elemental entities of space and the rest.
shots.B12C363S58H02: Note 880: verses 4 to 7 occur in Manusmriti, corresponding to its verses 75 to 78.
shots.B12C363S58H03: Note 881: the living soul is called Purusha, the resident of the body, because Avidya covers it and it takes a case of primordial matter shaped by acts.
shots.B12C363S58H04: Note 882: the seven entities combine into the limbs, then into the full body with its parts, and the subtle body receives the residue of acts, so creation runs in a series.
shots.B12C363S58H05: Note 883: the six and ten parts are the five gross elements and the eleven senses, the gross body forms first, then the subtle body, and then the Soul enters to witness.
shots.B12C363S59H01: Note 884: this refers to the variety of beings and of the relations between them.
shots.B12C363S59H02: Note 885: anubhe is explained as beyond both, and the Sattwasthas are those who regard Brahma as the sole cause.
shots.B12C363S59H03: Note 886: the Vedas are speech, so the Creator uttered words before creating, and the note notes a close resemblance to the first chapter of Genesis.
shots.B12C363S59H04: Note 887: all things were made well by Brahma, and the note again compares the words of Genesis, where God saw that things were good.
shots.B12C363S59H05: Note 888: nama means the Rigveda, bheda means the wife, tapah means penance, karma means daily rites, yama means sacrifice, akhya means good works, aloka means three kinds of meditation, and siddhi means liberation in this life.
shots.B12C363S60H01: Note 889: gahanam means the inconceivable Brahma, and vedavadeshu means the words of the Vedas.
shots.B12C363S60H02: Note 890: in the other ages people perform Vedic acts from low motives, and even in the Kali age such rites are known but done for sordid gain.
shots.B12C363S60H03: Note 891: the construction of this verse is set out, following the commentator.
shots.B12C363S60H04: Note 892: mind is the essence of all the manifest, and the swallowing up is the dissolution of the outer universe, but the section seems to describe the yogin's withdrawal of the senses.
shots.B12C363S60H05: Note 893: verses 16 and 17 are a yoga mystery, and the translator compares them to a proposition of the Principia that a reader must study first.
shots.B12C363S61H01: Note 894: jatakarma is a rite with Vedic mantras after a child's birth, and many such rites follow until the end of pupilage.
shots.B12C363S61H02: Note 895: no fee is charged for tuition, though the pupil may give a final fee after studies, set by the teacher.
shots.B12C363S61H03: Note 896: by children one pays the debt to ancestors, by study the debt to the Rishis, and by sacrifice the debt to the gods.
shots.B12C363S61H04: Note 897: taking anything from a daughter's father-in-law or relatives is a deadly sin, and those who sell their daughters in marriage are counted fallen.
shots.B12C363S61H05: Note 898: a householder must honour the gods and the Pitris, and a Brahmin has no means for this but accepting gifts, so such acceptance is not sinful.
shots.B12C363S62H01: Note 899: kritadapi is explained as cooked food.
shots.B12C363S62H02: Note 900: no gift is too valuable for such persons.
shots.B12C363S62H03: Note 901: the first and fourth verses are triplets in the Bengal texts.
shots.B12C363S62H05: Note 903: the note praises the image of the trees of benevolence that creatures carried down the river of Time may catch hold of, and says the Burdwan translator misunderstands the image.
shots.B12C363S63H01: Note 904: K.P. Singha misunderstands this verse, and the Burdwan translator is also inaccurate.
shots.B12C363S63H02: Note 905: sets out the conditions of yoga: a clean solitary place, abstention from food and amusements, faith in the scriptures, pure food, control of the senses, and reflection on birth, death, and sorrow.
shots.B12C363S63H03: Note 906: explains the parts of the chariot as images of virtues, naming the seat, fence, pole, axle, yoke, wheel, rim, hub, and goad.
shots.B12C363S63H04: Note 907: following Hamilton's faculties, dharana is the representative faculty by which the mind is held on one image, and yogins train it first.
shots.B12C363S63H05: Note 908: the seven kinds of dharana belong to earth, wind, space, water, fire, consciousness, and understanding.
shots.B12C363S64H01: Note 909: these are explained further below.
shots.B12C363S64H02: Note 910: the construction of these lines is difficult, and the note says yogatah means according to rules, and vikrama means the order of conceptions.
shots.B12C363S64H03: Note 911: pasyatah means of that which sees, namely the Atman or Soul.
shots.B12C363S64H04: Note 912: the Understanding is called the soul of the five elements and of individuality because these rest on it.
shots.B12C363S64H05: Note 913: all that is manifest springs from the Unmanifest Supreme Soul, which the yogin sees in everything.
shots.B12C363S65H01: Note 914: na kritina means kriti eva, and nirakriti means regardless of dress, and K.P. Singha misrenders both.
shots.B12C363S65H02: Note 915: the man who has neither friend nor foe regards all creatures with equal benevolence, and takes praise and blame alike.
shots.B12C363S65H03: Note 916: extraordinary powers come to yogins, and one who is led by them falls into hell, while one who transcends them gains liberation.
shots.B12C363S65H04: Note 917: dhirah means one who meditates, and santi means liberation, and the note says the speaker prefers Sankhya here.
shots.B12C363S65H05: Note 918: compare the Gita, chapter 5, verses 4 and 5.
shots.B12C363S66H01: Note 919: brahmanam is an Arsha form of brahmam.
shots.B12C363S66H02: Note 920: vidya is the teaching that dispels error, like seeing a cord as a snake, and nivritti is the doctrine of the Sunyavadins and Lokayatikas, who seek annihilation.
shots.B12C363S66H03: Note 921: the construction is set out, and the commentator takes the speaker to be attacking the Sunyavadins, who say the world appears by its own nature.
shots.B12C363S66H04: Note 922: the Bombay text reads putwatrinamishikamva.
shots.B12C363S66H05: Note 923: enam is singular, and the speaker rejects both the Sunyavadin and Lokayatika views of Nature as the cause, since both are false.
shots.B12C363S67H01: Note 924: both vernacular translators skip paribhava, which means the existence of the others, and the two terms refer to the Nihilists and the Lokayatikas.
shots.B12C363S67H02: Note 925: wisdom achieves ends by applying means, and nature does not build palaces, so exertion answers both Nihilists and Lokayatikas.
shots.B12C363S67H03: Note 926: para means the Chit or Soul, avara means all else, and prajna, jnana, and vidya are equivalent.
shots.B12C363S67H04: Note 927: cheshta means intelligent energy, both mental and physical, that distinguishes things.
shots.B12C363S67H05: Note 928: the itarani are birds of the air, khechara, not Pisachas, though Pisachas may belong to that class.
shots.B12C363S68H01: Note 929: the foremost are foremost, and the middling are observers of caste duties, so popular opinion is taken first before the higher view.
shots.B12C363S68H02: Note 930: the Vedas were not yet written down, so their contents rested in the memory of those who knew them.
shots.B12C363S68H03: Note 931: knowledge of the Soul means understanding birth and death, and avoiding rebirth, while the ignorant keep going round in rebirths.
shots.B12C363S68H04: Note 932: the phrase means the power that comes of yoga.
shots.B12C363S68H05: Note 933: para means high, often Brahma or the Soul, and the Burdwan rendering as other scriptures is wrong.
shots.B12C363S69H01: Note 934: one should see everything as one's own, and yoga leads to this, and the true Brahmana who realises it is a god on earth; adhiyajna and adhidaivata mean the Soul.
shots.B12C363S69H02: Note 935: the difference between anta and nidhan is not clear, and K.P. Singha's rendering is correct while the Burdwan version is nonsense.
shots.B12C363S69H03: Note 936: the question is whether karma is obligatory or optional, and since knowledge is needed for liberation, acts may be needed as means to it.
shots.B12C363S69H04: Note 937: the note sets out the construction of the difficult first line, and admires Nilakantha's patience.
shots.B12C363S69H05: Note 938: daiva is explained as fate or time, which the translator renders as necessity, while vritti means conduct and avivekam means a combination of the three.
shots.B12C363S70H01: Note 939: inspired with doubt refers to doubts about the Srutis, and tranquil souls are those free of doubt.
shots.B12C363S70H02: Note 940: in the Treta and later ages people devoted themselves to one Veda only, while the men of the Krita age treated all the Vedas as one.
shots.B12C363S70H03: Note 941: by penance the living soul gains the power to create and reaches Brahma and universal power.
shots.B12C363S70H04: Note 942: this verse answers the question of which knowledge is meant, since in the Vedanta knowledge leads to Brahma, which is hidden even from those who study the rites.
shots.B12C363S70H05: Note 943: the second line corresponds to verse 87 of Chapter 2 of the Manusmriti.
shots.B12C363S71H01: Note 944: they are seen and not seen is an idiom meaning becoming invisible.
shots.B12C363S71H02: Note 945: kine give no sweet milk, the soil ceases to be fertile, water loses its sweetness, and herbs lose their healing power.
shots.B12C363S71H03: Note 946: the commentator links swadharmasthah with asramah, but the translator prefers the more obvious construction.
shots.B12C363S71H04: Note 947: varshati means nourishes, and angani are the observances of yoga and of rites and vows, which the Vedas cause to grow.
shots.B12C363S71H05: Note 948: prabhava is origin and sthanam is support, which the translators wrongly ran together, and swabhavena means by Brahma's own nature.
shots.B12C363S72H01: Note 949: yatha in the first line means yat prakarakam, of that kind.
shots.B12C363S72H02: Note 950: the four words indicate the four modes of life.
shots.B12C363S72H03: Note 951: the ignorant take the great non-self entities for the self or its possessions.
shots.B12C363S72H04: Note 952: the Yoga view of the soul as the enjoyer but not the actor is wrong, and the Sankhya view that the soul neither acts nor enjoys is true, since the deities in the senses act and enjoy.
shots.B12C363S72H05: Note 953: bhutatma is rendered as knowledge, following the commentator's phrase the living being with the intellect as its vehicle.
shots.B12C363S73H01: Note 954: niyama and visarga are explained as destruction and creation, though the translator prefers restraining and employing.
shots.B12C363S73H02: Note 955: the objects of the senses exist in the heart as concepts, and swabhava means attributes such as heat and cold.
shots.B12C363S73H03: Note 956: a very difficult verse on the body, knowledge, and the three attributes, which the note says is the body's image in a dream, with Prakriti as the true refuge of knowledge.
shots.B12C363S73H04: Note 957: such men behold Brahma in all things, and abhijanah means disciples or a family of disciples.
shots.B12C363S73H05: Note 958: the word tatam means pervaded, not spread, as the Gita uses it.
shots.B12C363S74H01: Note 959: the Vedas teach that all is one's soul, and the degree of realising this is the degree of attaining Brahma.
shots.B12C363S74H02: Note 960: the track of such a person is as invisible as the sky, and even the gods are stupefied about the object he seeks.
shots.B12C363S74H03: Note 961: the thing in which Time is cooked is Brahma.
shots.B12C363S74H04: Note 962: Brahma is not found in any particular spot, however holy.
shots.B12C363S75H01: Note 964: niyatah means unwavering and vasi means without the fault of an adjunct, while hansa means moving, hence gatimati.
shots.B12C363S75H02: Note 965: the Soul residing in the body is identical with the Supreme Soul, which only men of wisdom know.
shots.B12C363S75H03: Note 966: the construction shows there is no difference between the individual and the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C363S75H04: Note 967: sattwena is explained as by intelligence or knowledge.
shots.B12C363S75H05: Note 968: the brilliant seed is Brahma, and the essence of all this is Brahma's juice.
shots.B12C363S76H01: Note 969: Brahma opened his eyes to become many, and by his glance he became the Soul of all things mobile and immobile.
shots.B12C363S76H02: Note 970: the commentator reads Brahmanah padam as Prakriti, but the translator keeps the obvious sense.
shots.B12C363S76H03: Note 971: parimitam kalam is explained as six months, as the Srutis say.
shots.B12C363S76H04: Note 972: these verses set out the yoga ideal and its powers, but a yogin who is led away by these powers falls into hell; pramoha, brahma, and avarta are technical terms, and equality with the wind means speed and power to move through the sky.
shots.B12C363S76H05: Note 973: a chaitya is a sacred tree standing on its roots with a raised platform around it, and vrikshagra means in front of a tree.
shots.B12C363S77H01: Note 974: the commentator says one should imitate the wind by being unattached, and aniketah means without a house or fixed abode.
shots.B12C363S77H02: Note 975: savda-brahma is the mystic syllable Om, and K.P. Singha takes it as a sign that such a man transcends Vedic rites.
shots.B12C363S77H03: Note 976: the Sudra order is meant as inferior, and Vyasa says all classes may take up the path of yoga, though only the three higher orders study Sankhya.
shots.B12C363S77H04: Note 977: fixed senses means senses fixed on the mind and the mind on the understanding, while ajaram means unchanging and subtlety means incapable of being grasped.
shots.B12C363S77H05: Note 978: anu anudrisya is taken as following the teacher's words, and abhutagatim means until the destruction of all beings.
shots.B12C363S78H01: Note 979: the Vedas proclaim both acts and knowledge, and acts are not laid down for one who has knowledge.
shots.B12C363S78H02: Note 980: the highest duty, explained by the commentator, is to see the self through yoga.
shots.B12C363S78H03: Note 981: na vartate does not mean annihilated but refers to one who does not know himself as I am.
shots.B12C363S78H04: Note 982: by mind and by act is explained as by resolve.
shots.B12C363S78H05: Note 983: the man of acts is like the new moon, which grows and decays.
shots.B12C363S79H01: Note 984: this has been explained in an earlier section.
shots.B12C363S79H02: Note 985: the soul in the body is untouched by its attributes, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf that does not soak it, and the phrase means a soul whose mind is restrained by yoga.
shots.B12C363S79H03: Note 986: the three attributes have the nature of Jiva, which is an accident of the Soul, and the Soul comes from the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C363S79H04: Note 987: two creations are named: the twenty-four entities from Prakriti, and a derivative creation of senses and objects that binds the individual.
shots.B12C363S79H05: Note 988: the course of righteousness is regulated by the character of the Yuga that sets in.
shots.B12C363S80H01: Note 989: Suka asks how two apparently conflicting declarations are one, and wants his father to explain more clearly.
shots.B12C363S80H02: Note 990: the course of conduct of human beings means the distinction between right and wrong, and the phrase vimuktatma is taken to mean one who has cast off the body.
shots.B12C363S80H03: Note 991: the translator does not follow the commentator on this line.
shots.B12C363S80H04: Note 992: when the huts are smokeless and the husking rod is silent, the mendicant is unlikely to receive much alms.
shots.B12C363S80H05: Note 993: if two declarations conflict, both cannot be scriptural, so the question is how the authority of both can be kept.
shots.B12C363S81H01: Note 994: the Burdwan translator blunders in rendering jaghanyasayi, since jaghanya means later in time.
shots.B12C363S81H02: Note 995: the disciple should not clamour for lessons but approach the preceptor only when summoned, and both vernacular translators misread this.
shots.B12C363S81H03: Note 996: the disciple should cast humble glances and not stare boldly.
shots.B12C363S81H04: Note 997: learning was never sold, and the final fee is a token of gratitude, with the story of Galava as a warning about pressing the fee.
shots.B12C363S81H05: Note 998: the fourth kind of conduct, kapoti or unchha, is gathering the seeds of grain fallen from the ears and left by the reapers.
shots.B12C363S82H01: Note 999: each of the four kinds of gathering is more meritorious than the one before, so the fourth is first in merit.
shots.B12C363S82H02: Note 1000: a householder who cooks must share the food with a student, a wanderer, or a guest, and eating all of it is a grave sin.
shots.B12C363S82H03: Note 1001: the commentator says relatives are named because disputes over inheritance are likely with them.
shots.B12C363S82H04: Note 1002: those named, if duly honoured, can send the householder to the places indicated or make him comfortable there.
shots.B12C363S82H05: Note 1003: the three forms of domesticity are the kumbhadhanya, the aswastana or unchhasila, and the kapoti, and the Burdwan version misnames them.
shots.B12C363S83H01: Note 1004: the Burdwan version of this verse is incorrect.
shots.B12C363S83H02: Note 1005: a cow is sacred, and forest recluses kept cows for merit and for the ghee used in sacrifice, with the story of Vasishtha's cow.
shots.B12C363S83H03: Note 1006: the five sacrifices are the Agnihotra, Darsapurnamasi, Chaturmasya, Pasu, and Soma.
shots.B12C363S83H04: Note 1007: the Burdwan translator misunderstands abhravakasah, which Wilson explains correctly.
shots.B12C363S83H05: Note 1008: the grain eaten is not cleaned with a regular husking or cleaning apparatus.
shots.B12C363S84H01: Note 1009: only a very small portion of the grain comes out for drink or mixes with the water.
shots.B12C363S84H02: Note 1010: yathavasah and akritacramah are adjectives of Sudivatandi, not names of Rishis, as the Burdwan translator took them.
shots.B12C363S84H03: Note 1011: the sage's wishes were immediately fulfilled, whether they were blessings or curses.
shots.B12C363S84H04: Note 1012: niranandah is explained as free from the troubles of lunar penance and similar rites.
shots.B12C363S84H05: Note 1013: anakstrah means luminous, different from the stars, and anadhrishyah means fearless.
shots.B12C363S85H01: Note 1014: atmayaji performs his own funeral rites, atmakrida takes pleasure in the self, and atmasraya takes refuge in the self.
shots.B12C363S85H02: Note 1015: examples of such sacrifices are the Brahma-yajna and similar rites.
shots.B12C363S85H03: Note 1016: once ordinary sacrifice has purified the mind, the sacrificer offers into the self, meaning yoga, and no longer needs visible fires.
shots.B12C363S85H04: Note 1017: orthodox twice-born men still offer five small mouthfuls to the five vital breaths before eating.
shots.B12C363S85H05: Note 1018: vapya means causing a shave, which a renouncer must have, and the Burdwan translator wrongly reads parivyapta.
shots.B12C363S86H01: Note 1019: abhaya means giving freedom from fear, that is a life of total harmlessness, which is the great duty of the fourth stage.
shots.B12C363S86H02: Note 1020: yama includes universal benevolence, truth, faith, celibacy, and detachment, and niyama includes purity, contentment, study, and meditation, and the renouncer should seek the Soul and drop caste marks.
shots.B12C363S86H03: Note 1021: the commentator says the first line answers the son's question, and the speaker then gives the straight path to Brahma.
shots.B12C363S86H04: Note 1022: bhava-samahitah means one whose mind is composed.
shots.B12C363S86H05: Note 1023: the skull is to be used as a drinking vessel, and kuchela means faded, reddish-brown rags.
shots.B12C363S87H01: Note 1024: as elephants in a well cannot get out, so a man whose hard words do not stir him is fit for mendicancy.
shots.B12C363S87H02: Note 1025: the yogin withdraws his senses and mind by pratyahara so that a crowded place looks empty to him.
shots.B12C363S87H03: Note 1026: the mendicant should never eat to full satiety, but leave his hunger only partly satisfied.
shots.B12C363S87H04: Note 1027: the commentator reads kaunjara as a yogin in samadhi, and the fruits of yoga absorb every other fruit, even Indra's rank.
shots.B12C363S87H05: Note 1028: the single duty of harmlessness, the fourth stage, gives the merit that all the other duties give together.
shots.B12C363S88H01: Note 1029: haryartham means for the sake of Hari, meaning a disciple or attendant who takes away merit, and another reading gives for the happiness of others.
shots.B12C363S88H02: Note 1030: all acts, whether general or religious, involve injury to others.
shots.B12C363S88H03: Note 1031: tikshnam tanum means the religion of sacrifices and acts, and the line means that he attains liberation, from which creatures are free from fear.
shots.B12C363S88H04: Note 1032: a tentative version is offered that follows the words of the original.
shots.B12C363S88H05: Note 1033: the images apply to the Supreme Soul: vaster than the firmament, golden as pure knowledge, born of the egg, with many feathers for its limbs, and luminous with rays.
shots.B12C363S89H01: Note 1034: a man who understands the wheel of Time deserves universal regard, and its joints are the sacred lunar days.
shots.B12C363S89H02: Note 1035: unconsciousness, the sleep of dreamless slumber, is the origin of the universe, and jiva feeds the deities and senses, which in turn are swallowed by that open mouth.
shots.B12C363S89H03: Note 1036: smriti is memory, so one whose smriti is lost has confounded right and wrong, and atmanah sampradanena means surrender to one's passions.
shots.B12C363S89H04: Note 1037: chittam is the gross understanding, sattwa is the subtle one that thinks of Brahma, and kalanjara means one who subdues Time.
shots.B12C363S89H05: Note 1038: purification is transcending the sense of duality, righteousness is inferior to liberation, and atmani sthitwa means living in one's true nature.
shots.B12C363S90H01: Note 1039: atmanam here means the Jiva-soul and atmani means the Supreme Soul, and the second line keeps the same distinction.
shots.B12C363S90H02: Note 1040: Brahmanas who have finished their Vedic study and entered the householder stage, with faith and pure conduct, are meant.
shots.B12C363S90H03: Note 1041: adhyatma here means the twenty-seven usual topics of philosophy, including the organs, the breaths, the elements, desire, acts, and avidya.
shots.B12C363S90H04: Note 1042: the second clause means what one sees in the desire that is the cause.
shots.B12C363S90H05: Note 1043: mind, understanding, and nature come from their previous states, and in their functions they seize particular attributes such as scent and form.
shots.B12C363S91H01: Note 1044: the senses and mind are the understanding in a particular shape, the mind cherishes and discards impressions, and the understanding reaches certainty.
shots.B12C363S91H02: Note 1045: the phrase from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head means the whole person, the self that says I.
shots.B12C363S91H03: Note 1046: the verse establishes that the attributes of form, and the senses and mind that apprehend them, are the understanding itself.
shots.B12C363S91H04: Note 1047: the three attributes come from their counterparts in a previous life, and so affect the objects of the senses.
shots.B12C363S91H05: Note 1048: the last word in the first line is aprabodhita, not prabodhita.
shots.B12C363S92H01: Note 1049: the word atman is used in several senses, and the place decides which.
shots.B12C363S92H02: Note 1050: vela means tide or current, and the understanding can transcend the three attributes by yoga.
shots.B12C363S92H03: Note 1051: the Bengal texts give this as a single line, while the Bombay text makes verse 9 a triplet, and medhyani means knowledge of forms.
shots.B12C363S92H04: Note 1052: the note reads the theory as a kind of idealism, in which the tree is only an image formed in the mind by vision.
shots.B12C363S92H05: Note 1053: the speaker opposes the view that qualities inhere in objects, and the wife's limbs simile shows they follow the mind, like the spokes of a wheel.
shots.B12C363S93H01: Note 1054: the version is offered tentatively, and compares verse 42 of section 194.
shots.B12C363S93H02: Note 1055: once the darkness of the understanding is dispelled, the soul becomes visible.
shots.B12C363S93H03: Note 1056: this is one who adopts Sannyasa, the last stage, after passing through the earlier ones.
shots.B12C363S93H04: Note 1057: gunan means objects, Sattivadin means one who is good, and vikriyatah means undergoing change.
shots.B12C363S93H05: Note 1058: the commentator says the gunas are not destroyed by knowledge in the way a pot is broken, but bind as a rope or snake does, so they can return.
shots.B12C363S94H01: Note 1059: the two opinions make little practical difference, and conduct is not much changed by either.
shots.B12C363S94H02: Note 1060: janmasamartham is competence by birth or by the duties of one's order, and parayanam means what leads to liberation.
shots.B12C363S94H03: Note 1061: the Bengal reading buddhah is preferred over the Bombay reading suddhah.
shots.B12C363S94H04: Note 1062: lokam means objects of enjoyment, such as a wife, aturam means afflicted with faults, and ubhayam kritakritam means grief and no grief.
shots.B12C363S94H05: Note 1063: many verses match section 194 with verbal changes, some slight and some making a material difference.
shots.B12C363S95H01: Note 1064: pastures means all external and inner objects that the senses and mind attend to, whose home is Brahma.
shots.B12C363S95H02: Note 1065: the word atma in the first line is indefinite, and the translator takes the inner Soul to be the Chit unmodified by birth and attributes.
shots.B12C363S95H03: Note 1066: abhavapratipattyartham is explained as for attaining the unborn, meaning the soul.
